subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
question: Trace the history of microbiology. Describe the contributions of Antonie van Leeuwenhoek, Louis Pasteur, Joseph Lister and Robert Koch.

diagram.caption: Pasteur's swan-neck flask experiment disproving spontaneous generation

answer_html:
Introduction Microbiology is the study of living things too small to be seen with the naked eye – bacteria, viruses, fungi and parasites. For thousands of years people suffered epidemics of plague, cholera and smallpox without knowing that tiny germs caused them. The history of microbiology is the story of how a few curious scientists, using simple microscopes and careful experiments, proved that "specific germs cause specific diseases" and showed us how to prevent them. Every hand wash, sterile dressing and vaccine a nurse gives today rests on their work.

A. Phases in the history of microbiology

  1. Period of speculation (before 1670) – diseases were blamed on bad air ("miasma"), curses or imbalance of body humours. Girolamo Fracastoro (1546) suggested that invisible "seeds" (contagium) spread disease by direct contact, by objects (fomites) and through the air – an idea far ahead of its time.
  2. Period of observation (1670s–1850s) – the microscope revealed the hidden world of microbes (Leeuwenhoek).
  3. Period of experimentation – the "Golden Age" (1857–1914) – Pasteur and Koch proved the germ theory, developed culture methods and vaccines; most major bacterial pathogens were discovered in these years.
  4. Modern period (1900s onwards) – discovery of viruses, antibiotics, immunology, electron microscopy, molecular biology, PCR and genome sequencing.

B. Antonie van Leeuwenhoek (1632–1723) – "Father of bacteriology and protozoology"

  1. A Dutch cloth merchant who made more than 400 simple single-lens microscopes with a magnification of about 200–300 times.
  2. In 1676 he was the first person to see and describe bacteria, protozoa and sperm, which he called "animalcules" (little animals).
  3. He drew accurate pictures of cocci, bacilli and spiral forms from scrapings of his own teeth and from rain water.
  4. He sent his observations as letters to the Royal Society of London.
  5. Importance: he proved that an invisible world of microbes really exists, though he did not link them to disease.

C. Louis Pasteur (1822–1895) – "Father of modern microbiology" A French chemist whose experiments changed medicine for ever.

  1. Disproved spontaneous generation – with his swan-neck flask experiment (1861) he showed that boiled broth stays clear when dust and germs are trapped in the curved neck, and becomes cloudy only when the neck is broken. Life comes only from pre-existing life.
  2. Fermentation is caused by microbes – he showed that yeasts produce alcohol and other microbes turn wine and milk sour.
  3. Pasteurisation – gentle heating of wine and milk to kill spoilage and disease-causing organisms (still used for milk – 63 °C for 30 minutes or 72 °C for 15–20 seconds).
  4. Germ theory of disease – he proved that microbes cause diseases such as the silkworm disease (pébrine) and puerperal fever.
  5. Vaccines from attenuated (weakened) microbes – chicken cholera vaccine (1880), anthrax vaccine (1881) and the rabies vaccine (1885), first given to a boy, Joseph Meister, bitten by a rabid dog. He coined the word "vaccine" in honour of Edward Jenner.
  6. Sterilisation – introduced the hot air oven and, with Chamberland, the autoclave and steam sterilisation.
  7. Coined the terms "aerobes" and "anaerobes"; founded the Pasteur Institute, Paris (1888).

D. Joseph Lister (1827–1912) – "Father of antiseptic surgery"

  1. A British surgeon who was disturbed by the high death rate from wound infection (sepsis) after operations.
  2. Inspired by Pasteur's germ theory, in 1867 he used carbolic acid (phenol) to clean wounds, dressings, instruments and his hands, and sprayed it in the operating room.
  3. Post-operative infections and deaths fell dramatically.
  4. Importance: he laid the foundation of antiseptic and aseptic techniques – scrubbing, sterile gloves and instruments – that every OT nurse follows today. (Earlier, in 1847, Ignaz Semmelweis in Vienna had reduced deaths from childbed fever by making doctors wash hands in chlorinated lime – the first proof of the value of hand hygiene.)

E. Robert Koch (1843–1910) – "Father of bacteriology / medical microbiology" A German physician who turned microbiology into an exact science.

  1. Anthrax (1876) – proved that Bacillus anthracis causes anthrax; the first proof that a specific organism causes a specific disease.
  2. Tuberculosis (1882) – discovered Mycobacterium tuberculosis; announced on 24 March 1882, now observed as World TB Day.
  3. Cholera (1883) – identified Vibrio cholerae ("comma bacillus").
  4. Solid culture media – introduced gelatin and then agar (suggested by Fanny Hesse) for growing bacteria; his assistant Julius Petri designed the Petri dish. This made pure culture possible.
  5. Staining and photography – methods of staining bacteria with aniline dyes and the first microphotographs of bacteria.
  6. Koch's postulates (1884) – criteria to prove that an organism causes a disease.
  7. Koch phenomenon and tuberculin – the basis of the tuberculin (Mantoux) test.
  8. Awarded the Nobel Prize in 1905.

F. Other milestones (memory list) | Scientist | Contribution | |---|---| | Edward Jenner (1796) | Smallpox vaccination using cowpox | | Hans Christian Gram (1884) | Gram staining | | Elie Metchnikoff (1883) | Phagocytosis – cell-mediated immunity | | Ivanovsky (1892) | First virus (tobacco mosaic virus) shown to be filterable | | Ronald Ross (1897) | Malaria transmitted by mosquito – discovered at Secunderabad, India | | W. M. Haffkine (1890s) | Cholera and plague vaccines in India | | Paul Ehrlich (1910) | Salvarsan for syphilis – "magic bullet", father of chemotherapy | | Alexander Fleming (1928) | Penicillin | | Ruska and Knoll (1931) | Electron microscope | | Kary Mullis (1983) | Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) |

G. Nursing importance

  1. Hand hygiene, asepsis, sterilisation and pasteurisation – all nursing routines – come directly from Semmelweis, Lister and Pasteur.
  2. Specimen collection and culture reports depend on Koch's pure-culture methods.
  3. Vaccines that nurses give under the immunisation programme follow the principle discovered by Jenner and Pasteur.

Conclusion From Leeuwenhoek's "animalcules" to Koch's postulates, these pioneers proved that germs cause disease and can be controlled. A nurse who knows this history understands why every infection-control step matters.

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
question: Explain the importance and relevance of microbiology in nursing.
answer_html:
Introduction Nurses are with patients 24 hours a day – they touch wounds, insert catheters, give injections, handle blood and dispose of waste. Every one of these acts can either spread or stop germs. Microbiology gives the nurse the scientific reason behind each infection-control practice, so that care is safe for the patient, the nurse and the community.

1. Understanding the cause of disease

  • Knowing the organism, its source, mode of spread and incubation period helps the nurse plan care and isolation (e.g., airborne precautions for TB and measles, contact precautions for MRSA).
  • Helps her recognise early signs of infection – fever, pus, foul-smelling urine, redness of a cannula site.
  • Explains why some patients (newborns, elderly, diabetics, HIV-positive, patients on chemotherapy) get opportunistic infections.

2. Prevention of hospital-acquired infections (HAI)

  • Hand hygiene at the five moments, standard precautions and correct use of PPE.
  • Asepsis in catheterisation, dressings, injections, IV cannulation and suctioning.
  • Following care bundles for urinary catheters, central lines, ventilators and surgical wounds.
  • Isolation and barrier nursing of infectious patients; cohorting during outbreaks.

3. Sterilisation and disinfection

  • Selecting the right method for each article (autoclave for instruments, high-level disinfection for endoscopes, 1% hypochlorite for blood spills).
  • Checking sterility indicators, expiry dates and pack integrity before use.
  • Safe preparation and dilution of disinfectants.

4. Collection and transport of specimens

  • Correct specimen, correct time, correct container – e.g., blood culture before the first antibiotic dose, early-morning sputum for AFB, mid-stream urine.
  • Aseptic collection to avoid contamination, proper labelling, quick transport and safe packing.
  • A wrongly collected specimen gives a false report and wrong treatment.

5. Interpreting laboratory reports

  • Understanding Gram stain, culture and sensitivity reports, Widal, HBsAg, HIV and dengue tests.
  • Reporting critical results (positive blood culture, AFB-positive sputum) to the doctor immediately.

6. Rational use of antibiotics (antimicrobial stewardship)

  • Giving antibiotics at the correct time and dose, completing the course and watching for side effects.
  • Educating patients not to self-medicate – helps to prevent antimicrobial resistance (MRSA, ESBL, CRE).

7. Immunisation

  • Knowledge of vaccine types, cold chain, schedule and contraindications for the Universal Immunisation Programme.
  • Immunisation of health workers against hepatitis B, influenza and tetanus.

8. Biomedical waste and laundry management

  • Segregating waste in colour-coded bins as per BMW Management Rules 2016; safe disposal of sharps.
  • Handling soiled linen safely.

9. Occupational safety of the nurse

  • Prevention and first aid for needle-stick injuries, post-exposure prophylaxis for HIV and hepatitis B.
  • Protection from TB, COVID-19 and other airborne infections.

10. Community and public health nursing

  • Health education on safe drinking water, food hygiene, sanitation and vector control to prevent cholera, typhoid, hepatitis A, malaria and dengue.
  • Participating in national programmes – NTEP (tuberculosis), NACP (HIV), NCVBDC (vector-borne diseases), IDSP (disease surveillance).
  • Outbreak investigation and contact tracing.

11. Food, water and nutrition

  • Hygienic food handling in hospital kitchens, milk pasteurisation, safe infant feeding and preparation of ORS with clean water.

12. Research and evidence-based practice

  • Surveillance data on HAI rates, hand-hygiene audits and infection-control research help improve nursing practice.

Example from the ward A diabetic patient develops fever on day 3 of a urinary catheter. A nurse trained in microbiology suspects CAUTI, collects a urine sample aseptically from the sampling port (not from the bag), labels and sends it promptly, reports to the doctor and reviews whether the catheter is still needed – preventing a serious bloodstream infection.

13. Special care areas

  • Operation theatre – sterile technique, surgical scrub, OT fumigation/cleaning, sterility of packs and implants.
  • ICU and NICU – prevention of ventilator-associated pneumonia, central-line infections and neonatal sepsis; strict hand hygiene for every touch.
  • Dialysis and blood bank – screening for HBV, HCV and HIV, separate machines for HBsAg-positive patients, safe handling of blood.
  • Burns and oncology wards – protective (reverse) isolation for patients with low immunity.

14. Epidemics and disasters

  • During outbreaks (cholera, dengue, COVID-19) the nurse helps in case finding, isolation, specimen collection, disinfection, vaccination drives and health education.
  • After floods she watches for leptospirosis, typhoid and diarrhoeal diseases.

15. Quality and legal responsibility

  • Hospital accreditation (NABH) and the Kayakalp award scheme assess hand hygiene, BMW segregation, cleanliness and HAI surveillance – areas where nurses play the main role.
  • Wrong disposal of biomedical waste or negligence in asepsis can lead to legal action.

Summary – nursing activity and the microbiology principle behind it | Nursing activity | Principle | |---|---| | Hand washing before and after patient contact | Removes transient flora; breaks contact transmission | | Autoclaving instruments | Moist heat kills spores | | Early-morning sputum for AFB | More bacilli collected overnight | | Blood culture before antibiotics | Antibiotics prevent growth in culture | | Cold chain for vaccines | Vaccines lose potency with heat | | Colour-coded waste bins | Correct treatment of infectious waste |

Conclusion Microbiology is the "why" behind nursing's "how". It turns routine practices into conscious, scientific actions that protect patients, nurses and the community from infection.

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
question: Describe the normal microbial flora of the human body and its importance.
answer_html:
Definition Normal (commensal) flora are the microorganisms that live regularly on the skin and mucous membranes of healthy people without causing disease. They colonise the baby soon after birth and remain throughout life.

1. Types

  • Resident flora – fixed organisms always present at a site (e.g., Staphylococcus epidermidis on skin).
  • Transient flora – picked up from the environment and present for hours to weeks (e.g., organisms on a nurse's hands after touching a patient); easily removed by hand washing.

2. Normal flora at different sites | Site | Common organisms | |---|---| | Skin | S. epidermidis, Cutibacterium (Propionibacterium) acnes, diphtheroids, Candida | | Nose | S. aureus (20–30% of people are carriers), diphtheroids | | Mouth and throat | Viridans streptococci, Neisseria, anaerobes, Candida | | Large intestine | Bacteroides (most numerous), E. coli, enterococci, lactobacilli, clostridia | | Vagina | Lactobacilli (Döderlein's bacilli) keeping pH acidic (4–4.5) | | Anterior urethra | S. epidermidis, diphtheroids |

Sterile sites: blood, CSF, lower respiratory tract, urinary bladder, uterus and body cavities.

3. Beneficial roles

  • Colonisation resistance – they occupy space and nutrients and prevent pathogens from settling.
  • Produce acids and bacteriocins that inhibit harmful organisms.
  • Intestinal bacteria synthesise vitamin K and some B vitamins.
  • Stimulate the immune system and production of natural antibodies.
  • Help in digestion of some foods.

4. Harmful roles

  • Cause opportunistic or endogenous infections when they reach another site or when immunity falls – E. coli causing UTI, S. epidermidis infecting IV lines, viridans streptococci causing endocarditis.
  • Antibiotics disturb the flora, allowing Candida (thrush) or Clostridioides difficile (diarrhoea) to overgrow.
  • Streptococcus mutans causes dental caries.

5. Nursing importance

  • Skin antisepsis before injections, cannulation and surgery.
  • Perineal care from front to back to prevent UTI.
  • Mouth care in unconscious and ventilated patients.
  • Avoiding unnecessary antibiotics; probiotics/curd may help restore gut flora.

6. Factors that alter normal flora

  • Broad-spectrum antibiotics, steroids and anticancer drugs.
  • Hospitalisation – patients soon become colonised with hospital strains (MRSA, multidrug-resistant Gram-negatives).
  • Change in pH (menopause, diabetes), poor oral hygiene, nasogastric tubes and catheters.

7. Normal flora and hospital infection Most hospital infections are endogenous – caused by the patient's own flora entering a wound, the bladder or the bloodstream through a device. This is why skin preparation with chlorhexidine, catheter care and oral care in ventilated patients are emphasised.

Conclusion Normal flora are useful partners while they stay in place; the nurse's aseptic care keeps them from becoming invaders.

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
question: Explain the following basic terms in microbiology: pathogen, commensal, opportunist, pathogenicity, virulence, colonisation, infection and infectious disease.
answer_html:
Introduction Before studying individual organisms, a nurse must understand the words used to describe how microbes and humans interact. These terms appear in every laboratory report and infection-control policy.

1. Pathogen

  • A microorganism capable of producing disease, e.g., Salmonella Typhi, Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
  • Primary (frank) pathogens cause disease in healthy people.

2. Commensal

  • An organism that lives on or in the body without harming it, e.g., E. coli in the colon, S. epidermidis on the skin.
  • Forms part of the normal flora.

3. Opportunist (opportunistic pathogen)

  • A commensal or environmental organism that causes disease only when host defences are lowered – in HIV/AIDS, diabetes, cancer chemotherapy, burns or when devices bypass the skin.
  • Examples: Candida, Pneumocystis jirovecii, Pseudomonas aeruginosa.

4. Pathogenicity

  • The ability of a species to cause disease – a qualitative property ("Can it cause disease?").
  • M. tuberculosis is pathogenic; Lactobacillus normally is not.

5. Virulence

  • The degree of pathogenicity of a particular strain – a quantitative property ("How severe?").
  • Measured in the laboratory as LD50 (dose that kills 50% of test animals) or ID50.
  • Depends on virulence factors: capsule, adhesins (pili), toxins, enzymes (coagulase, hyaluronidase), ability to invade and to resist phagocytosis.
  • Attenuation = reduction of virulence (used to make live vaccines such as BCG); exaltation = increase.

6. Colonisation

  • Presence and multiplication of microbes on a body surface without tissue invasion or illness – e.g., MRSA in the nose of a staff member. A colonised person can still spread the organism.

7. Infection

  • Entry, establishment and multiplication of a pathogen in the tissues of the host, producing a response.
  • May be subclinical (inapparent) – detected only by antibodies – or clinical.
  • Types: primary, secondary, cross-infection, nosocomial (hospital-acquired), endogenous, exogenous, latent (TB, herpes), iatrogenic.

8. Infectious disease

  • Infection that produces signs and symptoms (clinical illness). A communicable disease is one that spreads from person to person.

Simple memory aid Colonisation → Infection → Disease: "living on → living in → harming."

Nursing importance These terms guide isolation decisions, screening of carriers, care of immunocompromised patients and the interpretation of culture reports.

Conclusion Clear understanding of these terms helps the nurse think scientifically about every case of infection.

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
question: Explain Koch's postulates and their importance.
answer_html:
Introduction In 1884 Robert Koch (with Friedrich Loeffler) laid down a set of rules to decide whether a particular microbe is the real cause of a disease. These rules, called Koch's postulates, gave scientific proof to the germ theory.

1. The postulates

  1. The organism must be present in every case of the disease and in the lesions, and should not be found in healthy persons.
  2. It must be isolated in pure culture on artificial media.
  3. The pure culture, when inoculated into a susceptible animal, must reproduce the same disease.
  4. The organism must be re-isolated in pure culture from the experimentally infected animal.

Additional (fifth) postulate added later: specific antibodies against the organism should be demonstrable in the patient's serum.

2. Example – anthrax Koch found Bacillus anthracis in the blood of every animal dying of anthrax, grew it in pure culture, injected it into mice which developed anthrax, and recovered the same bacilli from them.

3. Importance

  • Gave a logical method of proving causation and ended guesswork about disease.
  • Led to the rapid discovery of the causes of TB, cholera, diphtheria, typhoid and plague in the "golden age".
  • Introduced the habit of working with pure cultures, still the basis of diagnostic microbiology.
  • Guides the search for causes of new diseases (e.g., SARS-CoV-2 was confirmed by isolation and animal studies).

4. Exceptions (in brief)

  • Some organisms cannot be grown on artificial media (M. leprae, Treponema pallidum).
  • Healthy carriers exist (typhoid, polio, cholera).
  • Many organisms have no suitable animal model.

5. Molecular Koch's postulates (Falkow, 1988) Applied to the genes of virulence: the gene should be found in disease-causing strains; inactivating it should reduce virulence; restoring it should restore virulence.

6. Postulates for viruses (Rivers' postulates, 1937) As viruses cannot grow on artificial media, Thomas Rivers modified the rules: the virus must be found in the host cells or body fluids at the time of disease, must be grown in living cells (cell culture, eggs), must be filterable, must produce the disease in a susceptible host, and specific antibodies must appear.

7. Nursing relevance Koch's idea that a disease has a definite cause underlies specimen collection before treatment – a correctly collected specimen helps the laboratory isolate the true causative organism.

Conclusion Koch's postulates remain the classic framework for linking a microbe to a disease, even though modern methods have widened them.

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
question: Define microbiology.
answer_html:
Definition Microbiology (Greek mikros = small, bios = life, logos = study) is the branch of biology that deals with the study of microorganisms – living things too small to be seen with the naked eye, such as bacteria, viruses, fungi, protozoa and microscopic algae.

It studies their:

  • Structure, physiology and classification
  • Growth, reproduction and genetics
  • Role in health, disease and the environment
  • Methods of control (sterilisation, disinfection, antimicrobials, vaccines)

Medical microbiology deals with microbes that cause disease in humans and with their diagnosis, treatment and prevention.

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
question: Mention the contributions of Robert Koch to microbiology.
answer_html:
Robert Koch (1843–1910) – German physician, "father of bacteriology".

Contributions

  1. Proved that Bacillus anthracis causes anthrax (1876) – first proof that a specific germ causes a specific disease.
  2. Discovered Mycobacterium tuberculosis (1882) – 24 March is World TB Day.
  3. Discovered Vibrio cholerae (1883).
  4. Introduced solid culture media (agar) and the pure culture technique.
  5. Developed methods of staining and photographing bacteria.
  6. Formulated Koch's postulates (1884).
  7. Described the Koch phenomenon and prepared tuberculin (basis of the Mantoux test). He received the Nobel Prize in 1905.

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
question: Enumerate the limitations of Koch's postulates.
answer_html:
Koch's postulates cannot be fulfilled in every infection. Limitations:

  1. Some organisms cannot be grown on artificial media – Mycobacterium leprae, Treponema pallidum, and all viruses.
  2. No suitable animal model for some human pathogens (e.g., Salmonella Typhi, gonococcus).
  3. Asymptomatic carriers exist (typhoid, cholera, polio), so the organism is found in healthy persons.
  4. One organism can cause many diseases (S. pyogenes – sore throat, cellulitis, scarlet fever) and one disease can be caused by many organisms (pneumonia, meningitis).
  5. Some diseases are polymicrobial or depend on host factors (opportunistic infections).
  6. Deliberately infecting humans is unethical.

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
question: List the branches of microbiology.
answer_html:
Branches of microbiology

  1. Bacteriology – study of bacteria
  2. Virology – study of viruses
  3. Mycology – study of fungi
  4. Parasitology – protozoa (protozoology) and helminths (helminthology)
  5. Immunology – body's defence against infection
  6. Medical/clinical microbiology – diagnosis and control of infections
  7. Public health/epidemiological microbiology
  8. Food and dairy microbiology
  9. Industrial and pharmaceutical microbiology – antibiotics, vaccines
  10. Environmental, soil and agricultural microbiology
  11. Microbial genetics and molecular microbiology

Relevance to nursing: medical microbiology, immunology and public health microbiology are directly used in infection control, immunisation and community health programmes.

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
question: Write the contributions of Louis Pasteur.
answer_html:
Louis Pasteur (1822–1895) – French chemist, "father of modern microbiology".

Contributions

  1. Disproved spontaneous generation (swan-neck flask experiment).
  2. Proved that fermentation is caused by microbes.
  3. Introduced pasteurisation of milk and wine.
  4. Established the germ theory of disease.
  5. Developed vaccines for chicken cholera, anthrax and rabies (1885); coined the term "vaccine".
  6. Introduced sterilisation by hot air oven and autoclave (with Chamberland).
  7. Coined the terms aerobes and anaerobes; founded the Pasteur Institute.

He also showed that microbes cause silkworm disease and puerperal sepsis, laying the scientific base for aseptic nursing practice.

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
unit_title: Section A: General Characteristics of Microbes
question: Describe the classification of microorganisms. Explain the morphology and growth of bacteria.

diagram.caption: Bacterial growth curve
labels: log number of viable cells vs time

answer_html:
(a) Classification and types of microbes (5 marks)

Introduction Microorganisms are a very large and varied group. Grouping them helps us to study, identify and treat them. Medically important microbes are classified into bacteria, viruses, fungi and parasites, with a few special groups.

1. Broad classification of living organisms

  • Whittaker's five kingdoms (1969): Monera (bacteria), Protista (protozoa, algae), Fungi, Plantae, Animalia.
  • Woese's three domains (1990): Bacteria, Archaea and Eukarya.
  • Microbes are also divided into prokaryotes (no true nucleus – bacteria) and eukaryotes (true nucleus – fungi, protozoa, helminths).

2. Types of medically important microbes | Group | Key features | Examples | |---|---|---| | Bacteria | Prokaryotic, unicellular, cell wall, multiply by binary fission | S. aureus, E. coli, M. tuberculosis | | Rickettsiae, Chlamydiae | Very small bacteria, obligate intracellular | Scrub typhus, trachoma | | Mycoplasma | Bacteria without cell wall, pleomorphic | Atypical pneumonia | | Viruses | Not cells; DNA or RNA only, protein coat; obligate intracellular | HIV, hepatitis B, rabies | | Fungi | Eukaryotic; yeasts and moulds; chitin cell wall | Candida, Aspergillus, dermatophytes | | Protozoa | Unicellular eukaryotic parasites | Plasmodium, Entamoeba histolytica | | Helminths | Multicellular worms | Roundworm, hookworm, tapeworm | | Prions | Infectious proteins without nucleic acid | Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease |

3. Classification of bacteria (based on)

  1. Shape – cocci, bacilli, vibrios, spirilla, spirochaetes, actinomycetes.
  2. Gram staining – Gram-positive (violet) and Gram-negative (pink).
  3. Oxygen requirement – obligate aerobes (M. tuberculosis), facultative anaerobes (E. coli, staphylococci), microaerophiles (Campylobacter, H. pylori), obligate anaerobes (Clostridium, Bacteroides).
  4. Temperature – psychrophiles (15–20 °C), mesophiles (25–40 °C; all human pathogens, optimum 37 °C), thermophiles (55–80 °C).
  5. Spore formation – spore-forming (Bacillus, Clostridium) and non-spore-forming.
  6. Motility, capsule, nutrition and biochemical reactions.
  7. Bacteria are named by the binomial system (genus + species, e.g., Staphylococcus aureus) and classified in Bergey's Manual.

(b) Morphology and growth of bacteria (5 marks)

4. Size and shape

  • Bacteria are measured in micrometres (µm); most are 0.5–1 µm wide and 2–5 µm long. Seen only with a microscope (oil-immersion lens, ×1000).
  • Shapes and arrangements:
    • Cocci (spherical) – diplococci (pneumococci, gonococci), chains (streptococci), clusters (staphylococci), tetrads, sarcinae (packets of eight).
    • Bacilli (rods) – single, chains, Chinese-letter pattern (Corynebacterium diphtheriae), coccobacilli (Brucella).
    • Vibrios – comma-shaped (V. cholerae).
    • Spirilla – rigid spirals; spirochaetes – flexible spirals (Treponema, Leptospira).
    • Actinomycetes – branching filaments; Mycoplasma – no fixed shape.

5. Reproduction

  • Bacteria multiply by binary fission – one cell divides into two identical daughter cells.
  • Generation time = time taken to double: E. coli about 20 minutes, M. tuberculosis about 14–18 hours, M. leprae about 12 days. This explains why TB cultures take weeks.

6. Bacterial growth curve When bacteria are put into a fresh broth and counted at intervals, the curve shows four phases:

  1. Lag phase – bacteria adapt, enlarge and make enzymes; no increase in number.
  2. Log (exponential) phase – rapid division at a constant rate; cells show typical shape and staining and are most sensitive to antibiotics.
  3. Stationary phase – nutrients run out and toxic products collect; rate of division equals rate of death. Spores, exotoxins and antibiotics are produced here.
  4. Decline (death) phase – death exceeds division; abnormal "involution" forms appear.

7. Factors affecting growth – nutrients, oxygen, CO₂, temperature, pH (most pathogens 7.2–7.6), moisture, osmotic pressure and light.

Nursing importance

  • Rapid doubling explains how a small contamination of IV fluid or feed can become dangerous within hours – so prepared feeds and infusions must be used within the safe time.
  • Slow growth of TB bacilli explains long treatment and delayed culture reports.

8. Comparison of special groups of bacteria | Feature | Rickettsiae | Chlamydiae | Mycoplasma | |---|---|---|---| | Cell wall | Present (Gram-negative type) | Present but lacks peptidoglycan | Absent | | Growth | Obligate intracellular | Obligate intracellular | Grows on special artificial media | | Transmission | Arthropods (lice, fleas, ticks, mites) | Direct contact, sexual | Droplets, sexual | | Disease | Scrub typhus, epidemic typhus | Trachoma, genital infection | Atypical pneumonia | | Drug of choice | Doxycycline | Doxycycline/azithromycin | Macrolides (not penicillin) |

9. Measuring bacterial growth

  • Total count – counts both living and dead cells (counting chamber, turbidity).
  • Viable count – counts only living cells by colony counting on pour plates; urine culture reports such as "10⁵ CFU/ml" use this method.

10. Nursing points

  • Sending specimens quickly prevents overgrowth of contaminants in the lag/log phases at room temperature; urine should reach the laboratory within 1–2 hours or be refrigerated at 4 °C.

Conclusion Classification and morphology are the first clues used in the laboratory to identify an organism, and the growth curve explains how infections build up and how antibiotics act.

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
unit_title: Section A: General Characteristics of Microbes
question: Describe the structure of a bacterial cell with a neat labelled diagram.

diagram.caption: Structure of a bacterial cell

answer_html:
Introduction A bacterium is a single prokaryotic cell – it has no nuclear membrane, no mitochondria and no endoplasmic reticulum. Yet its few structures are very efficient and many of them are targets of antibiotics and virulence factors. The structures are grouped as outer layers, cytoplasmic contents and appendages.

A. Outer layers (cell envelope)

1. Capsule and slime layer

  • A gelatinous layer outside the cell wall, usually polysaccharide (polypeptide in Bacillus anthracis).
  • Well-defined = capsule; loose = slime layer.
  • Functions: protects bacteria from phagocytosis – an important virulence factor (S. pneumoniae, Klebsiella, Cryptococcus); helps attachment to surfaces and medical devices (biofilm).
  • Demonstrated by negative staining (India ink) and the Quellung (capsule swelling) reaction.
  • Capsular antigens are used in vaccines (pneumococcal, Hib, meningococcal).

2. Cell wall

  • Rigid layer 10–25 nm thick that gives shape and protects against bursting in dilute fluids.
  • Made of peptidoglycan (murein) – chains of N-acetylglucosamine and N-acetylmuramic acid linked by peptide bridges.
  • Gram-positive wall: thick peptidoglycan with teichoic acids.
  • Gram-negative wall: thin peptidoglycan plus an outer membrane containing lipopolysaccharide (LPS – endotoxin) and porins.
  • Importance: basis of Gram staining; site of action of penicillins and cephalosporins (inhibit cell-wall synthesis) and of lysozyme in tears.
  • Cell-wall-deficient forms: protoplasts, spheroplasts, L-forms; Mycoplasma naturally has no cell wall (hence resistant to penicillin).

3. Cytoplasmic (plasma) membrane

  • Thin phospholipid–protein bilayer under the cell wall; no sterols (except Mycoplasma).
  • Functions: selective permeability, active transport of nutrients, respiration (energy production) – bacteria have no mitochondria – and synthesis of cell-wall components.
  • Mesosomes – infoldings of the membrane, possibly involved in cell division.
  • Target of polymyxins.

B. Cytoplasmic contents

4. Cytoplasm – watery colloid of proteins, enzymes, nutrients and salts; no cytoplasmic streaming.

5. Ribosomes

  • 70S type (50S + 30S subunits) – the sites of protein synthesis.
  • Differ from human 80S ribosomes, so antibiotics such as aminoglycosides and tetracyclines (30S) and macrolides and chloramphenicol (50S) act selectively on bacteria.

6. Nucleoid (nuclear body)

  • A single, circular, double-stranded DNA chromosome lying free in the cytoplasm without a nuclear membrane or nucleolus.
  • Carries all essential genetic information.

7. Plasmids

  • Small circular pieces of extra-chromosomal DNA that replicate independently.
  • Carry genes for antibiotic resistance (R-plasmids), toxins and virulence; transferred to other bacteria by conjugation – a major reason for the spread of drug resistance in hospitals.

8. Inclusion granules – stored food: volutin (metachromatic) granules of C. diphtheriae (seen with Albert's stain), glycogen, lipid droplets.

C. Appendages

9. Flagella

  • Long, thin, whip-like threads (3–20 µm) of protein flagellin, arising from a basal body; organs of motility.
  • Arrangement: monotrichous (one polar – Vibrio cholerae), lophotrichous (tuft at one end), amphitrichous (at both ends), peritrichous (all around – E. coli, Salmonella Typhi).
  • Flagellar "H" antigens are used in the Widal test.

10. Fimbriae (pili)

  • Short, fine, hair-like protein projections, more numerous than flagella.
  • Common pili help adhesion to host cells (e.g., E. coli to the bladder lining, gonococci to genital mucosa).
  • Sex pili transfer DNA (plasmids) during conjugation.

11. Spores (endospores) – highly resistant resting forms formed inside some Gram-positive bacilli (Bacillus, Clostridium) under unfavourable conditions.

Summary table | Structure | Main function | Clinical relevance | |---|---|---| | Capsule | Anti-phagocytic | Virulence; vaccines | | Cell wall | Shape, protection | Gram stain; penicillin target | | Cell membrane | Transport, energy | Polymyxin target | | Ribosome (70S) | Protein synthesis | Aminoglycosides, macrolides | | Plasmid | Extra genes | Drug resistance spread | | Flagella | Motility | H antigen | | Pili | Adhesion, conjugation | Colonisation (UTI) | | Spore | Survival | Resists boiling – needs autoclaving |

Nursing importance

  • Understanding structures explains why some antibiotics fail (e.g., penicillin on Mycoplasma), why spores need autoclaving, and why biofilms on catheters make infections hard to treat – so catheters must be removed as soon as possible.

D. Biofilm – a community structure

  • Bacteria attach to surfaces (catheters, IV lines, prosthetic valves, endotracheal tubes) and produce a slimy matrix, forming a biofilm.
  • Inside a biofilm bacteria are protected from antibiotics, disinfectants and white cells, and infections become persistent.
  • Prevention: insert devices aseptically, keep them for the shortest time, follow care bundles and change devices as per policy.

E. Flagella versus pili | Feature | Flagella | Pili (fimbriae) | |---|---|---| | Size | Long, thick | Short, thin | | Number | Few | Many (100–500) | | Function | Motility | Adhesion, conjugation | | Antigen | H antigen | Fimbrial antigens | | Origin | Basal body in membrane | Cell membrane |

Conclusion Though simple, every part of the bacterial cell has a role in survival or disease and offers a point of attack for drugs, vaccines and sterilisation methods.

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
unit_title: Section A: General Characteristics of Microbes
question: Describe the principle and procedure of Gram staining, including the differentiation (decolourisation) step. Draw and explain the differences between Gram-positive and Gram-negative cell walls.

diagram.caption: Gram-positive and Gram-negative cell walls

answer_html:
Introduction Gram staining is the most important and most commonly used differential stain in microbiology. It was developed by the Danish physician Hans Christian Gram in 1884. It divides bacteria into two large groups – Gram-positive (violet/purple) and Gram-negative (pink/red) – within a few minutes, and gives the doctor an early clue for starting treatment before culture reports arrive.

1. Principle

  • All bacteria first take up the primary stain crystal violet.
  • Gram's iodine acts as a mordant; it combines with crystal violet to form a large crystal violet–iodine (CV–I) complex inside the cell.
  • When decolouriser (acetone or alcohol) is applied:
    • In Gram-positive bacteria the thick, multilayered peptidoglycan gets dehydrated, its pores shrink and the CV–I complex is trapped – cells stay violet.
    • In Gram-negative bacteria the decolouriser dissolves the lipid-rich outer membrane, and the thin peptidoglycan cannot hold the complex – the dye is washed out and the cells become colourless.
  • The counterstain (safranin) then stains the colourless Gram-negative cells pink/red.

2. Requirements Clean grease-free glass slides, inoculating loop, spirit lamp/Bunsen burner, staining rack, crystal violet (1%), Gram's iodine, decolouriser (acetone or 95% ethyl alcohol), safranin (0.5%) or dilute carbol fuchsin, wash bottle with water, blotting paper, cedar-wood or immersion oil, microscope.

3. Procedure

  1. Prepare the smear – spread a thin, even film of the specimen (pus, sputum, CSF deposit) or colony emulsified in saline on the slide.
  2. Air-dry and heat-fix by passing the slide (smear side up) quickly 2–3 times through a flame; this kills and sticks the organisms to the slide.
  3. Primary stain – cover with crystal violet for 1 minute; wash gently with water.
  4. Mordant – flood with Gram's iodine for 1 minute; wash.
  5. Decolourisation (differentiation step) – tilt the slide and pour acetone (2–3 seconds) or alcohol (about 10–30 seconds) drop by drop until no more violet colour runs off; wash immediately with water.
  6. Counterstain – apply safranin for 30 seconds–1 minute; wash.
  7. Blot dry and examine under the oil-immersion objective (×100).

4. The differentiation (decolourisation) step – the critical step

  • It is this step that "differentiates" the two groups.
  • Over-decolourisation (too long) → Gram-positive cells lose colour and appear falsely Gram-negative.
  • Under-decolourisation (too short or thick smear) → Gram-negative cells retain violet and appear falsely Gram-positive.
  • Hence the smear must be thin, the time short and controlled, and known control organisms (S. aureus and E. coli) should be stained regularly.

5. Results and interpretation | Result | Colour | Examples | |---|---|---| | Gram-positive cocci in clusters | Violet | Staphylococcus | | Gram-positive cocci in chains | Violet | Streptococcus | | Gram-positive bacilli | Violet | Clostridium, Bacillus, Corynebacterium | | Gram-negative diplococci | Pink | Neisseria | | Gram-negative bacilli | Pink | E. coli, Klebsiella, Salmonella, Pseudomonas | | Gram-negative curved rods | Pink | Vibrio cholerae | Pus cells are also seen and reported, e.g., "plenty of pus cells with Gram-positive cocci in clusters".

6. Differences between Gram-positive and Gram-negative cell walls | Feature | Gram-positive | Gram-negative | |---|---|---| | Thickness of wall | Thick (20–80 nm) | Thin (about 10 nm) | | Peptidoglycan | Many layers (up to 40), 50–90% of wall | 1–2 layers, about 10% of wall | | Teichoic and lipoteichoic acids | Present | Absent | | Outer membrane | Absent | Present (phospholipid, proteins) | | Lipopolysaccharide (endotoxin) | Absent | Present (lipid A) | | Periplasmic space | Absent/narrow | Present between membranes | | Porins | Absent | Present | | Lipid content | Low (1–4%) | High (10–20%) | | Sensitivity to penicillin and lysozyme | More sensitive | Less sensitive (outer membrane barrier) | | Toxin produced | Mostly exotoxins | Endotoxin (plus some exotoxins) | | Gram reaction | Violet | Pink |

7. Uses (applications)

  • Rapid preliminary identification of bacteria from specimens (CSF in meningitis, pus, sputum, urethral discharge in gonorrhoea).
  • Guides empirical antibiotic therapy before culture results.
  • Checks the quality of sputum specimens (many pus cells, few epithelial cells).
  • Helps select culture media and further tests.

8. Limitations

  • Some organisms do not stain well: Mycobacterium (needs Ziehl–Neelsen stain), Treponema (too thin), Mycoplasma (no wall), Chlamydia and Rickettsia.
  • Old cultures and antibiotic-treated bacteria may appear Gram-variable.

Nursing importance

  • Collect specimens before antibiotics and send them quickly so that a reliable Gram stain is possible.
  • A Gram stain report of CSF or blood culture is a critical result – inform the doctor at once so that treatment can start.

Conclusion Gram staining is a simple, cheap, ten-minute test, yet it divides bacteria into two great groups, reflects basic differences in their cell walls and guides life-saving early treatment.

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
unit_title: Section A: General Characteristics of Microbes
question: Explain the bacterial spore with a labelled diagram.

diagram.caption: Structure of a bacterial endospore and positions of spores

answer_html:
Definition A bacterial spore (endospore) is a highly resistant, dormant (resting) form produced inside the cell by some Gram-positive bacilli – mainly Bacillus and Clostridium – when conditions become unfavourable (lack of nutrients). One bacterium forms only one spore, so sporulation is a method of survival, not reproduction.

1. Structure (from inside out)

  1. Core – contains DNA, ribosomes and enzymes in a dehydrated state, with calcium dipicolinate (gives heat resistance).
  2. Inner membrane (future cell membrane).
  3. Cortex – thick layer of special peptidoglycan; keeps the core dry.
  4. Outer membrane.
  5. Spore coat – tough, keratin-like protein; makes the spore impermeable to chemicals.
  6. Exosporium – outermost thin lipoprotein layer (in some species).

2. Sporulation and germination

  • Sporulation takes about 6–8 hours and passes through several stages.
  • In favourable conditions the spore germinates (activation → initiation → outgrowth) into a vegetative cell.

3. Shape and position (useful in identification) | Position | Example | |---|---| | Central, non-bulging | Bacillus anthracis | | Subterminal, oval | Clostridium perfringens, C. botulinum | | Terminal, spherical – "drumstick" | Clostridium tetani | | Terminal, oval – "tennis racket" | Clostridium tertium |

4. Resistance

  • Resist boiling, drying, radiation and many disinfectants for years; survive in soil for decades.
  • Killed reliably by autoclaving at 121 °C for 15 minutes and by sporicidal chemicals (glutaraldehyde, hydrogen peroxide, peracetic acid, ethylene oxide).

5. Demonstration

  • Gram stain – unstained refractile areas.
  • Schaeffer–Fulton (malachite green) stain – green spores, red vegetative cells; modified Ziehl–Neelsen stain – red spores.

6. Importance

  • Geobacillus stearothermophilus spores are used as biological indicators to check autoclaves.
  • Diseases spread by spores: tetanus, gas gangrene, botulism, anthrax and hospital diarrhoea due to Clostridioides difficile (alcohol hand rubs do not kill these spores – wash hands with soap and water).

7. Difference between spore and vegetative cell | Spore | Vegetative cell | |---|---| | Dormant, no metabolism | Active metabolism and division | | Very low water content | High water content | | Contains calcium dipicolinate | Absent | | Resistant to heat, drying, chemicals | Easily killed | | Thick cortex and coat | Thin wall | | Does not stain easily | Stains readily |

8. Nursing points

  • Deep, soil-contaminated wounds need thorough cleaning, debridement and tetanus prophylaxis.
  • Instruments must be autoclaved, not merely boiled; check that the biological indicator report is satisfactory.
  • In C. difficile outbreaks, clean surfaces with chlorine-based (sporicidal) disinfectants.

Conclusion Spores are the toughest form of life known; sterilisation methods are therefore designed to destroy spores.

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
unit_title: Section A: General Characteristics of Microbes
question: Classify culture media with examples. Add a note on media preparation and the uses of blood agar.
answer_html:
Definition A culture medium is a nutrient preparation (solid or liquid) used to grow microorganisms in the laboratory for identification and antibiotic sensitivity testing.

1. Classification based on consistency

  • Solid media – contain agar 1.5–2% (a seaweed product with no food value; melts at about 95 °C, sets at about 42 °C), e.g., nutrient agar.
  • Semi-solid media – 0.2–0.5% agar, for motility tests.
  • Liquid media (broth) – nutrient broth, peptone water; used for blood culture and biochemical tests.

2. Classification based on composition

  • Simple/basal – peptone water, nutrient broth, nutrient agar.
  • Complex – special ingredients added.
  • Synthetic/defined – exact chemical composition known (research use).

3. Classification based on purpose (most important) | Type | Purpose | Examples | |---|---|---| | Enriched | Solid medium with blood/serum for fastidious organisms | Blood agar, chocolate agar, Loeffler's serum slope | | Enrichment | Liquid; favours the wanted organism over others | Selenite F broth (Salmonella), alkaline peptone water (Vibrio) | | Selective | Solid; inhibits unwanted organisms | DCA, XLD, TCBS (Vibrio), Lowenstein–Jensen (TB), Sabouraud's dextrose agar (fungi) | | Differential (indicator) | Shows a visible difference in colonies | MacConkey agar (lactose fermenters pink), blood agar (haemolysis), CLED | | Transport | Keeps organisms alive during transport | Stuart's, Amies, Cary–Blair, VR medium (Vibrio), buffered glycerol saline | | Anaerobic | Grows anaerobes | Robertson's cooked meat broth, thioglycollate broth | | Sugar media | Fermentation tests | Glucose, lactose, sucrose with Andrade's indicator |

4. Preparation of culture media (outline)

  1. Weigh dehydrated medium and dissolve in distilled water.
  2. Adjust pH to 7.2–7.4.
  3. Sterilise by autoclaving (121 °C, 15 minutes); heat-sensitive items (sugars, serum) by filtration; egg media (LJ) by inspissation.
  4. Cool to 45–50 °C, then add sterile blood or supplements.
  5. Pour about 15–20 ml into sterile Petri dishes aseptically; allow to set and dry.
  6. Quality control – incubate a few plates overnight for sterility and test with control strains.
  7. Label with name and date; store at 2–8 °C.

5. Uses of blood agar Blood agar = nutrient agar + 5–10% sterile sheep blood.

  1. Enriched medium for fastidious organisms – streptococci, pneumococci.
  2. Differential medium – shows type of haemolysis: β (complete, clear zone) – S. pyogenes, S. aureus; α (partial, greenish) – S. pneumoniae, viridans streptococci; γ (none) – enterococci.
  3. Routine primary culture of most clinical specimens (pus, throat swab, sputum).
  4. Shows swarming of Proteus, satellitism of Haemophilus, and is used for the CAMP test.
  5. Base for preparing chocolate agar.

Conclusion Choosing the right medium is the key to isolating the right organism; nurses help by sending specimens in the correct transport medium.

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
unit_title: Section A: General Characteristics of Microbes
question: Describe the methods of culturing bacteria, including pure culture techniques.

diagram.caption: Four-quadrant (four-flame) streak plate method

answer_html:
Introduction Culture methods are techniques of inoculating specimens on media so that bacteria grow in a form suitable for study. The aim is usually to get isolated colonies that can be picked as a pure culture (growth of only one type of organism).

1. Streak culture (surface plating) – most common

  • A loopful of specimen is spread over one area of a plate and then streaked in successive areas (four-quadrant or four-flame method), flaming the loop between areas.
  • Gradually thins the inoculum so that isolated colonies appear in the last streaks.
  • Used for routine culture of pus, urine, sputum.

2. Lawn (carpet) culture

  • The inoculum is spread evenly over the whole plate with a swab, giving uniform growth.
  • Used for antibiotic sensitivity testing (Kirby–Bauer disc diffusion) and bacteriophage typing.

3. Stroke culture

  • Streaking on the surface of an agar slope in a tube.
  • Gives a pure growth for slide agglutination and biochemical tests.

4. Stab culture

  • Medium in a tube is stabbed with a straight wire.
  • Used for motility testing, gelatin liquefaction and maintaining stock cultures.

5. Pour plate culture

  • Diluted specimen is mixed with melted, cooled agar (45 °C) and poured into a Petri dish; colonies grow throughout the agar.
  • Used to find the viable bacterial count – e.g., in water and milk; urine colony count.

6. Liquid (broth) culture

  • Inoculation into broth – growth shows as turbidity.
  • Useful for large volumes such as blood culture and for specimens with few organisms; but pure culture cannot be identified directly.

7. Anaerobic culture

  • In McIntosh–Fildes jar, GasPak system or cooked meat broth for anaerobes such as Clostridium.

8. Methods of obtaining pure culture

  1. Streak plating and picking a single isolated colony (commonest).
  2. Pour plate / dilution methods.
  3. Selective and enrichment media to suppress other organisms.
  4. Use of special conditions – heat (to keep only spore-formers), specific pH, anaerobiosis.
  5. Animal inoculation (e.g., guinea pig for TB – historical).
  6. Single-cell isolation by micromanipulator (research).

Precautions Aseptic technique, flaming loops, labelling plates, incubating at 37 °C for 18–24 hours, biosafety cabinets for dangerous organisms.

Conclusion Correct culture methods give pure colonies – the starting point for identification and sensitivity reports that guide treatment.

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
unit_title: Section A: General Characteristics of Microbes
question: Explain the nutritional requirements and nutritional types of bacteria.
answer_html:
Introduction Like all living cells, bacteria need food for energy and for building their cells. Knowing their nutrition helps us grow them in culture media and also deny them food and moisture in hospitals.

1. Basic nutritional requirements

  1. Water – about 80% of the cell weight; dry conditions stop growth.
  2. Carbon source – organic compounds (sugars, proteins) for most pathogens.
  3. Nitrogen – amino acids, peptones, ammonium salts; for proteins and nucleic acids.
  4. Hydrogen and oxygen – from water and organic matter.
  5. Phosphorus and sulphur – for nucleic acids, ATP and amino acids.
  6. Minerals – potassium, magnesium, calcium, iron (bacteria use siderophores to steal iron), trace elements.
  7. Growth factors – vitamins and other substances some bacteria cannot make, e.g., Haemophilus influenzae needs X factor (haemin) and V factor (NAD).
  8. Energy source – light or chemical compounds.

2. Nutritional types | Basis | Type | Meaning | Example | |---|---|---|---| | Energy source | Phototrophs | Use sunlight | Photosynthetic bacteria | | | Chemotrophs | Use chemical reactions | All pathogenic bacteria | | Carbon source | Autotrophs | Use CO₂ | Soil bacteria (nitrifying) | | | Heterotrophs | Need organic carbon | All pathogens | | Electron donor | Lithotrophs | Inorganic | Sulphur bacteria | | | Organotrophs | Organic | Pathogens | Thus pathogenic bacteria are chemo-organo-heterotrophs.

  • Prototrophs grow on simple media; auxotrophs need extra growth factors.
  • Fastidious organisms need special enriched media (gonococci, H. influenzae).
  • Saprophytes live on dead matter; parasites on living hosts; obligate intracellular parasites (rickettsiae, chlamydiae, viruses) grow only in living cells.

3. Requirement of gases

  • Obligate aerobes – need oxygen (M. tuberculosis, Pseudomonas).
  • Facultative anaerobes – grow with or without oxygen (E. coli, S. aureus).
  • Microaerophiles – low oxygen (Campylobacter, H. pylori).
  • Obligate anaerobes – killed by oxygen (Clostridium, Bacteroides).
  • Capnophiles – need 5–10% CO₂ (Neisseria gonorrhoeae, Brucella abortus).

4. Uptake of nutrients Passive diffusion, facilitated diffusion, active transport and group translocation through the cell membrane.

Nursing importance

  • Moist, warm, protein-rich places (wet dressings, stagnant water in humidifiers, leftover feeds) favour growth – keep equipment dry and clean.
  • Anaerobic deep wounds favour tetanus and gas gangrene – thorough wound debridement is essential.

5. Application in culture media Culture media are prepared by supplying these requirements – peptone (nitrogen), meat extract (vitamins, minerals), sugars (energy), salts and water, with blood or serum for fastidious organisms, at the correct pH and temperature.

Conclusion Bacterial nutrition explains how media are designed and why cleanliness and dryness check bacterial growth.

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
unit_title: Section A: General Characteristics of Microbes
question: Describe the Ziehl–Neelsen (acid-fast) staining method.
answer_html:
Introduction Some bacteria, especially Mycobacterium tuberculosis and M. leprae, have a cell wall rich in mycolic acid (a waxy lipid). They do not take up Gram stain easily, but once stained with hot carbol fuchsin they resist decolourisation by acid – hence called acid-fast bacilli (AFB). The Ziehl–Neelsen (ZN) stain is the basic test for diagnosis of tuberculosis.

1. Principle

  • Strong carbol fuchsin (with phenol) is driven into the waxy wall by heating.
  • The mycolic acid holds the dye even after treatment with 20% sulphuric acid (acid-fast).
  • Non-acid-fast organisms and cells lose the red dye and take up the blue counterstain.

2. Reagents Strong carbol fuchsin, 20% sulphuric acid (5% for M. leprae) or acid–alcohol (3% HCl in 95% ethanol), methylene blue (counterstain), water.

3. Procedure

  1. Prepare a thin smear from the purulent part of sputum (about 2 × 3 cm), air-dry and heat-fix.
  2. Flood with carbol fuchsin and heat gently from below until steam rises – do not boil – for 5 minutes, adding stain to prevent drying.
  3. Wash with water.
  4. Decolourise with 20% sulphuric acid, repeating until the smear is faint pink (about 2–4 minutes); wash.
  5. Counterstain with methylene blue for 30 seconds–1 minute; wash and dry.
  6. Examine under the oil-immersion lens – at least 100 fields.

4. Result

  • AFB – bright red, slender, slightly curved, beaded rods on a blue background.
  • Pus cells and other bacteria appear blue.

5. Grading of sputum smears (NTEP / IUATLD) | Finding | Report | |---|---| | No AFB in 100 fields | Negative | | 1–9 AFB in 100 fields | Scanty (number recorded) | | 10–99 AFB in 100 fields | 1+ | | 1–10 AFB per field (in 50 fields) | 2+ | | More than 10 AFB per field (in 20 fields) | 3+ |

6. Uses

  • Diagnosis and follow-up of pulmonary TB; leprosy (slit-skin smears); Nocardia (modified stain); spore staining (modified).
  • Fluorescent (auramine–rhodamine, LED) microscopy is a faster alternative now used widely; CBNAAT/Truenat detect TB DNA and drug resistance.

Nursing role Teach the patient to give a good early-morning, deep-coughed sputum (not saliva), in a wide-mouthed, leak-proof container, in an open area away from others; label and send quickly.

Conclusion ZN staining is cheap and quick and remains a cornerstone of TB diagnosis in India.

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
unit_title: Section A: General Characteristics of Microbes
question: Explain the anaerobic methods of culture.

diagram.caption: McIntosh and Fildes anaerobic jar
labels: lid with inlet and outlet valves

answer_html:
Introduction Anaerobes such as Clostridium tetani, C. perfringens and Bacteroides cannot grow in the presence of oxygen. Special methods are needed to remove or exclude oxygen so that these organisms can be cultured from deep wounds, abscesses and gangrenous tissue.

1. Exclusion of oxygen (simple methods)

  • Deep stab culture or shake culture in agar.
  • Sealing the medium with a layer of paraffin or agar.
  • Boiling the medium just before use to drive out dissolved oxygen.

2. Use of reducing substances in media

  • Robertson's cooked meat (RCM) broth – pieces of cooked meat contain glutathione and unsaturated fatty acids that absorb oxygen; anaerobes grow in it.
  • Thioglycollate broth, cysteine, glucose and ascorbic acid also lower oxygen.

3. Displacement of oxygen

  • Candle jar – burning candle uses up oxygen and adds CO₂ (useful only for capnophiles, not for strict anaerobes).

4. McIntosh and Fildes anaerobic jar (classic method)

  • A strong metal or glass jar with an airtight lid having inlet and outlet valves and a palladium catalyst (alumina pellets coated with palladium) under the lid.
  • Inoculated plates are placed inside, air is evacuated and hydrogen is filled in; the catalyst makes hydrogen combine with remaining oxygen to form water.
  • Indicator – reduced methylene blue (colourless when anaerobic, blue if oxygen is present) or resazurin.

5. GasPak system (modern, convenient)

  • A disposable sachet containing sodium borohydride and sodium bicarbonate with citric acid; on adding water it releases hydrogen and CO₂.
  • With a palladium catalyst in the jar, oxygen is removed. Used widely in laboratories.

6. Anaerobic glove box / workstation

  • A closed chamber filled with a gas mixture (nitrogen, hydrogen, CO₂) where work is done through gloves; best for research and large laboratories.

7. Biological method

  • Growing aerobic organisms alongside anaerobes so that the aerobes consume oxygen (rarely used).

Specimen care (nurse's role)

  • Anaerobic specimens should be aspirated pus or tissue, not dry swabs; send in an anaerobic transport medium or a capped syringe without air, and transport immediately.

Anaerobic infections of clinical importance Tetanus, gas gangrene, botulism, C. difficile diarrhoea, lung and brain abscess, peritonitis after bowel perforation, aspiration pneumonia and pelvic abscess. Foul-smelling pus, gas in tissues and black discharge suggest anaerobes.

Conclusion Anaerobic methods allow diagnosis of serious infections like gas gangrene and tetanus; correct collection by the nurse is as important as the laboratory method.

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
unit_title: Section A: General Characteristics of Microbes
question: Describe the bacterial flagella and the methods of demonstrating motility.

diagram.caption: Arrangements of bacterial flagella

answer_html:
Introduction Flagella are long, thin, thread-like appendages that make bacteria motile. Motility helps bacteria reach nutrients and host tissues, and the pattern of motility is useful in identification.

1. Structure

  • Made of a protein called flagellin; 3–20 µm long and only 12–30 nm thick (too thin to see by ordinary microscopy without special stains).
  • Three parts: filament, hook and basal body (anchored in the cell wall and membrane – acts as a rotary motor).
  • Bacteria move by rotation of flagella.

2. Arrangement | Type | Description | Example | |---|---|---| | Atrichous | No flagella | Shigella, Klebsiella | | Monotrichous | Single polar flagellum | Vibrio cholerae | | Lophotrichous | Tuft at one end | Pseudomonas fluorescens | | Amphitrichous | Flagellum at both ends | Alcaligenes faecalis | | Peritrichous | All over the surface | E. coli, Salmonella Typhi, Proteus | Spirochaetes move by endoflagella (axial filaments) lying under an outer sheath.

3. Functions and importance

  • Motility towards nutrients (chemotaxis) and spread in tissues (e.g., Proteus in the urinary tract).
  • Flagellar "H" antigens are used for serotyping Salmonella and in the Widal test.
  • Characteristic motility aids identification: darting (V. cholerae), tumbling (Listeria), swarming (Proteus), corkscrew (spirochaetes).

4. Methods of demonstrating motility

  1. Hanging drop preparation – a drop of young broth culture on a coverslip is inverted over a cavity slide (ring of petroleum jelly) and examined under the high-power lens with reduced light; true motility (directional movement) is seen, as distinct from Brownian movement (vibration in one place).
  2. Wet mount – a drop between slide and coverslip.
  3. Semi-solid agar (motility medium) – stab inoculation; motile organisms spread out and make the medium cloudy; non-motile grow only along the stab line.
  4. Craigie's tube method – separates motile phases (used for Salmonella).
  5. Dark-ground microscopy – for spirochaetes (T. pallidum) and Vibrio.
  6. Flagella staining (Leifson's, silver impregnation) and electron microscopy to see the flagella themselves.

5. True motility versus Brownian movement | True motility | Brownian movement | |---|---| | Organism moves from one place to another | Vibrates in the same place | | Due to flagella | Due to bombardment by water molecules | | Seen only in living organisms | Seen in dead cells and particles too | | Directional, purposeful | Random, oscillating |

Conclusion Flagella are organs of motility and important antigens; simple motility tests give quick clues to the identity of bacteria.

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
unit_title: Section A: General Characteristics of Microbes
question: Explain the KOH mount and lactophenol cotton blue (LPCB) preparation used in the diagnosis of fungal infections.
answer_html:
Introduction Direct microscopy is the quickest way to diagnose fungal infections. Two simple wet preparations are used in every laboratory: the potassium hydroxide (KOH) mount for clinical specimens and the lactophenol cotton blue (LPCB) mount for identifying fungi grown in culture.

A. KOH mount

  1. Principle – 10% KOH (20–40% for nails) dissolves keratin, epithelial cells and debris, but fungal cell walls (chitin) resist it, so the fungal elements become clearly visible.
  2. Specimens – skin scrapings from the active edge of a lesion, nail clippings, hair stumps, corneal scrapings, sputum, pus, tissue.
  3. Procedure
    • Place the specimen on a clean slide; add a drop of KOH and a coverslip.
    • Leave for 10–30 minutes (warm gently) to clear; nails may need longer.
    • Examine under the low- and high-power objectives with reduced light.
  4. Findings
    • Thin, branched, septate hyphae – dermatophytes (ringworm), Aspergillus.
    • Budding yeast cells with pseudohyphae – Candida.
    • Short hyphae and round yeasts ("spaghetti and meatballs") – Malassezia (pityriasis versicolor).
    • Broad, ribbon-like aseptate hyphae – Mucor/Rhizopus (mucormycosis).
  5. Adding calcofluor white makes fungi glow under a fluorescence microscope.

B. Lactophenol cotton blue (LPCB) mount

  1. Composition and role of each component
    • Phenol – kills the fungi (safe to handle).
    • Lactic acid – preserves fungal structures and clears the preparation.
    • Glycerol – prevents drying; makes a semi-permanent mount.
    • Cotton blue – stains the chitin of fungal walls blue.
  2. Procedure – a small piece of fungal growth from culture (e.g., on Sabouraud dextrose agar) is teased apart with needles in a drop of LPCB on a slide, covered with a coverslip and examined.
  3. Uses
    • Identification of moulds by the shape of hyphae, conidia and fruiting bodies – e.g., Aspergillus (conidial head), Penicillium (brush-like), Mucor (sporangia), dermatophytes (macro- and microconidia).
    • Slide cultures and teaching preparations.

Comparison | KOH mount | LPCB mount | |---|---| | Direct examination of clinical specimen | Examination of growth from culture | | Clears tissue | Stains and preserves fungus | | Rapid screening | Identification of species |

C. Other rapid methods in mycology

  • India ink preparation of CSF – capsulated yeasts of Cryptococcus neoformans in HIV patients.
  • Gram stain – Candida appears as Gram-positive budding yeasts.
  • Culture on Sabouraud dextrose agar (SDA) at 25 °C and 37 °C for identification.
  • Germ tube test – Candida albicans forms germ tubes in serum within 2 hours.

Conclusion These two simple mounts give a rapid and inexpensive diagnosis of most fungal infections.

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
unit_title: Section A: General Characteristics of Microbes
question: Explain the laboratory methods used for the identification of microorganisms.
answer_html:
Introduction To treat an infection correctly the laboratory must answer two questions: "Which organism is it?" and "Which drug will kill it?" Several methods are used step by step, starting with the quickest.

1. Microscopy

  • Wet mounts – hanging drop (motility), saline and iodine mounts (parasites), KOH (fungi), India ink (Cryptococcus).
  • Stained smears – Gram stain, Ziehl–Neelsen (AFB), Albert's (diphtheria), Giemsa/Leishman (malaria parasites).
  • Special microscopes – dark-ground (spirochaetes), fluorescence (auramine for TB), electron microscope (viruses).

2. Culture

  • Growth on suitable media (blood agar, MacConkey, selective media) under correct conditions.
  • Colony characters – size, shape, colour, haemolysis, lactose fermentation, smell, swarming.

3. Biochemical tests

  • Sugar fermentation, catalase (staphylococci +, streptococci −), coagulase (S. aureus), oxidase (Pseudomonas, Vibrio), indole, urease, citrate, H₂S (IMViC tests for Enterobacteriaceae).
  • Automated systems (VITEK) and MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry identify organisms within hours.

4. Serological (antigen–antibody) methods

  • Detecting antigen of the organism – slide agglutination with specific antisera (Salmonella, Vibrio), latex tests, rapid antigen tests (malaria, dengue NS1, COVID-19).
  • Detecting antibodies in the patient's serum – Widal, VDRL, ELISA for HIV/HBsAg, ASO.

5. Molecular methods

  • PCR, real-time PCR, CBNAAT/Truenat (TB and rifampicin resistance), line probe assay, gene sequencing – fast and highly sensitive.

6. Antimicrobial susceptibility testing

  • Kirby–Bauer disc diffusion, MIC by E-test or broth dilution, automated systems – guide the choice of antibiotic.

7. Animal inoculation and other tests

  • Toxigenicity tests (Elek's test for diphtheria), mouse tests for toxins; rarely used now.
  • Typing methods (phage typing, molecular typing) to trace hospital outbreaks.

Nursing role Correct specimen, collected aseptically before antibiotics, properly labelled with clinical details and sent quickly – the accuracy of all these methods depends on it.

8. Example – workflow of a urine culture

  1. Mid-stream urine received within 1–2 hours.
  2. Wet mount for pus cells; Gram stain if needed.
  3. Culture on CLED or blood agar and MacConkey with a calibrated loop; incubate 18–24 hours.
  4. Colony count – ≥10⁵ CFU/ml of a single organism suggests significant bacteriuria.
  5. Identification by colony characters and biochemical tests (e.g., E. coli).
  6. Antibiotic sensitivity by disc diffusion; report sent in 48–72 hours.

Conclusion Identification moves from quick microscopy to culture, biochemical, serological and molecular tests – each step adding certainty that leads to targeted treatment.

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
unit_title: Section A: General Characteristics of Microbes
question: Write the morphological classification of bacteria.
answer_html:
Based on shape, bacteria are classified as:

  1. Cocci (spherical) – diplococci (Pneumococcus, Neisseria), streptococci (chains), staphylococci (clusters), tetrads, sarcinae.
  2. Bacilli (rod-shaped) – E. coli, Salmonella; coccobacilli (Brucella); Chinese-letter arrangement (C. diphtheriae).
  3. Vibrios (comma-shaped) – Vibrio cholerae.
  4. Spirilla (rigid spirals) – Spirillum minus.
  5. Spirochaetes (flexible spirals) – Treponema, Borrelia, Leptospira.
  6. Actinomycetes (branching filaments) – Actinomyces, Nocardia.
  7. Mycoplasma – no cell wall, no fixed shape (pleomorphic).

Shape and arrangement are seen in a Gram-stained smear and give the first clue to the identity of the organism.

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
unit_title: Section A: General Characteristics of Microbes
question: Write the factors influencing microbial growth.
answer_html:
Factors influencing microbial growth

  1. Nutrients – carbon, nitrogen, minerals, growth factors.
  2. Temperature – most pathogens grow best at 37 °C (mesophiles).
  3. Oxygen – aerobes, anaerobes, facultative, microaerophilic organisms.
  4. Carbon dioxide – 5–10% for capnophiles (gonococci).
  5. pH – most pathogens 7.2–7.6; V. cholerae prefers alkaline pH (8.2–8.6).
  6. Moisture – water is essential; drying stops growth.
  7. Osmotic pressure/salt – S. aureus tolerates high salt.
  8. Light and radiation – darkness favours growth; UV light kills.
  9. Blood and body fluids – act as rich nutrients.

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
unit_title: Section A: General Characteristics of Microbes
question: List the uses of lactophenol cotton blue stain.
answer_html:
Lactophenol cotton blue (LPCB) is a mounting fluid and stain for fungi. Uses

  1. Identification of moulds grown in culture by studying hyphae, spores and fruiting bodies (e.g., Aspergillus, Penicillium, Mucor, dermatophytes).
  2. Staining fungal cell walls (chitin) blue for clear visibility.
  3. Kills the fungus (phenol) – makes handling safe.
  4. Preserves fungal structures (lactic acid) and prevents drying (glycerol) – semi-permanent mounts.
  5. Used in slide culture and teaching/reference slides.

Composition: phenol, lactic acid, glycerol and cotton blue dye in distilled water.

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
unit_title: Section A: General Characteristics of Microbes
question: What are amphitrichous bacteria? Give two examples.
answer_html:
Amphitrichous bacteria are bacteria that have a single flagellum (or a tuft of flagella) at each of the two opposite ends (poles) of the cell.

Examples

  1. Alcaligenes faecalis
  2. Campylobacter jejuni (single polar flagellum at one or both ends) (Tufts at both ends are seen in Spirillum species – sometimes called amphilophotrichous.)

Other arrangements for comparison: monotrichous (Vibrio cholerae), lophotrichous (Pseudomonas fluorescens), peritrichous (E. coli).

Flagellar arrangement is studied by flagella staining or electron microscopy and helps in identifying bacteria.

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
unit_title: Section A: General Characteristics of Microbes
question: Differentiate between prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells.
answer_html:
Feature Prokaryotic cell Eukaryotic cell
Nucleus No nuclear membrane (nucleoid) True nucleus with membrane
Chromosome Single, circular DNA Multiple, linear chromosomes
Ribosomes 70S 80S (70S in mitochondria)
Mitochondria, ER, Golgi Absent Present
Cell wall Peptidoglycan Chitin (fungi) or absent (protozoa)
Sterols in membrane Absent Present
Division Binary fission Mitosis/meiosis
Size Small (0.5–5 µm) Larger (10–100 µm)
Cytoplasmic streaming Absent Present
Lysosomes and vacuoles Absent Present
Histones with DNA Absent Present
Examples Bacteria Fungi, protozoa, helminths, human cells

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
unit_title: Section A: General Characteristics of Microbes
question: What are plasmids? State their significance.
answer_html:
Plasmids are small, circular, double-stranded extra-chromosomal DNA molecules found in the bacterial cytoplasm. They replicate independently of the chromosome and are not essential for survival.

Significance

  1. R-plasmids (resistance factors) carry genes for antibiotic resistance (e.g., ESBL, carbapenemase genes) and spread them between bacteria by conjugation – a major cause of multidrug resistance in hospitals.
  2. Carry genes for toxins and virulence (e.g., enterotoxins of E. coli, tetanus toxin).
  3. Used as vectors in genetic engineering (production of insulin, hepatitis B vaccine).
  4. Useful in plasmid typing of outbreak strains.

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
question: Describe the morphology, pathogenesis and laboratory diagnosis of *Treponema pallidum*.

diagram.caption: *Treponema pallidum* under dark-ground microscopy and stages of syphilis
labels: thin spiral organism with regular coils
secondary rash on palms and soles

answer_html:
Introduction Treponema pallidum (subspecies pallidum) is a spirochaete that causes syphilis, a chronic sexually transmitted infection that can affect almost every organ. It was discovered by Schaudinn and Hoffmann in 1905. Syphilis in pregnancy can kill the fetus or cause congenital syphilis, so every antenatal mother in India is screened for it under the national programme for elimination of mother-to-child transmission of HIV and syphilis.

A. Morphology (3 marks)

  1. Shape – thin, delicate, spiral organism with 6–14 regular, tight coils and tapering, pointed ends.
  2. Size – 6–15 µm long but only 0.1–0.2 µm thick – too thin to be seen by ordinary light microscopy or Gram stain.
  3. Motility – actively motile with three characteristic movements: rotation (corkscrew) around the long axis, flexion (bending) and translation (forward movement), produced by endoflagella (axial filaments) lying between the cell wall and outer sheath.
  4. Staining – stains poorly; seen by dark-ground (dark-field) microscopy, silver impregnation (Fontana stain in smears, Levaditi stain in tissues) and direct fluorescent antibody staining.
  5. Culture – cannot be grown on artificial media; maintained by inoculation in rabbit testes (Nichols strain), which provides antigen for tests.
  6. Resistance – very delicate; killed quickly by drying, heat (41–42 °C), soap and common disinfectants. It survives in blood stored at 4 °C for 1–3 days, so fresh blood transfusion can transmit it; storage beyond 72 hours makes it safe.

B. Modes of transmission

  • Sexual contact – the commonest route (genital, anal, oral).
  • Vertical (transplacental) – from the infected mother to the fetus, usually after the fourth month of pregnancy.
  • Blood transfusion with fresh blood.
  • Direct contact with lesions (rarely health workers) and accidental inoculation.

C. Pathogenesis and clinical stages (4 marks)

  1. Entry – spirochaetes enter through minute abrasions of skin or intact mucous membranes.
  2. Spread – they multiply locally and within hours reach the lymph nodes and bloodstream, so syphilis is a systemic disease from the start.
  3. Incubation period – 9–90 days (average 3 weeks).
  4. Primary syphilis
    • A painless, indurated, clean-based ulcer – the hard chancre – at the site of entry (penis, vulva, cervix, anus, lips).
    • Painless, rubbery, enlarged regional lymph nodes.
    • The chancre heals in 3–6 weeks even without treatment, giving a false sense of cure.
  5. Secondary syphilis (6–12 weeks after infection)
    • Due to widespread multiplication of the organism.
    • Generalised skin rash, typically on the palms and soles; mucous patches and "snail-track" ulcers in the mouth; condylomata lata (moist warty lesions) in the genital region; patchy hair loss; fever, malaise, generalised lymphadenopathy.
    • This is the most infectious stage.
  6. Latent syphilis – no symptoms; only serological tests are positive. Early latent (within 1–2 years) may relapse; late latent is usually not infectious except from mother to fetus.
  7. Tertiary (late) syphilis – in about one-third of untreated patients, 10–30 years later.
    • Gummas – destructive granulomatous lesions of skin, bone, liver.
    • Cardiovascular syphilis – aortitis, aortic aneurysm, aortic regurgitation.
    • Neurosyphilis – tabes dorsalis, general paresis of the insane, meningovascular syphilis.
    • The pathology is mainly due to immune reaction (endarteritis obliterans) rather than toxins (T. pallidum produces no toxin).
  8. Congenital syphilis – abortion, stillbirth or an infected baby.
    • Early (before 2 years): snuffles (nasal discharge), skin rash, hepatosplenomegaly, bone changes.
    • Late: Hutchinson's triad – notched incisor teeth, interstitial keratitis and eighth-nerve deafness; saddle nose, sabre tibia.

D. Laboratory diagnosis (3 marks)

1. Specimens

  • Serous exudate from the chancre or moist secondary lesions (clean the lesion with saline, squeeze gently and collect the clear fluid).
  • Lymph node aspirate.
  • Blood (serum) for serology; CSF in suspected neurosyphilis.

2. Direct demonstration (useful in primary and secondary stages)

  • Dark-ground microscopy – thin, bright, actively motile spirochaetes with characteristic movements on a dark background. Not suitable for mouth lesions because harmless oral treponemes look similar.
  • Direct fluorescent antibody test (DFA-TP).
  • Silver staining of tissue sections; PCR in specialised centres.

3. Serological tests (mainstay of diagnosis) (a) Non-treponemal (reagin) tests – detect antibodies (reagin) against cardiolipin antigen.

  • VDRL (Venereal Disease Research Laboratory) test – slide flocculation test; gives a titre (e.g., 1:16).
  • RPR (Rapid Plasma Reagin) card test – uses charcoal particles; good for field screening.
  • Uses: screening (antenatal, blood donors), monitoring the response to treatment (titre falls after cure), CSF-VDRL for neurosyphilis.
  • Limitations: biological false-positive reactions in malaria, viral infections, leprosy, pregnancy, SLE, old age; prozone phenomenon (false negative with very high antibody in secondary syphilis – overcome by diluting serum).

(b) Treponemal tests – use T. pallidum antigen; specific, used for confirmation.

  • TPHA (T. pallidum haemagglutination assay) and TPPA (particle agglutination).
