  • FTA-ABS (fluorescent treponemal antibody absorption) – earliest to become positive; IgM FTA-ABS for congenital syphilis.
  • ELISA/CLIA and rapid immunochromatographic tests (dual HIV–syphilis rapid tests used in antenatal clinics).
  • Remain positive for life, so not used to monitor treatment.

Interpretation table | VDRL/RPR | TPHA | Interpretation | |---|---|---| | Positive | Positive | Active (or recently treated) syphilis | | Positive | Negative | Biological false positive | | Negative | Positive | Treated old syphilis or very early/late syphilis | | Negative | Negative | No syphilis (or incubation period) |

E. Treatment and prevention (in brief)

  • Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units IM, single dose for early syphilis (weekly × 3 for late); aqueous penicillin IV for neurosyphilis; doxycycline if allergic (not in pregnancy).
  • Jarisch–Herxheimer reaction – fever, chills and myalgia a few hours after the first dose, due to release of treponemal products; reassure and give antipyretics.
  • Partner notification and treatment, HIV testing, condom use, antenatal screening of all mothers, screening of blood donors.

Nursing importance

  • Wear gloves while examining or dressing lesions; lesions of primary and secondary syphilis are highly infectious.
  • Counsel patients with respect and confidentiality; refer to Suraksha clinics (STI/RTI clinics under NACO).
  • Ensure every pregnant woman is screened in the first visit and treated early to prevent congenital syphilis.

Conclusion T. pallidum is a fragile, uncultivable spirochaete that causes a life-long, multisystem disease. Dark-ground microscopy in early lesions and VDRL/TPHA serology form the basis of diagnosis, and a single injection of penicillin can cure early disease.

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
question: Describe the general properties, pathogenesis and laboratory diagnosis of *Mycobacterium tuberculosis*.

diagram.caption: Pathogenesis of tuberculosis – primary (Ghon) complex and secondary TB

answer_html:
Introduction Mycobacterium tuberculosis causes tuberculosis (TB), the world's leading infectious killer. India carries the largest share of the global TB burden, and the National TB Elimination Programme (NTEP) aims to end TB. The organism was discovered by Robert Koch in 1882 – hence called Koch's bacillus.

A. General properties (2 marks)

  1. Morphology – slender, straight or slightly curved rods, 1–4 µm × 0.2–0.5 µm; often beaded or barred; occur singly, in pairs or in small clumps.
  2. Non-motile, non-sporing, non-capsulated.
  3. Acid-fast – the cell wall is rich in mycolic acid (waxy lipid); stains red by the Ziehl–Neelsen method and is weakly Gram-positive.
  4. Obligate aerobe – grows best in oxygen-rich areas such as the apex of the lung.
  5. Very slow growth – generation time about 14–18 hours; colonies take 2–8 weeks to appear.
  6. Culture – on Lowenstein–Jensen (LJ) medium (egg, glycerol, asparagine, mineral salts and malachite green to suppress contaminants); colonies are dry, rough, buff-coloured and tough ("rough, tough and buff"). Liquid culture (MGIT) gives results in 1–2 weeks.
  7. Resistance – survives in dried sputum for weeks; resistant to drying, acids and alkalis (used to decontaminate sputum by Petroff's method); killed by sunlight (UV light), pasteurisation and 5% phenol in 24 hours; heat 60 °C for 15–20 minutes.

B. Virulence factors

  • Cord factor (trehalose dimycolate) – bacilli grow in serpentine cords; toxic to cells.
  • Mycolic acid and sulphatides – prevent fusion of phagosome and lysosome, so bacilli survive inside macrophages.
  • Lipoarabinomannan – suppresses macrophage activity.
  • Ability to remain dormant (latent) for years.

C. Mode of spread

  • Droplet nuclei (1–5 µm) produced when a patient with sputum-positive pulmonary TB coughs, sneezes or talks; they remain suspended in air for hours.
  • Rarely by ingestion of unpasteurised milk (M. bovis), through skin or transplacentally.

D. Pathogenesis (4 marks) 1. Primary tuberculosis (first infection, usually in childhood)

  • Inhaled bacilli reach the alveoli and are engulfed by alveolar macrophages, but they multiply inside them.
  • A small inflammatory lesion forms just below the pleura – the Ghon focus.
  • Bacilli travel through lymphatics to the hilar lymph nodes.
  • Ghon focus + lymphangitis + enlarged hilar nodes = primary (Ghon) complex.
  • In 3–8 weeks cell-mediated immunity and delayed hypersensitivity develop (the Mantoux test turns positive).
  • Activated macrophages form granulomas (tubercles) – central caseous necrosis surrounded by epithelioid cells, Langhans giant cells and lymphocytes.
  • In most people the lesion heals by fibrosis and calcification, but a few viable bacilli remain dormant – latent TB infection.
  • In infants, malnourished or HIV-positive persons, the infection may spread – progressive primary TB, miliary TB, TB meningitis.

2. Secondary (post-primary, reactivation) tuberculosis – usually in adults

  • Occurs by reactivation of dormant bacilli when immunity falls (HIV, diabetes, malnutrition, steroids, old age) or by reinfection.
  • Lesions develop in the apex of the lung (high oxygen).
  • Because of hypersensitivity there is extensive caseation; caseous material liquefies and is coughed out, forming cavities full of bacilli – the patient becomes highly infectious.
  • Erosion of vessels causes haemoptysis; spread through bronchi produces new lesions; bloodstream spread causes miliary TB and extrapulmonary TB (lymph nodes, pleura, spine – Pott's spine, kidney, meninges, intestine).

E. Laboratory diagnosis (4 marks)

1. Specimens

  • Pulmonary TB: two sputum samples (one spot and one early-morning) collected in a sterile, wide-mouthed, screw-capped container; for children – gastric aspirate or induced sputum; bronchoalveolar lavage.
  • Extrapulmonary: pus, lymph node aspirate (FNAC), pleural fluid, CSF, urine (three early-morning samples), tissue biopsy.

2. Microscopy

  • Ziehl–Neelsen staining – red, beaded acid-fast bacilli on blue background; graded as scanty, 1+, 2+, 3+.
  • Fluorescence (auramine–rhodamine) microscopy with LED – bacilli glow yellow-green; faster screening.
  • About 5,000–10,000 bacilli per ml of sputum are needed for a positive smear, so a negative smear does not rule out TB.

3. Molecular tests (rapid, recommended upfront under NTEP)

  • CBNAAT (GeneXpert MTB/RIF) – cartridge-based nucleic acid amplification test; detects TB DNA and rifampicin resistance in about 2 hours.
  • Truenat – Indian chip-based, battery-operated PCR suitable for peripheral laboratories.
  • Line probe assay (LPA) – detects resistance to rifampicin, isoniazid and second-line drugs.

4. Culture

  • LJ medium – colonies in 2–8 weeks; confirmatory (gold standard).
  • Liquid culture – MGIT 960 automated system – 1–2 weeks.
  • Specimens are first decontaminated (e.g., with 4% NaOH – Petroff's method).

5. Drug susceptibility testing (DST) – on culture or by molecular methods, to detect MDR-TB (resistant to isoniazid and rifampicin) and XDR-TB.

6. Other tests

  • Tuberculin (Mantoux) test and interferon-gamma release assays (IGRA) – indicate infection, mainly for latent TB and children.
  • Chest X-ray – infiltrates, cavities in the upper zones, miliary mottling.
  • Histopathology – caseating granulomas; ADA levels in pleural or ascitic fluid.

F. Treatment and prevention (in brief)

  • Drug-sensitive TB: 2 months HRZE + 4 months HRE (isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide, ethambutol) given daily under NTEP with fixed-dose combinations.
  • BCG vaccine at birth protects children against severe forms (TB meningitis, miliary TB).
  • Ni-kshay Poshan Yojana gives nutritional support to patients; TB preventive therapy for contacts.

Nursing importance

  • Teach cough etiquette – cover mouth, use a mask, dispose of sputum safely (in a covered container with disinfectant or by burning).
  • Keep wards well ventilated; use an N95 respirator while caring for infectious patients and during sputum induction.
  • Collect sputum correctly – deep cough, not saliva – in an open area.
  • Ensure treatment adherence, monitor side effects and trace contacts.

Conclusion M. tuberculosis is a slow-growing, acid-fast, intracellular bacillus that causes disease mainly through the body's own cell-mediated reaction. Rapid molecular tests along with microscopy and culture now allow early diagnosis and detection of drug resistance – the key to ending TB.

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
question: Describe the general properties, modes of transmission and serological markers (with a graph) of hepatitis B virus.

diagram.caption: Serological markers in acute hepatitis B (graph)
labels: weeks after exposure on x-axis; HBsAg
anti-HBs curves; symptoms and ALT peak; window period

answer_html:
Introduction Hepatitis B virus (HBV) causes acute and chronic hepatitis, cirrhosis and liver cancer. It is about 100 times more infectious than HIV and is a major occupational hazard for nurses. Fortunately, a safe and effective vaccine is available. HBsAg was first discovered by Baruch Blumberg (1965) as the "Australia antigen".

A. General properties of the virus (2 marks)

  1. Family – Hepadnaviridae; a DNA virus that replicates through an RNA intermediate using reverse transcriptase.
  2. Structure – the Dane particle (42 nm)
    • Outer envelope carrying the surface antigen (HBsAg).
    • Inner core (nucleocapsid, 27 nm) made of core antigen (HBcAg).
    • Inside the core: partially double-stranded circular DNA and DNA polymerase.
    • HBeAg – a soluble protein secreted from infected cells; indicates active replication.
  3. Infected blood also contains huge numbers of small spherical (22 nm) and tubular particles made only of HBsAg; they are not infectious but are detected in tests.
  4. Cannot be grown in ordinary cell cultures.
  5. Resistance – relatively stable; survives on surfaces for 7 days at room temperature; destroyed by autoclaving, boiling for 10 minutes, 1% sodium hypochlorite and 2% glutaraldehyde.

B. Modes of transmission (3 marks)

  1. Parenteral (blood-borne)
    • Transfusion of unscreened blood and blood products.
    • Needle-stick and sharp injuries in health workers (risk 6–30% from an HBeAg-positive source).
    • Sharing needles among injecting drug users; unsafe injections, reuse of syringes.
    • Haemodialysis, tattooing, ear-piercing, razors and toothbrushes shared.
  2. Sexual – through semen and vaginal secretions; commoner with multiple partners.
  3. Vertical (perinatal) – from an infected mother to the baby, mainly during delivery; if the mother is HBeAg-positive, up to 90% of babies get infected and most become chronic carriers.
  4. Horizontal – among household contacts and children through cuts and sores.
  5. It is not spread by food, water, coughing or casual contact. - Incubation period: 30–180 days (average about 60–90 days). - Chronicity depends on age: about 90% of infected newborns, 30% of young children and only 5% of adults become chronic carriers.

C. Serological markers (5 marks) | Marker | Meaning | |---|---| | HBsAg | First marker to appear (2–8 weeks after exposure, before symptoms); indicates current infection. Persistence beyond 6 months = chronic infection/carrier | | HBeAg | Active viral replication and high infectivity | | HBV DNA | Viral load; most sensitive indicator of replication; used to decide and monitor treatment | | IgM anti-HBc | Acute (recent) infection; the only marker in the window period | | IgG (total) anti-HBc | Past or chronic infection; persists for life (not produced by vaccine) | | Anti-HBe | Seroconversion; falling replication and lower infectivity | | Anti-HBs | Recovery and immunity; the only marker present after vaccination (≥10 mIU/ml is protective) |

Description of the graph (acute hepatitis B with recovery)

  • 0–4 weeks: HBV DNA and then HBsAg appear in blood; HBeAg follows.
  • 6–12 weeks: symptoms (jaundice) and ALT peak; IgM anti-HBc rises.
  • About 16–24 weeks: HBsAg and HBeAg disappear; anti-HBe appears.
  • Window period: the gap after HBsAg disappears and before anti-HBs appears – only IgM anti-HBc is positive. Testing only HBsAg in this period gives a false-negative result.
  • After 24–32 weeks: anti-HBs appears and stays for years; IgG anti-HBc remains for life.
  • In chronic infection the HBsAg curve does not fall – it stays positive beyond 6 months, anti-HBs never appears, and HBeAg may persist.

Interpretation of common patterns | HBsAg | IgM anti-HBc | Total anti-HBc | Anti-HBs | Interpretation | |---|---|---|---|---| | + | + | + | − | Acute hepatitis B | | + | − | + | − | Chronic infection | | − | + | + | − | Window period (recent infection) | | − | − | + | + | Recovered with immunity | | − | − | − | + | Immune due to vaccination | | − | − | − | − | Susceptible – needs vaccination |

D. Prevention (in brief)

  • Hepatitis B vaccine (recombinant HBsAg) – birth dose within 24 hours plus three doses in the pentavalent vaccine at 6, 10 and 14 weeks under UIP; health workers – 3 doses at 0, 1 and 6 months, with anti-HBs check.
  • Newborns of HBsAg-positive mothers: hepatitis B immunoglobulin (HBIG) and vaccine within 12 hours of birth.
  • Screening of blood, safe injections, standard precautions, safe sex.

Nursing importance

  • Treat all blood as potentially infectious; never recap needles; report needle-stick injuries at once.
  • Know your own anti-HBs status; take a booster/series if non-immune.
  • Use separate dialysis machines for HBsAg-positive patients; clean blood spills with 1% hypochlorite.

Conclusion HBV is a highly infectious, blood-borne DNA virus. Its serological markers tell us whether infection is acute, chronic or past and whether a person is immune – knowledge every nurse needs for safe practice and counselling.

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
question: Describe the structure, modes of transmission, pathogenesis and laboratory diagnosis of HIV.

diagram.caption: Structure of human immunodeficiency virus

answer_html:
Introduction Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) causes acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS) by gradually destroying the body's CD4 T-helper cells. In India the National AIDS Control Programme (NACP) provides free testing and lifelong antiretroviral therapy (ART). Nurses care for people living with HIV in every setting and must also protect themselves from occupational exposure.

A. Structure

  1. Family – Retroviridae, genus Lentivirus; two types – HIV-1 (worldwide, including India) and HIV-2 (mainly West Africa, less virulent).
  2. Shape and size – spherical, 100–120 nm.
  3. Envelope – lipid bilayer from the host cell with glycoprotein spikes: gp120 (attaches to CD4) and gp41 (helps fusion).
  4. Matrix protein (p17) lines the envelope.
  5. Capsid (core) – cone-shaped, made of p24 antigen (detected in 4th-generation tests).
  6. Inside the core: two identical copies of single-stranded RNA and enzymes – reverse transcriptase, integrase and protease (targets of ART drugs).
  7. Resistance – fragile outside the body; killed by heat (56 °C for 30 minutes), 70% alcohol, 1% hypochlorite and 2% glutaraldehyde.

B. Modes of transmission

  1. Sexual – unprotected vaginal or anal intercourse; the commonest route in India.
  2. Parenteral – transfusion of infected blood (risk over 90%), sharing needles among injecting drug users, unsafe injections.
  3. Vertical (parent-to-child) – during pregnancy, delivery or breastfeeding (25–40% without intervention; below 2% with ART).
  4. Occupational – needle-stick injury (risk about 0.3%), mucous membrane splash (about 0.09%). - HIV is not spread by hugging, sharing utensils, toilets, swimming pools or mosquito bites.

C. Pathogenesis

  1. Attachment – gp120 binds to the CD4 receptor and a co-receptor (CCR5 or CXCR4) on T-helper cells, macrophages and dendritic cells.
  2. Fusion and entry – gp41 fuses the envelope with the cell membrane.
  3. Reverse transcription – viral RNA is converted into DNA.
  4. Integration – viral DNA (provirus) is inserted into the host DNA by integrase; the cell is infected for life (latency).
  5. Replication and budding – new virions are assembled, matured by protease and released, killing CD4 cells.
  6. Course of infection
    • Acute (primary) HIV infection – 2–4 weeks after exposure; flu-like illness, high viral load, highly infectious.
    • Clinical latency (asymptomatic stage) – may last 8–10 years; slow fall of CD4 cells (normal 500–1,500 cells/µl).
    • Symptomatic stage – weight loss, chronic diarrhoea, fever, oral thrush, herpes zoster.
    • AIDS – CD4 count below 200 cells/µl or AIDS-defining illnesses: tuberculosis (commonest in India), Pneumocystis pneumonia, cryptococcal meningitis, toxoplasmosis, CMV retinitis, Kaposi's sarcoma, lymphoma.
  7. Loss of CD4 cells cripples both cell-mediated and humoral immunity, leading to opportunistic infections.

D. Laboratory diagnosis

  1. Pre-test counselling and informed consent; confidentiality as per the HIV and AIDS (Prevention and Control) Act, 2017.
  2. Specimen – venous blood (serum/plasma); dried blood spot for infants.
  3. Antibody detection
    • ELISA and rapid tests (immunochromatographic, dot-blot).
    • NACO testing strategy – a person is declared HIV-positive only when the serum is reactive in three different tests based on different principles/antigens.
    • 4th-generation tests detect both p24 antigen and antibodies, shortening the window period (time between infection and detectable antibodies, usually 3–12 weeks; about 2–4 weeks with 4th-generation tests).
    • Western blot – older confirmatory test.
  4. Virus/genome detection
    • HIV DNA PCR – for early infant diagnosis at 6 weeks (antibodies from the mother persist in babies up to 18 months, so antibody tests are not reliable).
    • Viral load (HIV RNA) – to monitor ART success (target: suppressed, below 1,000 copies/ml).
  5. Immunological monitoring – CD4 count by flow cytometry.
  6. Tests for opportunistic infections and drug resistance testing.

E. Prevention and control (in brief)

  • Safe sex (condoms), screening of all blood, sterile needles, standard precautions.
  • Prevention of parent-to-child transmission – lifelong ART for the mother, nevirapine syrup for the baby, safe delivery.
  • Post-exposure prophylaxis (TLD for 28 days) within 72 hours (ideally 2 hours).
  • "Test and treat" – ART for every diagnosed person regardless of CD4 count; UNAIDS 95-95-95 targets.

Nursing importance

  • Follow standard precautions with every patient; never recap needles.
  • Provide non-judgemental, confidential care; avoid stigma and discrimination.
  • Teach ART adherence, nutrition, prevention of opportunistic infections and safe practices.

Conclusion HIV is a fragile retrovirus that integrates into CD4 cells and slowly destroys immunity. Early testing by NACO's three-test strategy, ART and strict standard precautions have changed HIV from a fatal disease into a manageable chronic condition.

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
question: Describe the morphology, virulence factors, diseases and laboratory diagnosis of *Staphylococcus aureus*.

diagram.caption: *Staphylococcus aureus* – Gram-positive cocci in grape-like clusters and golden colonies
labels: pus cells; golden-yellow colonies on nutrient agar; beta-haemolysis on blood agar

answer_html:
Introduction Staphylococcus aureus (Greek staphyle = bunch of grapes; Latin aureus = golden) is the commonest cause of pus-forming (pyogenic) infections and one of the commonest causes of hospital-acquired infections. About 20–30% of healthy people carry it in the nose, including health workers. Its methicillin-resistant strain, MRSA, is a serious hospital problem.

A. Morphology and cultural characters

  1. Gram-positive cocci, about 1 µm in diameter, arranged in grape-like clusters.
  2. Non-motile, non-sporing; some strains have a capsule.
  3. Facultative anaerobe; grows on ordinary media at 37 °C.
  4. Nutrient agar – smooth, opaque colonies with golden-yellow pigment.
  5. Blood agar – colonies with beta (complete) haemolysis.
  6. Mannitol salt agar – a selective medium with 7.5% NaCl; S. aureus ferments mannitol and forms yellow colonies (used to screen carriers).
  7. Biochemical – catalase positive (differentiates from streptococci), coagulase positive (differentiates from S. epidermidis), DNase positive, ferments mannitol.
  8. Fairly resistant – survives drying for months and tolerates heat (60 °C for 30 minutes); killed by most disinfectants.

B. Virulence factors 1. Cell-surface factors

  • Protein A – binds the Fc part of IgG, preventing opsonisation.
  • Clumping factor (bound coagulase), capsule and teichoic acid – adhesion and resistance to phagocytosis.

2. Enzymes

  • Coagulase – clots plasma; fibrin coat protects bacteria; localises infection (abscess).
  • Catalase – destroys hydrogen peroxide made by phagocytes.
  • Hyaluronidase ("spreading factor"), staphylokinase (fibrinolysin), lipase, nuclease.
  • Penicillinase (beta-lactamase) – destroys penicillin.

3. Toxins

  • Haemolysins (alpha, beta, gamma, delta) – damage RBCs and tissue cells.
  • Leucocidin (Panton–Valentine leucocidin) – kills white cells; seen in severe skin infections and necrotising pneumonia.
  • Enterotoxins – heat-stable; cause food poisoning (vomiting within 2–6 hours of eating contaminated milk products, sweets, meat).
  • Toxic shock syndrome toxin-1 (TSST-1) – a superantigen; causes high fever, rash, shock.
  • Exfoliative toxin – causes staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome in newborns.

C. Diseases caused

  1. Skin and soft tissue – boils (furuncle), carbuncle, stye, impetigo, folliculitis, abscess, cellulitis, wound infection, breast abscess in lactating mothers.
  2. Deep infections – osteomyelitis (commonest cause) and septic arthritis, pneumonia (especially after influenza), lung abscess, endocarditis (in IV drug users and on prosthetic valves), bacteraemia and sepsis, meningitis, UTI (rare).
  3. Toxin-mediated – food poisoning, toxic shock syndrome, scalded skin syndrome.
  4. Hospital-acquired – surgical site infections, IV-line infections, ventilator pneumonia, infections in burns – often by MRSA.

D. Laboratory diagnosis

  1. Specimens – pus, wound swab, blood (for culture), sputum, CSF, urine; vomit, faeces and food remnants in food poisoning; nasal swabs from staff to detect carriers during outbreaks.
  2. Direct microscopy – Gram-stained smear of pus shows pus cells with Gram-positive cocci in clusters.
  3. Culture – blood agar and MacConkey agar (small pink colonies); mannitol salt agar for heavily contaminated specimens and carriers; blood culture in broth bottles or automated systems.
  4. Identification – colony characters, catalase test, coagulase test (slide and tube), DNase test, mannitol fermentation.
  5. Antibiotic sensitivity testing – disc diffusion; cefoxitin disc test to detect MRSA; PCR for the mecA gene.
  6. Typing (phage typing, molecular methods) to trace sources of hospital outbreaks.

E. Treatment and prevention (in brief)

  • Penicillinase-resistant penicillins (cloxacillin), cephalosporins; MRSA – vancomycin, linezolid, teicoplanin; drainage of abscesses.
  • Nasal decolonisation of carriers with mupirocin; chlorhexidine bathing in outbreaks.
  • Hand hygiene, contact precautions for MRSA, aseptic wound care and food hygiene.

Nursing importance

  • Staff with boils or skin infections should not work in OT, nursery or kitchen until treated.
  • Keep MRSA patients in a single room or cohort; use dedicated equipment (stethoscope, BP cuff).
  • Proper wound dressing technique and hand hygiene prevent cross-infection.

F. Differences between S. aureus and S. epidermidis | Feature | S. aureus | S. epidermidis | |---|---|---| | Colony pigment | Golden yellow | White | | Haemolysis on blood agar | Beta-haemolytic | Usually non-haemolytic | | Coagulase | Positive | Negative | | Mannitol fermentation | Positive | Negative | | DNase | Positive | Negative | | Normal habitat | Nose (carriers), skin | Skin (normal flora) | | Disease | Boils, abscess, osteomyelitis, sepsis, food poisoning | Infections of IV lines, prosthetic valves and joints (biofilm) |

G. MRSA in brief

  • Methicillin-resistant S. aureus carries the mecA gene, which produces an altered penicillin-binding protein (PBP2a); it is resistant to all beta-lactam antibiotics (penicillins, cephalosporins, carbapenems).
  • Hospital MRSA spreads mainly on the hands of staff and through shared equipment; community MRSA causes severe skin infections in healthy people.
  • Control: hand hygiene, screening of high-risk patients, contact precautions, decolonisation and antibiotic stewardship.

Conclusion S. aureus is a hardy, toxin-producing coccus that causes infections from simple boils to fatal sepsis. Coagulase and catalase tests identify it, and strict hand hygiene and contact precautions control its spread in hospitals.

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
question: Write a note on the laboratory diagnosis of enteric (typhoid) fever, including the Widal test.
answer_html:
Introduction Enteric fever (typhoid and paratyphoid) is caused by Salmonella enterica serotype Typhi and Paratyphi A and B. It spreads by the faeco-oral route through contaminated water and food and is common in India. Correct timing of specimens is the key to diagnosis.

1. Bacteriological diagnosis – "BASU" (first week to fourth week) | Week | Best test | |---|---| | 1st | Blood culture (positive in 70–90% in the first week) | | 2nd | Antibodies – Widal test | | 3rd | Stool culture | | 4th | Urine culture |

2. Blood culture (test of choice)

  • 5–10 ml of blood (2–3 ml in children) collected aseptically before starting antibiotics, inoculated into bile broth or brain-heart infusion broth (1:5–1:10 ratio) or automated bottles.
  • Subcultured on MacConkey agar – pale, non-lactose-fermenting colonies.
  • Bone marrow culture – most sensitive, positive even after antibiotics.
  • Clot culture is an alternative.

3. Stool and urine culture

  • Stool enriched in selenite F broth, then cultured on DCA, XLD or Wilson–Blair bismuth sulphite medium (black colonies with metallic sheen).
  • Useful to detect carriers (food handlers).

4. Identification Motile, Gram-negative bacilli; non-lactose fermenter; produce small amounts of H₂S; confirmed by slide agglutination with specific O, H and Vi antisera. Antibiotic sensitivity is tested (resistance to fluoroquinolones is common).

5. Widal test (serological)

  • Principle – a tube agglutination test that detects antibodies in the patient's serum against O (somatic) and H (flagellar) antigens of S. Typhi and H antigens of S. Paratyphi A and B (AH, BH).
  • Procedure – serial dilutions of serum (1:20 to 1:640) are mixed with standard antigen suspensions and incubated (O antigen – granular agglutination; H antigen – loose, cottony clumps).
  • Timing – antibodies appear by the end of the first week and peak in the third–fourth week.
  • Interpretation – a fourfold rise in titre in paired sera taken 7–10 days apart is diagnostic. In a single sample, titres of O ≥1:160 and H ≥1:160 are usually taken as significant in India (local baseline matters).
  • Limitations – false positives due to past infection, vaccination (raises H mainly), other infections (malaria, cross-reacting Salmonella) and the anamnestic reaction; false negatives if tested too early or after early antibiotics. A slide (rapid) Widal is less reliable.

6. Other tests

  • Typhidot / IgM rapid tests and Tubex (detect antibodies to outer-membrane proteins or O antigen).
  • Total leucocyte count – leucopenia with relative lymphocytosis; raised liver enzymes.
  • PCR in reference laboratories.

Nursing role Collect blood culture with strict asepsis before antibiotics; send promptly; label with day of fever. Teach hand washing, safe water and food hygiene; typhoid conjugate vaccine is available.

Conclusion Blood culture in the first week is the gold standard; the Widal test is supportive and must be interpreted with care.

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
question: Differentiate between endotoxin and exotoxin.
answer_html:
Introduction Toxins are poisonous products of bacteria that damage the host. Exotoxins are proteins secreted by living bacteria, while endotoxins are part of the cell wall of Gram-negative bacteria, released when the bacteria die and break up.

Differences | Feature | Exotoxin | Endotoxin | |---|---|---| | Source | Mainly Gram-positive bacteria (also some Gram-negative) | Only Gram-negative bacteria | | Location | Secreted outside the cell | Part of the outer membrane (cell wall) | | Release | By living cells | On death and lysis of cells | | Chemical nature | Protein (polypeptide) | Lipopolysaccharide (lipid A is the toxic part) | | Heat stability | Heat-labile (destroyed at 60–80 °C) – except staphylococcal enterotoxin | Heat-stable (withstands autoclaving; needs 180 °C for hours) | | Toxicity | Highly potent (microgram doses fatal) | Less potent (milligram doses) | | Action | Specific – on particular cells (nerves, gut, heart) | Non-specific – fever, shock, DIC | | Mode of action | Enzymatic; often A–B type | Releases IL-1, TNF from macrophages; activates complement and clotting | | Antigenicity | Strongly antigenic; neutralised by antitoxin | Weakly antigenic; not neutralised | | Conversion to toxoid | Yes (by formalin) – used as vaccines | No | | Vaccine available | Yes (tetanus, diphtheria toxoids) | No | | Genes | Often on plasmids or bacteriophages | Chromosomal | | Fever | Usually not | Pyrogenic – causes fever | | Detection | Neutralisation tests, Elek's test | Limulus amoebocyte lysate (LAL) test | | Examples | Tetanus, diphtheria, botulinum, cholera toxins, staphylococcal enterotoxin | E. coli, Salmonella, Klebsiella, Pseudomonas, meningococcus |

Diseases

  • Exotoxin-mediated: tetanus (spastic paralysis), botulism (flaccid paralysis), diphtheria (myocarditis), cholera (watery diarrhoea), food poisoning, toxic shock syndrome.
  • Endotoxin-mediated: fever, septic (endotoxic) shock, disseminated intravascular coagulation, Waterhouse–Friderichsen syndrome (meningococcal).

Nursing importance

  • IV fluids and injections must be pyrogen-free (tested by LAL test); a contaminated infusion can cause rigors and shock.
  • Toxoid vaccines (TT/Td, DPT) and antitoxins (antitetanus and antidiphtheria serum) are based on exotoxins.
  • Monitor Gram-negative sepsis patients closely for fever, hypotension and bleeding.

Recognising endotoxic (septic) shock at the bedside Sudden high fever with rigors, rapid pulse, falling blood pressure, cold clammy or warm flushed skin, reduced urine output and confusion in a patient with Gram-negative infection (urinary, abdominal, ventilator pneumonia) – inform the doctor at once, start the sepsis protocol (blood culture, fluids, antibiotics within 1 hour) as ordered.

Conclusion Exotoxins are potent, specific, heat-labile proteins that can be made into toxoids; endotoxins are heat-stable lipopolysaccharides that cause fever and shock.

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
question: Describe the virulence factors of *Streptococcus pyogenes* with its laboratory diagnosis.
answer_html:
Introduction Streptococcus pyogenes (group A beta-haemolytic streptococcus, GAS) causes sore throat, skin infections and serious complications such as acute rheumatic fever and post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis. They are Gram-positive cocci in chains, catalase negative and beta-haemolytic.

1. Virulence factors (a) Surface components

  • Capsule of hyaluronic acid – anti-phagocytic; non-antigenic because it resembles human tissue.
  • M protein – the most important virulence factor; prevents phagocytosis; more than 100 types; antibodies to M protein give type-specific immunity; cross-reacts with heart tissue (basis of rheumatic fever).
  • Lipoteichoic acid and F protein – adhesion to throat epithelium.

(b) Toxins

  • Streptolysin O – oxygen-labile haemolysin; strongly antigenic – the ASO (antistreptolysin O) titre is raised after infection.
  • Streptolysin S – oxygen-stable, non-antigenic; causes the beta-haemolysis on blood agar plates.
  • Pyrogenic (erythrogenic) exotoxins – cause the rash of scarlet fever; act as superantigens in streptococcal toxic shock syndrome.

(c) Enzymes

  • Streptokinase – dissolves fibrin clots, helps spread (also used as a thrombolytic drug in myocardial infarction).
  • Streptodornase (DNase) – liquefies pus; anti-DNase B antibodies rise after skin infections.
  • Hyaluronidase – "spreading factor"; NADase; C5a peptidase.

2. Diseases

  • Suppurative: pharyngitis and tonsillitis, impetigo, erysipelas, cellulitis, necrotising fasciitis, wound infection, puerperal sepsis, otitis media, scarlet fever.
  • Non-suppurative sequelae: acute rheumatic fever (2–3 weeks after sore throat) and acute glomerulonephritis (after throat or skin infection).

3. Laboratory diagnosis

  1. Specimens – throat swab (two swabs, rubbing both tonsils and posterior pharynx), pus, blood.
  2. Gram stain of pus – Gram-positive cocci in chains (not useful for throat swabs because of normal streptococci).
  3. Culture – 5% sheep blood agar, incubated at 37 °C with 5–10% CO₂ – small, pinpoint colonies with a wide zone of beta-haemolysis.
  4. Identification – catalase negative, sensitive to bacitracin, PYR positive, Lancefield group A by latex agglutination.
  5. Rapid antigen detection tests on throat swabs.
  6. Serology (for rheumatic fever and glomerulonephritis) – ASO titre above 200 IU/ml, anti-DNase B, streptozyme test.
  7. Sensitivity testing – penicillin is still uniformly effective.

Nursing importance

  • Treat sore throat in children with a full course of penicillin to prevent rheumatic fever.
  • Children with rheumatic heart disease need regular benzathine penicillin prophylaxis.
  • Strict asepsis in labour rooms prevents puerperal sepsis.

Conclusion M protein, toxins and spreading enzymes make S. pyogenes a dangerous pathogen; culture, bacitracin sensitivity and ASO titre form the basis of diagnosis.

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
question: Describe the structure of a virus with a neat diagram.

diagram.caption: Structure of a virus – naked and enveloped
labels: glycoprotein spikes (peplomers); icosahedral and helical symmetry

answer_html:
Introduction Viruses are the smallest infectious agents (20–300 nm), visible only with an electron microscope. They are not cells; they contain only one type of nucleic acid – DNA or RNA – inside a protein coat, and can multiply only inside living cells (obligate intracellular parasites).

1. Basic components

  1. Nucleic acid (genome)
    • Either DNA or RNA (never both); single- or double-stranded, linear or circular.
    • Carries the genetic information and is the infective part.
  2. Capsid
    • A protein coat that surrounds and protects the nucleic acid.
    • Made of many identical subunits called capsomeres.
    • Helps attachment to host cells and is antigenic (stimulates antibodies).
  3. Nucleocapsid – nucleic acid + capsid together.
  4. Envelope (only in some viruses)
    • A lipoprotein membrane derived from the host cell membrane during budding.
    • Carries glycoprotein spikes (peplomers) – e.g., haemagglutinin and neuraminidase of influenza virus, gp120 of HIV.
    • Enveloped viruses (HIV, HBV, influenza, herpes, SARS-CoV-2) are easily killed by alcohol, soap and detergents; naked viruses (polio, hepatitis A, rotavirus, norovirus) are more resistant.
  5. Enzymes in some viruses – reverse transcriptase (HIV), RNA polymerase (influenza, rabies).

2. Symmetry of the capsid | Type | Description | Examples | |---|---|---| | Icosahedral (cubical) | 20 triangular faces, 12 corners | Adenovirus, herpesvirus, poliovirus | | Helical | Capsomeres arranged in a spiral around the nucleic acid | Influenza, measles, rabies (bullet-shaped) | | Complex | Neither pattern | Poxvirus, bacteriophage (head and tail) |

3. Size Parvovirus about 20 nm (smallest), poliovirus 28 nm, HIV 100–120 nm, poxvirus about 300 nm (largest).

4. Steps of viral replication (in brief) Adsorption (attachment) → penetration → uncoating → synthesis of nucleic acid and proteins → assembly (maturation) → release by cell lysis or budding.

5. Differences from bacteria

  • No cell wall, no ribosomes, no metabolism of their own.
  • Not affected by antibiotics; treated by antiviral drugs and prevented by vaccines.
  • Cannot be grown on culture media; grown in cell culture, embryonated eggs or animals.

Nursing importance

  • Alcohol hand rub is effective against enveloped viruses but soap and water is better for norovirus and rotavirus outbreaks.
  • Antibiotics should not be demanded for viral colds and flu – an important health-education point.

Conclusion A virus is simply nucleic acid in a protein coat, sometimes with an envelope; its structure decides how it spreads, how it can be killed and how vaccines are designed.

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
question: Classify fungi. Describe superficial and deep mycoses with examples.
answer_html:
Introduction Fungi are eukaryotic organisms with a rigid cell wall made of chitin and a cell membrane containing ergosterol (target of antifungal drugs). Most are harmless, but some cause infections called mycoses, which are increasing among diabetic, HIV-positive and ICU patients.

1. Morphological classification | Type | Features | Examples | |---|---|---| | Yeasts | Round/oval cells that reproduce by budding | Cryptococcus neoformans | | Yeast-like fungi | Yeast cells plus pseudohyphae | Candida albicans | | Moulds (filamentous) | Branching hyphae forming a mycelium | Aspergillus, Penicillium, Mucor, dermatophytes | | Dimorphic fungi | Yeast form in tissue at 37 °C, mould at 25 °C | Histoplasma, Sporothrix, Talaromyces marneffei |

2. Clinical classification of mycoses (a) Superficial mycoses – outermost layers of skin and hair; little tissue reaction.

  • Pityriasis versicolor (Malassezia furfur) – hypopigmented or brownish scaly patches on chest and back.
  • Tinea nigra, black and white piedra (nodules on hair).

(b) Cutaneous mycoses – keratinised skin, hair and nails.

  • Dermatophytoses (ringworm/tinea) by Trichophyton, Microsporum and Epidermophyton – tinea capitis (scalp), corporis (body), cruris (groin), pedis (athlete's foot), unguium (nails). Very common in India's hot, humid climate.
  • Cutaneous candidiasis – intertrigo, nappy rash, paronychia.

(c) Subcutaneous mycoses – through injury (thorn prick) in farmers and barefoot walkers.

  • Mycetoma (Madura foot) – swelling with discharging sinuses and grains.
  • Sporotrichosis, chromoblastomycosis, rhinosporidiosis (nasal polyps; common in South India).

(d) Deep (systemic) mycoses – internal organs.

  • Endemic (primary): histoplasmosis, blastomycosis, coccidioidomycosis.
  • Opportunistic – in low immunity:
    • Candidiasis – oral thrush, oesophagitis, vaginitis, candidaemia in ICU.
    • Cryptococcosis – meningitis in HIV/AIDS.
    • Aspergillosis – allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis, aspergilloma ("fungal ball" in old TB cavity), invasive aspergillosis in neutropenia.
    • Mucormycosis ("black fungus") – rhino-orbito-cerebral infection in uncontrolled diabetes and after steroid use (seen in the COVID-19 period in India).
    • Pneumocystis pneumonia in AIDS.

3. Laboratory diagnosis (brief) KOH mount, LPCB mount, India ink (Cryptococcus), culture on Sabouraud dextrose agar, germ tube test (C. albicans), histopathology, antigen tests (cryptococcal antigen, galactomannan).

Nursing importance

  • Keep skin folds dry; avoid sharing towels and combs; complete the full course of antifungal treatment.
  • Good oral care and blood-sugar control prevent candidiasis and mucormycosis; careful handling of oxygen humidifiers with sterile water.

Conclusion Fungi range from harmless skin dwellers to life-threatening invaders; classifying them by form and depth of infection guides diagnosis and treatment.

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
question: Describe the life cycle of the malaria parasite and the laboratory diagnosis of malaria.

diagram.caption: Life cycle of *Plasmodium* in man and mosquito

answer_html:
Introduction Malaria is caused by protozoa of the genus Plasmodium – mainly P. vivax and P. falciparum in India (also P. malariae, P. ovale, P. knowlesi). It is transmitted by the bite of the infected female Anopheles mosquito. India aims to eliminate malaria by 2030.

1. Hosts

  • Definitive host – female Anopheles mosquito (sexual cycle – sporogony).
  • Intermediate host – humans (asexual cycle – schizogony).

2. Human cycle

  1. Sporozoites injected by the mosquito reach the liver within 30 minutes.
  2. Pre-erythrocytic (liver) schizogony – they multiply in liver cells for 6–15 days, forming thousands of merozoites.
  3. In P. vivax and P. ovale, some sporozoites stay dormant as hypnozoites – cause relapses months later.
  4. Erythrocytic schizogony – merozoites enter RBCs → ring form → trophozoite → schizont → RBC bursts releasing new merozoites. The rupture causes the febrile paroxysm (cold, hot and sweating stages) every 48 hours (vivax, falciparum) or 72 hours (malariae).
  5. Some merozoites develop into male and female gametocytes, which are taken up by the mosquito. P. falciparum gametocytes are crescent (banana)-shaped.

3. Mosquito cycle

  1. Gametocytes taken with the blood meal form gametes in the mosquito stomach; fertilisation gives a zygote → ookinete.
  2. Ookinete penetrates the stomach wall → oocyst, which produces thousands of sporozoites.
  3. Sporozoites migrate to the salivary glands – the mosquito becomes infective in 10–14 days.

4. Laboratory diagnosis

  1. Peripheral blood smear (gold standard) – stained with Giemsa, Leishman or JSB stain; taken preferably during fever and before antimalarial drugs; repeated every 6–12 hours if negative.
    • Thick smear – more blood, RBCs lysed; more sensitive for detecting parasites and counting parasite density.
    • Thin smear – RBCs intact; used to identify the species.
    • P. falciparum: only ring forms and crescent gametocytes, multiple and accolé rings, RBCs not enlarged.
    • P. vivax: enlarged RBCs with Schüffner's dots, all stages seen.
  2. Rapid diagnostic tests (RDT) – detect HRP-2 (P. falciparum) and pLDH (P. vivax/pan) antigens; bivalent RDT kits used by ASHAs in villages.
  3. QBC (quantitative buffy coat) with acridine orange, PCR (species and low-density infection).
  4. Supportive – anaemia, thrombocytopenia, raised bilirubin.

Nursing importance Collect smears before giving drugs; ensure complete radical treatment (primaquine for 14 days in vivax after G6PD check); teach use of mosquito nets and elimination of breeding sites.

Conclusion Understanding the two-host life cycle explains malaria's fever pattern, relapses and the points where transmission can be broken.

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
question: Describe the morphology, pathogenesis and laboratory diagnosis of *Vibrio cholerae*.
answer_html:
Introduction Vibrio cholerae causes cholera, an acute diarrhoeal disease that can kill within hours by dehydration. It spreads through contaminated water and food, especially during floods and in crowded areas with poor sanitation. Serogroups O1 (biotypes classical and El Tor) and O139 (Bengal) cause epidemics.

1. Morphology and characters

  • Comma-shaped, curved Gram-negative rods, 1.5–3 µm long.
  • Actively motile with a single polar flagellum – darting ("shooting star") motility in hanging drop.
  • Non-sporing; oxidase positive.
  • Grows in alkaline pH (8.2–8.6); this is used in enrichment and selective media.
  • TCBS agar – yellow colonies (sucrose fermenting); alkaline peptone water – enrichment.

2. Pathogenesis

  1. Ingestion of a large number of vibrios (10⁸; fewer if stomach acid is low).
  2. Survivors reach the small intestine, attach to the mucosa by toxin-coregulated pili and multiply (no invasion).
  3. They produce cholera toxin (enterotoxin) – the B subunit binds to intestinal cells, the A subunit activates adenylate cyclase → raised cyclic AMP.
  4. This causes massive secretion of chloride and water and stops sodium absorption → profuse painless watery diarrhoea – "rice-water stools" with a fishy smell, up to 10–20 litres a day.
  5. Results: severe dehydration, hypovolaemic shock, acidosis, hypokalaemia (muscle cramps), kidney failure; death if untreated. - Incubation period: a few hours to 5 days.

3. Laboratory diagnosis

  1. Specimen – rice-water stool or rectal swab, collected before antibiotics.
  2. Transport – Venkatraman–Ramakrishnan (VR) medium or Cary–Blair medium if delay is expected.
  3. Direct microscopy – hanging drop shows darting motility, which stops on adding specific O1 antiserum (rapid diagnosis); Gram stain shows curved rods in "fish-in-stream" pattern.
  4. Enrichment in alkaline peptone water for 6–8 hours, then subculture.
  5. Culture – TCBS (yellow colonies) and MacConkey agar.
  6. Identification – oxidase test, string test, biochemical tests and slide agglutination with polyvalent O1 and O139 antisera; serotyping (Ogawa, Inaba).
  7. Rapid dipstick tests in outbreaks; antibiotic sensitivity testing.

4. Treatment and prevention (in brief)

  • Rehydration is life-saving – low-osmolarity ORS; IV Ringer's lactate for severe dehydration; antibiotics (doxycycline, azithromycin) shorten illness; zinc for children.
  • Safe drinking water (boiling, chlorination), sanitation, hand washing, food hygiene, oral cholera vaccine, notification to IDSP.

Nursing importance Record intake and output accurately (cholera cot), monitor signs of dehydration, disinfect stools and soiled linen with hypochlorite, and educate families about ORS.

Conclusion Cholera is a toxin-mediated, non-invasive disease where dehydration kills; rapid microscopy and culture on TCBS confirm it, and prompt rehydration saves lives.

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
question: Write a note on *Clostridium tetani*.
answer_html:
Introduction Clostridium tetani causes tetanus ("lockjaw"), a dangerous disease of muscle spasms caused by its powerful neurotoxin. Its spores are found everywhere in soil, dust and animal faeces. Tetanus is entirely preventable by immunisation; India was validated for maternal and neonatal tetanus elimination in 2015.

1. Morphology and characters

  • Long, slender Gram-positive bacillus (may appear Gram-variable in old cultures).
  • Terminal, round, bulging spores – giving a "drumstick" appearance.
  • Motile (peritrichous flagella); strict anaerobe.
  • Grows in Robertson's cooked meat broth; on blood agar shows a fine swarming growth.
  • Spores are highly resistant – survive in soil for years; killed by autoclaving.

2. Toxins

  • Tetanospasmin (neurotoxin) – one of the most potent toxins known; heat-labile; plasmid-coded.
  • It travels up the nerves to the spinal cord and brainstem and blocks the release of inhibitory transmitters (GABA and glycine) → uncontrolled muscle contraction (spastic paralysis).
  • Tetanolysin – a haemolysin of uncertain importance.

3. Pathogenesis and clinical features

  • Portal of entry: deep puncture wounds (nails, thorns), lacerations, burns, compound fractures, unclean delivery or abortion, umbilical stump (neonatal tetanus), chronic ear infection, unsterile injections.
  • Spores germinate in dead, anaerobic tissue; the organism stays local but the toxin spreads.
  • Incubation period 3–21 days (usually 6–10); shorter IP means worse prognosis.
  • Features: trismus (lockjaw), risus sardonicus (sardonic smile), neck stiffness, opisthotonus (arched back), painful generalised spasms triggered by noise, light or touch, dysphagia, autonomic instability. Consciousness is retained.
  • Neonatal tetanus – baby stops sucking on day 3–10, then has spasms.

4. Laboratory diagnosis

  • Diagnosis is mainly clinical.
  • Gram stain of wound material may show drumstick bacilli (not reliable).
  • Anaerobic culture and toxigenicity test in mice (rarely needed).

5. Treatment and prevention

  • Wound care – thorough cleaning and debridement.
  • Human tetanus immunoglobulin (or antitetanus serum after test dose) to neutralise free toxin; metronidazole or penicillin.
  • Sedation and muscle relaxants (diazepam), airway care, nutrition.
  • Active immunisation – DPT/pentavalent in infancy, boosters, Td at 10 and 16 years and Td in pregnancy; Td after injuries as per schedule.
  • Clean delivery practices ("the cleans": hands, surface, blade, cord tie, cord care).

Nursing care Nurse the patient in a quiet, dark room, minimise handling, keep suction and resuscitation ready, prevent aspiration, monitor breathing and give care during periods of sedation.

Conclusion C. tetani is a spore-forming anaerobe whose neurotoxin causes fatal spasms; toxoid immunisation and clean wound and delivery care prevent it.

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
question: Explain the role of rodents and vectors in the transmission of disease.
answer_html:
Introduction A vector is a living carrier, usually an arthropod (insect), that transmits infectious agents from one host to another. Rodents (rats, mice) act as reservoirs and carry vectors such as fleas and mites. Vector-borne diseases like malaria and dengue are major public health problems in India and are controlled under the National Center for Vector Borne Diseases Control (NCVBDC).

1. Types of transmission by vectors

  • Mechanical – the vector simply carries germs on its legs or body (housefly carrying typhoid bacilli).
  • Biological – the organism multiplies or develops inside the vector before it becomes infective (malaria parasite in Anopheles).

2. Important vectors and diseases | Vector | Diseases transmitted | |---|---| | Anopheles mosquito | Malaria | | Aedes aegypti/albopictus | Dengue, chikungunya, Zika, yellow fever | | Culex mosquito | Lymphatic filariasis, Japanese encephalitis | | Housefly | Typhoid, cholera, dysentery, diarrhoea, trachoma, conjunctivitis (mechanical) | | Cockroach | Diarrhoeal diseases (mechanical) | | Sandfly (Phlebotomus) | Kala-azar (visceral leishmaniasis) | | Rat flea (Xenopsylla cheopis) | Plague, murine typhus | | Body louse | Epidemic typhus, relapsing fever, trench fever | | Trombiculid mite (chigger) | Scrub typhus | | Itch mite | Scabies | | Ticks | Kyasanur forest disease (Karnataka), tick typhus, relapsing fever |

3. Role of rodents

  • Plague – rats harbour Yersinia pestis; rat fleas transmit it to humans.
  • Leptospirosis – rats excrete leptospires in urine that contaminates flood water and fields (common in Maharashtra, Kerala, Gujarat during monsoon).
  • Scrub typhus – rodents carry infected mites.
  • Rat-bite fever, salmonellosis (food contamination), hantavirus infections.
  • Rodents also damage food stores and hospital wiring.

4. Control measures

  1. Environmental – remove stagnant water (coolers, tyres, pots), weekly "dry day", proper drainage, waste disposal, covering water containers.
  2. Chemical – larvicides (temephos), indoor residual spraying, fogging during outbreaks, insecticide-treated long-lasting nets.
  3. Biological – larvivorous fish (Gambusia, guppy) in ponds.
  4. Personal protection – bed nets, repellents, full-sleeved clothing.
  5. Rodent control – rat-proof buildings and food stores, traps and poison baits; in plague areas kill fleas first before killing rats (otherwise fleas move to humans).
  6. Health education and community participation.

Nursing role Hospital pest control (screens, closed bins), early case detection and reporting, IEC on source reduction, and care of patients with vector-borne diseases.

Conclusion Vectors and rodents link the environment to human disease; controlling them is often the cheapest and most effective way to prevent infection.

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
question: Describe the life cycle and laboratory diagnosis of *Entamoeba histolytica*.

diagram.caption: Life cycle of *Entamoeba histolytica*

answer_html:
Introduction Entamoeba histolytica is an intestinal protozoan that causes amoebiasis – amoebic dysentery and amoebic liver abscess. It is common in India where sanitation is poor. Only one host (man) is needed to complete its life cycle.

1. Forms

  • Trophozoite – active, feeding form, 15–40 µm; one nucleus with a central karyosome; moves by pseudopodia; contains ingested red blood cells (diagnostic of E. histolytica).
  • Cyst – resistant, infective form, 10–15 µm, round, with 1–4 nuclei; the mature quadrinucleate cyst is infective; contains chromatoid bars.

2. Life cycle

  1. Infection – by swallowing mature quadrinucleate cysts in contaminated food, water or from dirty hands (faeco-oral route); flies help spread.
  2. Excystation – in the lower small intestine the cyst wall dissolves and eight small trophozoites are formed.
  3. Colonisation – trophozoites reach the large intestine (caecum, colon) and multiply by binary fission.
  4. Invasion – in some people they invade the mucosa using enzymes and form flask-shaped ulcers (narrow neck, broad base) → amoebic dysentery (stools with mucus and blood).
  5. Spread – through the portal vein to the liver (amoebic liver abscess with "anchovy sauce" pus), rarely to lungs and brain.
  6. Encystation – in the lumen, trophozoites round up and form cysts, which are passed in stool and survive in the environment for weeks. Asymptomatic cyst passers are the main source of infection.

3. Laboratory diagnosis

  1. Stool examination
    • Fresh stool (examined within 1 hour) – saline mount shows motile trophozoites with ingested RBCs; iodine mount shows cysts with nuclei.
    • Stool in dysentery: small amount, offensive, acidic, with mucus and blood; few pus cells, Charcot–Leyden crystals.
    • Repeat examination on three consecutive days; concentration techniques (formol–ether).
  2. Stool antigen detection (ELISA) and PCR – distinguish E. histolytica from the harmless E. dispar.
  3. Culture (Boeck–Drbohlav, Robinson's medium) – research use.
  4. Serology – antibodies (ELISA, IHA) are high in amoebic liver abscess.
  5. Imaging and aspiration – ultrasound of the liver; aspirated pus is chocolate-brown, with trophozoites at the abscess wall.
  6. Sigmoidoscopy – ulcers; scrapings show trophozoites.

4. Treatment and prevention (in brief) Metronidazole or tinidazole followed by a luminal drug (diloxanide furoate, paromomycin); boiling water (cysts resist chlorine), sanitary latrines, hand washing, food hygiene and screening of food handlers.

Nursing role Collect stool in a clean, wide-mouthed container and send immediately (trophozoites die quickly); teach hand washing and safe water.

Conclusion E. histolytica spreads by cysts and harms by invasive trophozoites; fresh stool examination is the simplest way to diagnose it.

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
question: What is an opportunistic infection? Give examples.
answer_html:
Definition An opportunistic infection is an infection caused by organisms of low virulence (often normal flora or environmental microbes) that rarely cause disease in healthy people but do so when the host's immunity is lowered.

Predisposing conditions HIV/AIDS, cancer and chemotherapy, organ transplant, long-term steroids, diabetes, extremes of age, burns, malnutrition and invasive devices.

Examples

  • Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia, oral/oesophageal candidiasis, cryptococcal meningitis, toxoplasmosis, CMV retinitis (in AIDS)
  • Tuberculosis – commonest in HIV patients in India
  • Pseudomonas in burns, Aspergillus in neutropenia, mucormycosis in uncontrolled diabetes

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
question: What are the modes of transmission of HIV?
answer_html:
Modes of transmission of HIV

  1. Sexual – unprotected vaginal, anal or oral intercourse with an infected person (commonest).
  2. Blood and blood products – transfusion of unscreened blood (risk over 90%).
  3. Sharing needles and syringes – injecting drug users; unsafe injections.
  4. Parent-to-child – during pregnancy, delivery or breastfeeding.
  5. Occupational – needle-stick injury (about 0.3%) or splash on mucous membranes in health workers.
  6. Organ and tissue transplantation, artificial insemination (if donors are not screened).

HIV is not transmitted by touching, hugging, sharing food, utensils or toilets, or by mosquitoes.

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
question: What are Negri bodies?
answer_html:
Negri bodies are eosinophilic (pink), round or oval intracytoplasmic inclusion bodies found in the nerve cells of the brain of humans and animals that die of rabies. They were described by Adelchi Negri (1903).

Key points

  • Seen mainly in the hippocampus (Ammon's horn) and Purkinje cells of the cerebellum.
  • Demonstrated by Seller's stain or H&E stain; contain viral antigen.
  • Their presence is diagnostic of rabies (post-mortem), though absence does not rule it out; fluorescent antibody testing is more sensitive.
  • Rabies virus is a bullet-shaped RNA virus (Rhabdoviridae).

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
question: Name the organisms causing diarrhoea.
answer_html:
Organisms causing diarrhoea Bacteria

  • Vibrio cholerae (cholera), diarrhoeagenic E. coli (ETEC, EPEC, EHEC), Shigella (bacillary dysentery), non-typhoidal Salmonella, Campylobacter jejuni, Clostridioides difficile (antibiotic-associated), toxins of S. aureus and Bacillus cereus (food poisoning).

Viruses

  • Rotavirus (commonest cause of severe diarrhoea in children under 5; prevented by rotavirus vaccine in UIP), norovirus, adenovirus 40/41, astrovirus.

Parasites

  • Giardia lamblia, Entamoeba histolytica, Cryptosporidium (in HIV), Cyclospora.

Helminths – Strongyloides, Trichuris (dysentery in heavy infection). Nursing point: collect stool before antibiotics, send fresh, and give ORS and zinc to children.

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
question: What are prions? Give examples of prion diseases.
answer_html:
Prions (proteinaceous infectious particles) are infectious agents made only of abnormally folded protein, without any nucleic acid. The abnormal prion protein converts normal brain proteins into the abnormal form, causing slow, fatal spongiform encephalopathies.

Examples

  • Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease (CJD) and variant CJD in humans
  • Kuru (Papua New Guinea), fatal familial insomnia
  • Mad cow disease (bovine spongiform encephalopathy), scrapie in sheep

Importance: prions resist ordinary sterilisation; instruments used on suspected cases need special treatment (e.g., autoclaving at 134 °C for 18 minutes with strong alkali) or disposal.

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
unit_title: Section A: Immunity, Hypersensitivity and Immunisation
question: Define and classify immunity with examples. Explain the mechanism of specific (acquired) immunity.

diagram.caption: Classification of immunity (flow chart)

answer_html:
Introduction Every day our body meets millions of microbes, yet we fall ill only occasionally. This protection is called immunity. A nurse uses the knowledge of immunity when she immunises a child, gives anti-rabies serum, cares for a patient with HIV or protects a cancer patient on chemotherapy.

Definition (1 mark) Immunity is the resistance of the body to infection and to the harmful effects of foreign substances (antigens), brought about by the combined action of physical barriers, cells and chemical substances of the immune system.

A. Classification of immunity (4 marks)

1. Innate (natural, native, non-specific) immunity Present from birth; does not depend on previous contact with the microbe; acts quickly but is not specific and has no memory.

  • (a) Species immunity – humans do not get many animal diseases (e.g., rinderpest, canine distemper).
  • (b) Racial immunity – some races resist certain diseases (e.g., people with sickle-cell trait resist falciparum malaria).
  • (c) Individual immunity – differs from person to person due to genetics, age, nutrition and hormones.

Mechanisms of innate immunity

  1. Anatomical barriers – intact skin, mucous membranes, cilia of the respiratory tract, coughing, sneezing, flow of urine and tears.
  2. Physiological and chemical barriers – acidity of the stomach (pH 1–2) and vagina, fatty acids of skin, lysozyme in tears and saliva, mucus, normal body temperature and fever.
  3. Normal flora – prevents colonisation by pathogens.
  4. Cellular defence – phagocytes (neutrophils, macrophages) engulf and kill microbes; natural killer (NK) cells kill virus-infected and tumour cells.
  5. Humoral factors – complement, interferons (antiviral), acute-phase proteins such as C-reactive protein, defensins.
  6. Inflammation – redness, heat, swelling and pain bring cells and fluid to the site.

2. Acquired (adaptive, specific) immunity Develops during life after exposure to an antigen; specific, has memory, and is stronger on repeated exposure.

(a) Active immunity – produced by the person's own immune system after antigenic stimulus.

  • Natural active – after clinical or subclinical infection (e.g., lifelong immunity after measles or chickenpox).
  • Artificial active – after vaccination (BCG, OPV, MR, hepatitis B, tetanus toxoid).

(b) Passive immunity – ready-made antibodies are transferred; no active role of the host.

  • Natural passive – maternal IgG crossing the placenta and IgA in breast milk (colostrum) protect the baby for the first few months.
  • Artificial passive – injection of antibodies: anti-rabies immunoglobulin, tetanus immunoglobulin, hepatitis B immunoglobulin, anti-snake venom, antidiphtheria serum.

(c) Other types

  • Local (mucosal) immunity – secretory IgA in gut and respiratory tract (oral polio vaccine induces it).
  • Herd immunity – protection of a community when a large proportion is immune.
  • Combined (active + passive) – e.g., rabies immunoglobulin with rabies vaccine; HBIG with hepatitis B vaccine for babies of HBsAg-positive mothers.

Comparison of active and passive immunity | Feature | Active immunity | Passive immunity | |---|---|---| | Produced by | Host's own immune system | Ready-made antibodies | | Onset | Slow (after a lag of 1–2 weeks) | Immediate | | Duration | Long-lasting (years) | Short (weeks to months) | | Memory | Present; booster effect | Absent | | Negative phase | May occur | Absent | | Use | Prophylaxis (prevention) | Immediate protection, treatment | | Example | Vaccines | Immunoglobulins, antisera, maternal antibodies |

B. Mechanism of specific (acquired) immunity (5 marks) Specific immunity is carried out by lymphocytes: B lymphocytes (mature in bone marrow) and T lymphocytes (mature in the thymus). It has two arms – humoral and cell-mediated – which work together.

Step 1 – Entry and recognition of antigen

  • Microbes or foreign substances (antigens) enter the body.
  • Antigen-presenting cells (APCs) – dendritic cells, macrophages and B cells – engulf the antigen, break it into small peptides and present them on MHC molecules on their surface.
  • MHC class II presents to CD4 T-helper cells; MHC class I presents to CD8 cytotoxic T cells.

Step 2 – Activation and clonal expansion

  • T-helper cells recognise the antigen–MHC complex and become activated; they release cytokines (interleukin-2, interferon-gamma, IL-4).
  • Only lymphocytes carrying receptors for that particular antigen are selected and multiply – clonal selection and expansion.

Step 3a – Humoral (antibody-mediated) immunity

  • Activated B cells, helped by T-helper cells, multiply and change into plasma cells, which secrete antibodies (immunoglobulins) into blood and body fluids.
  • Functions of antibodies:
    1. Neutralisation of toxins and viruses (e.g., antitetanus antibodies).
    2. Opsonisation – coating bacteria so phagocytes engulf them easily.
    3. Activation of complement – lysis of bacteria.
    4. Agglutination and precipitation of antigens.
    5. Antibody-dependent cell-mediated cytotoxicity (ADCC) by NK cells.
    6. Prevention of attachment of microbes to mucosa (secretory IgA).
  • Most effective against extracellular bacteria, toxins and viruses in blood.

Step 3b – Cell-mediated immunity (CMI)

  • CD8 cytotoxic T cells kill virus-infected cells, tumour cells and graft cells by releasing perforin and granzymes.
  • CD4 Th1 cells release cytokines that activate macrophages to kill intracellular organisms (TB, leprosy, Salmonella, fungi).
  • Responsible for delayed hypersensitivity (Mantoux reaction), graft rejection and tumour immunity.
  • Regulatory T cells control and switch off the response.

Step 4 – Memory

  • Some B and T cells become long-living memory cells. On second contact they respond faster and stronger – the basis of booster doses of vaccines.

Primary versus secondary immune response | Feature | Primary response | Secondary response | |---|---|---| | Lag period | Long (7–10 days) | Short (1–3 days) | | Main antibody | IgM | IgG | | Antibody level | Low, short-lived | High, prolonged | | Affinity of antibody | Low | High | | Antigen needed | Larger dose | Small dose |

Humoral versus cell-mediated immunity | Feature | Humoral | Cell-mediated | |---|---|---| | Cells | B cells → plasma cells | T cells | | Effector | Antibodies | Sensitised T cells, cytokines | | Acts against | Extracellular bacteria, toxins | Intracellular organisms, viruses, tumours | | Transfer | By serum | By lymphocytes | | Example | Protection after tetanus toxoid | Immunity in TB; Mantoux test |

Nursing importance

  • Follow the vaccination schedule and give boosters at the right time.
  • Protect patients with low immunity (HIV, chemotherapy, steroids, malnutrition) from infection – protective isolation, hand hygiene, safe food.
  • Encourage breastfeeding and colostrum for passive immunity of newborns.
  • Give immunoglobulins (rabies, tetanus, hepatitis B) promptly after exposure.

Conclusion Immunity has an innate, ready-to-act component and an acquired, specific component with memory. Through antibodies and sensitised T cells, specific immunity clears infection and provides the lasting protection that vaccines take advantage of.

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
unit_title: Section A: Immunity, Hypersensitivity and Immunisation
question: Define hypersensitivity. Describe the types of hypersensitivity reactions with examples.

diagram.caption: Mechanisms of the four types of hypersensitivity (Gell and Coombs)
labels: type I IgE on mast cell releasing histamine; type II antibody against cell surface with complement lysis; type III immune complexes deposited in vessel wall; type IV sensitised T cells and macrophages

answer_html:
Introduction The immune system normally protects us, but sometimes it reacts in an exaggerated or inappropriate way to harmless substances (pollen, drugs, food) or to infection, and damages our own tissues. Such harmful immune reactions are called hypersensitivity reactions. Nurses meet them every day – a patient reacting to an antibiotic injection, an asthmatic attack, a transfusion reaction or a positive Mantoux test.

Definition Hypersensitivity is an exaggerated or inappropriate immune response to an antigen (called an allergen) in a previously sensitised person, which results in tissue damage or disease.

Basic requirements

  • First exposure (sensitising dose) – no symptoms, but antibodies or sensitised T cells are formed.
  • Second exposure (shocking/eliciting dose) – reaction occurs.

Classification

  • Based on time: immediate (antibody-mediated; minutes to hours) and delayed (cell-mediated; 24–72 hours).
  • Gell and Coombs classification (1963) – four types; a fifth (stimulatory) type is sometimes added.

1. Type I – Anaphylactic (immediate) hypersensitivity

  • Mediated by IgE antibodies, which are fixed to mast cells and basophils.
  • Mechanism: on re-exposure, the allergen cross-links IgE on mast cells → degranulation → release of histamine, leukotrienes, prostaglandins, platelet-activating factor → vasodilation, increased capillary permeability, smooth-muscle contraction (bronchospasm), mucus secretion.
  • Time: within 2–30 minutes.
  • Examples
    • Systemic anaphylaxis – after penicillin injection, bee sting, peanut, anti-snake venom, contrast dye: hypotension, laryngeal oedema, bronchospasm, shock.
    • Local (atopic) reactions – allergic rhinitis (hay fever), bronchial asthma, urticaria, food allergy, atopic dermatitis.
  • Tests: skin-prick test, intradermal test dose before ASV or antiserum, serum IgE (RAST).
  • Treatment: adrenaline 0.5 mg IM (1:1000) in anaphylaxis, antihistamines, steroids, bronchodilators; avoid the allergen; desensitisation.

2. Type II – Cytotoxic (antibody-dependent) hypersensitivity

  • IgG or IgM antibodies react with antigens on the surface of cells (or tissues).
  • Mechanism: cell destruction by complement-mediated lysis, opsonisation and phagocytosis, or ADCC by NK cells.
  • Time: minutes to hours.
  • Examples
    • Incompatible (ABO) blood transfusion reaction – haemolysis, fever, haemoglobinuria, shock.
    • Haemolytic disease of the newborn (Rh incompatibility) – maternal anti-D IgG destroys fetal RBCs (prevented by anti-D immunoglobulin).
    • Autoimmune haemolytic anaemia, drug-induced thrombocytopenia.
    • Goodpasture's syndrome, myasthenia gravis, acute rheumatic fever (antibodies cross-reacting with heart).
  • Test: Coombs (antiglobulin) test.

3. Type III – Immune-complex hypersensitivity

  • Antigen–antibody (IgG) complexes form in the circulation or tissues and get deposited in blood-vessel walls, joints, kidneys and skin.
  • Mechanism: complexes activate complement → attract neutrophils → release of enzymes → vasculitis and tissue damage.
  • Time: 4–10 hours (Arthus), 1–2 weeks (serum sickness).
  • Examples
    • Arthus reaction – local oedema and necrosis at the site of repeated injections of antigen (e.g., frequent tetanus toxoid boosters).
    • Serum sickness – fever, rash, joint pain, lymphadenopathy 7–14 days after animal serum (ASV, ATS).
    • Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis, systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), rheumatoid arthritis, hypersensitivity pneumonitis (farmer's lung).

4. Type IV – Delayed (cell-mediated) hypersensitivity

  • No antibodies involved; mediated by sensitised T lymphocytes (CD4 Th1 and CD8 cells) and macrophages.
  • Mechanism: sensitised T cells meet the antigen and release cytokines that attract and activate macrophages → inflammation, induration, granuloma.
  • Time: 24–72 hours.
  • Examples
    • Tuberculin (Mantoux) reaction – induration at 48–72 hours.
    • Contact dermatitis – to nickel (jewellery), latex gloves, hair dye, cosmetics, plants.
    • Granulomatous reactions – tuberculosis, leprosy, sarcoidosis.
    • Graft (transplant) rejection, type 1 diabetes, multiple sclerosis.
  • Test: patch test for contact dermatitis; tuberculin test.

5. Type V – Stimulatory hypersensitivity (sometimes included)

  • Antibodies stimulate a receptor instead of destroying the cell – e.g., Graves' disease (antibodies stimulate TSH receptors → hyperthyroidism).

Summary table | Feature | Type I | Type II | Type III | Type IV | |---|---|---|---|---| | Name | Anaphylactic | Cytotoxic | Immune complex | Delayed / cell-mediated | | Mediator | IgE, mast cells | IgG/IgM, complement | IgG–antigen complexes | T cells, macrophages | | Onset | Minutes | Minutes–hours | Hours–days | 24–72 hours | | Transfer | By serum | By serum | By serum | By lymphocytes | | Examples | Anaphylaxis, asthma, urticaria | Transfusion reaction, Rh disease | Serum sickness, SLE, PSGN | Mantoux, contact dermatitis, graft rejection |

Nursing responsibilities

  1. Take a careful allergy history before giving any drug, blood or serum; record allergies prominently and use an allergy wristband.
  2. Give a test dose where advised (e.g., before antisera) and observe the patient for 20–30 minutes after injections of high-risk drugs.
  3. Keep an anaphylaxis kit (adrenaline, hydrocortisone, antihistamine, oxygen, airway) ready in every ward and immunisation session.
  4. During blood transfusion – correct identification, cross-matching, slow start and close observation in the first 15 minutes.
  5. Give anti-D immunoglobulin to Rh-negative mothers after delivery of an Rh-positive baby.
  6. Use latex-free gloves for latex-allergic patients and staff.
  7. Read Mantoux tests at 48–72 hours correctly.

Conclusion Hypersensitivity is the immune system's "friendly fire". Knowing the four types helps the nurse anticipate, prevent and promptly manage reactions ranging from a mild rash to life-threatening anaphylaxis.

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
unit_title: Section A: Immunity, Hypersensitivity and Immunisation
question: Explain antigen–antibody reactions – their general features, types and applications. List the serological tests with an example for each type.

diagram.caption: Principle of indirect ELISA
labels: colour change read by ELISA reader

answer_html:
Introduction When an antigen meets its specific antibody, they combine firmly like a lock and key. These antigen–antibody (Ag–Ab) reactions occur inside the body (protecting us) and can be reproduced in the laboratory. Tests based on them are called serological tests because they usually use serum. They are used to diagnose infections (typhoid, syphilis, HIV, hepatitis B, dengue), to group blood and to detect pregnancy.

A. General features of antigen–antibody reactions

  1. Specificity – an antibody reacts only with the antigen that stimulated it (or a very similar one – cross-reaction).
  2. Binding is by weak, non-covalent forces (hydrogen bonds, van der Waals and electrostatic forces) between the epitope of the antigen and the paratope of the antibody; the reaction is reversible.
  3. Whole molecules react, not fragments.
  4. Optimal proportions – visible reactions (precipitation, agglutination) occur best when antigen and antibody are in optimal ratio (zone of equivalence). Excess antibody gives the prozone phenomenon (false-negative); excess antigen gives the postzone.
  5. Reactions occur in two stages – primary (invisible combination) and secondary (visible effects such as clumping, precipitation, lysis).
  6. Can be qualitative (positive/negative) or quantitative (titre – the highest dilution of serum giving a reaction, e.g., Widal 1:160).
  7. Measurement depends on sensitivity (ability to detect small amounts) and specificity (no false positives).

B. Types of antigen–antibody reactions, with tests

1. Precipitation

  • A soluble antigen reacts with its antibody to form a visible precipitate.
  • Flocculation – precipitate remains suspended as floccules: VDRL test for syphilis.
  • Immunodiffusion in gel – Elek's test (toxigenicity of diphtheria bacilli), Ouchterlony double diffusion, single radial immunodiffusion (measuring immunoglobulin levels).
  • Immunoelectrophoresis, counter-current immunoelectrophoresis.

2. Agglutination

  • A particulate (cellular) antigen reacts with antibody to form visible clumps.
  • Slide agglutination – blood grouping, serotyping of Salmonella and Vibrio.
  • Tube agglutination – Widal test (typhoid), Weil–Felix test (rickettsial fever), standard agglutination test (brucellosis).
  • Passive (indirect) agglutination – antigen coated on latex or RBCs: latex tests for CRP, RA factor, ASO; TPHA for syphilis.
  • Coombs (antiglobulin) test – direct (antibody-coated RBCs in Rh disease) and indirect (cross-matching).

3. Complement fixation test (CFT)

  • Antigen–antibody complex "fixes" (uses up) complement; the absence of free complement is shown by the indicator system (sheep RBCs + haemolysin) – no haemolysis = positive.
  • Example: Wassermann reaction (old test for syphilis), CFT for some viral and rickettsial infections.

4. Neutralisation

  • Antibody neutralises the biological activity of a toxin or virus.
  • ASO test (antistreptolysin O neutralises haemolysis), Schick test (diphtheria immunity – historical), virus neutralisation tests, Nagler reaction (C. perfringens).

5. Opsonisation and immune adherence – coating of bacteria to promote phagocytosis (in vivo).

6. Labelled antibody techniques (most widely used today)

  • Immunofluorescence (IF) – antibody tagged with a fluorescent dye:
    • Direct IF – detects antigen in tissue (rabies antigen in corneal smear/brain).
    • Indirect IF – detects antibodies (FTA-ABS for syphilis, ANA for SLE).
  • Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) – antibody or antigen labelled with an enzyme; colour change on adding substrate. Examples: HIV antibody, HBsAg, anti-HCV, dengue NS1 and IgM, typhoid IgM. Highly sensitive; used in blood-bank screening.
  • Radioimmunoassay (RIA) – radioactive label; hormones, drug levels.
  • Chemiluminescence immunoassay (CLIA) – light-emitting label; automated tests for thyroid hormones, hepatitis markers.
  • Western blot (immunoblot) – confirmation of HIV (older practice).
  • Immunochromatographic (rapid/lateral flow) tests – card or strip tests read in 15–20 minutes: malaria antigen (HRP-2, pLDH), HIV, HBsAg, dengue, urine pregnancy test (hCG), COVID-19 antigen.

7. Other techniques

  • Flow cytometry – counting CD4 cells in HIV.
  • Immunoelectron microscopy – viruses.

Summary table – serological tests with examples | Type of reaction | Example test | Disease/use | |---|---|---| | Precipitation (flocculation) | VDRL, RPR | Syphilis | | Gel precipitation | Elek's test | Diphtheria toxin | | Agglutination (tube) | Widal | Typhoid | | Agglutination (slide) | Blood grouping | Transfusion | | Passive agglutination | TPHA, latex CRP/RA | Syphilis, inflammation, arthritis | | Antiglobulin | Coombs test | Rh disease, cross-match | | Complement fixation | Wassermann reaction | Syphilis (historic) | | Neutralisation | ASO titre | Rheumatic fever | | Immunofluorescence | FTA-ABS, rabies DFA | Syphilis, rabies | | ELISA | HIV, HBsAg, dengue IgM | Viral infections | | Rapid immunochromatography | Malaria RDT, pregnancy test | Bedside diagnosis |

C. Applications

  1. Diagnosis of infections – detecting antibodies (Widal, VDRL, HIV) or antigens (HBsAg, NS1, malaria antigen).
  2. Identification of organisms – serotyping of isolates (Salmonella, Vibrio, Shigella).
  3. Blood banking – grouping, cross-matching, screening donated blood for HIV, HBV, HCV, syphilis and malaria.
  4. Assessing immunity – anti-HBs titre after vaccination, rubella antibodies.
  5. Diagnosis of autoimmune diseases – RA factor, ANA.
  6. Measurement of hormones and drugs – hCG (pregnancy), thyroid hormones.
  7. Epidemiological surveys – seroprevalence studies (e.g., COVID-19 serosurveys).
  8. Forensic medicine – identifying bloodstains.

Nursing importance

  • Collect paired sera (acute and convalescent, 7–14 days apart) when the doctor needs to show a rising titre.
