  • Use plain (red-top) tubes for serum; avoid haemolysis; label and transport promptly; store serum at 4 °C if delayed.
  • Know the window period – a negative antibody test soon after exposure does not exclude infection.
  • Interpret rapid test results correctly and confirm positives as per national guidelines.

Conclusion Antigen–antibody reactions are specific, reversible combinations that can be seen in the laboratory as precipitation, agglutination, lysis or colour change. They form the basis of most diagnostic serological tests used in hospitals, blood banks and community programmes.

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
unit_title: Section A: Immunity, Hypersensitivity and Immunisation
question: Describe the structure, types and functions of immunoglobulins.

diagram.caption: Basic structure of an immunoglobulin (IgG) molecule

answer_html:
Definition Immunoglobulins (Ig) are glycoprotein molecules produced by plasma cells in response to an antigen; they react specifically with that antigen. All antibodies are immunoglobulins. They form about 20% of plasma proteins (gamma-globulin fraction).

1. Basic structure (Y-shaped monomer)

  1. Four polypeptide chains – two identical heavy (H) chains and two identical light (L) chains, joined by disulphide bonds.
  2. Light chains are of two types – kappa (κ) or lambda (λ); a molecule has only one type.
  3. Heavy chains decide the class: gamma (IgG), alpha (IgA), mu (IgM), delta (IgD), epsilon (IgE).
  4. Each chain has a variable region (V) at the tip – forms the antigen-binding site (paratope) – and a constant region (C).
  5. Hinge region – flexible part allowing the arms to move.
  6. Fragments (enzyme digestion by papain):
    • Two Fab fragments (fragment antigen-binding) – bind antigen.
    • One Fc fragment (fragment crystallisable) – binds complement, phagocytes and mast cells; responsible for placental transfer.

2. Classes of immunoglobulins | Class | Structure | % of total Ig | Special features | |---|---|---|---| | IgG | Monomer | 75–80% | Crosses placenta; main antibody of secondary response; neutralises toxins and viruses, opsonises, activates complement; longest half-life (about 23 days) | | IgA | Monomer in serum; dimer (secretory IgA) with J chain and secretory piece | 10–15% | Mucosal immunity – in saliva, tears, milk (colostrum), intestinal and respiratory secretions | | IgM | Pentamer – largest ("millionaire molecule") | 5–10% | First antibody in primary response and the first made by the fetus; best at agglutination and complement activation; does not cross placenta – IgM in a newborn means congenital infection; natural anti-A and anti-B are IgM | | IgD | Monomer | <1% | On surface of B cells – antigen receptor | | IgE | Monomer | Trace (0.004%) | Binds mast cells and basophils; type I hypersensitivity (allergy); defence against worms; raised in asthma |

3. Functions of immunoglobulins

  • Neutralisation of toxins and viruses; opsonisation; complement activation; agglutination; ADCC; protection of mucosa; allergy (IgE).

4. Clinical importance

  • IgM antibody indicates recent infection (dengue IgM, HAV IgM, IgM anti-HBc).
  • IgG indicates past infection or immunity.
  • Immunoglobulin preparations (HBIG, RIG, TIG, IVIG) give passive immunity.

Conclusion All immunoglobulins share a common Y-shaped structure but differ in their heavy chains, giving five classes with distinct roles in defence.

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
unit_title: Section A: Immunity, Hypersensitivity and Immunisation
question: Write a note on the Mantoux test.
answer_html:
Introduction The Mantoux test (tuberculin skin test) detects delayed (type IV) hypersensitivity to proteins of Mycobacterium tuberculosis. A positive test shows that the person has been infected (or vaccinated with BCG) at some time – it does not by itself prove active disease. It was devised by Charles Mantoux (1908).

1. Principle A person infected with tubercle bacilli develops sensitised T lymphocytes. When tuberculin is injected into the skin, these cells react and release cytokines, producing induration (hardening) at the site after 48–72 hours.

2. Material

  • Purified protein derivative (PPD) of tuberculin – 5 TU of PPD-S or 1–2 TU of PPD RT-23 in 0.1 ml.
  • Tuberculin syringe (1 ml) with a 26–27 G needle, spirit swab, ruler, record card.

3. Procedure

  1. Explain the procedure; check history of previous BCG, TB and immunosuppression.
  2. Select the flexor (inner) surface of the left forearm, about a third of the way down from the elbow; avoid veins and scars.
  3. Clean and allow to dry.
  4. Inject 0.1 ml intradermally with the bevel up; a pale wheal of 6–10 mm should appear.
  5. Do not massage or cover the site; record the date, time, batch and site.
  6. Ask the person to return after 48–72 hours.

4. Reading and interpretation

  • Measure only the induration (not redness), across the forearm, in millimetres, by palpation. | Induration | Interpretation | |---|---| | Less than 5 mm | Negative | | 5–9 mm | Doubtful (positive in HIV-positive, immunosuppressed, close contacts of TB) | | 10 mm or more | Positive – infected (or BCG effect) | | More than 15 mm / blistering | Strongly positive – suggests active infection, especially in children |

5. Causes of false results

  • False negative: very early infection, HIV, severe malnutrition, measles, steroids, cancer, miliary or overwhelming TB, old age, faulty technique (injection too deep, expired tuberculin).
  • False positive: BCG vaccination, infection with non-tuberculous mycobacteria, wrong reading.

6. Uses

  • Helps diagnose TB in children (along with symptoms, contact history and X-ray).
  • Detection of latent TB infection before starting biological therapy or in health workers.
  • Epidemiological surveys of TB infection in a community.
  • Interferon-gamma release assays (IGRA) are a blood-test alternative, not affected by BCG.

Nursing points Use proper intradermal technique, tell the person not to scratch the site, read on time, and record the result in millimetres (not just "positive").

Conclusion The Mantoux test is a simple measure of cell-mediated immunity to TB; it must be read correctly and interpreted along with the clinical picture.

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
unit_title: Section A: Immunity, Hypersensitivity and Immunisation
question: Write a note on the Universal Immunisation Programme (UIP).
answer_html:
Introduction The Universal Immunisation Programme (UIP) of the Government of India provides free vaccines to protect children and pregnant women against life-threatening diseases. It began in 1985 (after the Expanded Programme on Immunisation of 1978) and is one of the largest public health programmes in the world, reaching about 2.6 crore newborns and nearly 3 crore pregnant women every year.

1. Objectives

  • Rapidly increase immunisation coverage and maintain it.
  • Improve the quality of services, including cold chain and safe injections.
  • Achieve self-sufficiency in vaccine production.
  • Monitor performance and adverse events following immunisation (AEFI).

2. Diseases covered The UIP protects against 12 vaccine-preventable diseases nationally or in endemic areas: diphtheria, pertussis, tetanus, polio, measles, rubella, severe childhood tuberculosis, hepatitis B, Haemophilus influenzae type b infections (pneumonia, meningitis), rotavirus diarrhoea, pneumococcal pneumonia and Japanese encephalitis (in endemic districts).

3. National immunisation schedule (children) | Age | Vaccines | |---|---| | Birth | BCG, OPV-0, hepatitis B birth dose (within 24 hours) | | 6 weeks | OPV-1, Pentavalent-1, Rotavirus-1, fIPV-1, PCV-1 | | 10 weeks | OPV-2, Pentavalent-2, Rotavirus-2 | | 14 weeks | OPV-3, Pentavalent-3, Rotavirus-3, fIPV-2, PCV-2 | | 9–12 months | MR-1, JE-1, PCV booster, fIPV-3, vitamin A (1st dose) | | 16–24 months | MR-2, JE-2, DPT booster-1, OPV booster, vitamin A (2nd dose; then every 6 months up to 5 years) | | 5–6 years | DPT booster-2 | | 10 years and 16 years | Td | *JE in endemic districts.

Pregnant women: Td-1 early in pregnancy, Td-2 four weeks later (or one Td booster if vaccinated within the last 3 years).

4. Important initiatives

  • Mission Indradhanush (2014) and Intensified Mission Indradhanush – catch-up drives for unvaccinated and partially vaccinated children and pregnant women.
  • eVIN (electronic Vaccine Intelligence Network) – real-time monitoring of vaccine stock and cold-chain temperature.
  • U-WIN digital platform – registration and tracking of every vaccination.
  • Polio-free certification (2014), maternal and neonatal tetanus elimination (2015).

5. Role of the nurse/ANM

  • Plan immunisation sessions; due-list preparation with ASHAs; maintain the cold chain and open-vial policy.
  • Screen for contraindications, give correct dose, route and site; use AD syringes; dispose of sharps safely.
  • Counsel parents about the next due date and minor side effects; observe for 30 minutes after vaccination; report AEFI.
  • Keep accurate records (MCP card, registers, U-WIN).

Conclusion The UIP is the backbone of child survival in India; nurses are its front-line workers, ensuring that every child is "fully immunised" on time.

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
unit_title: Section A: Immunity, Hypersensitivity and Immunisation
question: Describe the BCG vaccine and its maintenance through the cold chain.

diagram.caption: Cold chain system for vaccines in India

answer_html:
A. BCG vaccine

  1. Nature – Bacille Calmette–Guérin, a live attenuated strain of Mycobacterium bovis developed by Calmette and Guérin (1921). India uses the Danish 1331 strain.
  2. Form – freeze-dried powder reconstituted with normal saline (diluent supplied); protected from light (amber vials).
  3. Dose and route – 0.05 ml intradermally for infants up to 1 month (0.1 ml after one month) given at birth or as early as possible up to 1 year, on the left upper arm at the insertion of the deltoid.
  4. Normal reaction – a small wheal; a papule appears in 2–3 weeks, becomes a pustule, breaks into a small ulcer and heals by 6–12 weeks leaving a small scar (keep the site clean; do not apply any ointment or dressing).
  5. Protection – mainly against severe childhood TB – TB meningitis and miliary TB; less effective against adult pulmonary TB.
  6. Complications – local abscess, enlarged axillary lymph nodes (lymphadenitis), keloid; disseminated BCG infection in immunodeficient babies.
  7. Contraindications – symptomatic HIV infection, known immunodeficiency, generalised eczema/skin infection.
  8. Reconstituted vaccine must be used within 4 hours or by the end of the session and then discarded (open-vial policy does not apply).

B. Cold chain Definition – the cold chain is the system of people, equipment and procedures used to store and transport vaccines at the recommended temperature from the manufacturer to the beneficiary.

1. Recommended temperature

  • Most vaccines (BCG, OPV at PHC level, MR, pentavalent, hepatitis B, Td, PCV, rotavirus, IPV): +2 °C to +8 °C.
  • OPV is stored frozen (−15 °C to −25 °C) at state and district stores.
  • Freeze-sensitive vaccines (hepatitis B, pentavalent, DPT, Td, IPV, PCV) must never be frozen – the shake test detects freeze damage.
  • Heat- and light-sensitive: OPV, MR, BCG.

2. Cold-chain equipment

  • Walk-in coolers and walk-in freezers – state and regional stores.
  • Ice-lined refrigerators (ILR) – store vaccines at +2 to +8 °C at district and PHC level; can keep cold during power cuts.
  • Deep freezers – freeze ice packs (and store OPV at higher levels).
  • Cold boxes – transport and emergency storage.
  • Vaccine carriers with 4 conditioned ice packs – carry vaccines to sub-centres and outreach sessions.
  • Day carriers, thermometers, temperature loggers; eVIN monitors temperature remotely.

3. Storage practices in the ILR

  • Keep the temperature log twice daily.
  • BCG, MR and OPV in the basket at the top; freeze-sensitive vaccines (hepatitis B, pentavalent, Td, IPV, PCV) in the lower basket, never touching the walls or bottom.
  • No food or drinks in the ILR; doors opened as little as possible.
  • Check expiry date and vaccine vial monitor (VVM); use "first expiry, first out".
  • Use conditioned ice packs (thawed until water is heard on shaking) to avoid freezing vaccines.

Nursing role Check VVM and expiry before use, keep BCG in the vaccine carrier away from sunlight, discard reconstituted BCG after 4 hours, and report any cold-chain break.

Conclusion BCG is a live vaccine that protects infants from severe TB, and like all vaccines it works only if its potency is protected by an unbroken cold chain.

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
unit_title: Section A: Immunity, Hypersensitivity and Immunisation
question: Classify vaccines with examples.
answer_html:
Definition A vaccine is a biological preparation of an organism, its part or product, made harmless, which when given stimulates active immunity against a specific disease without causing the disease.

1. Live attenuated vaccines

  • Contain living organisms whose virulence has been weakened.
  • Give strong, long-lasting immunity, often with a single dose; may cause mild infection.
  • Bacterial: BCG, oral typhoid (Ty21a).
  • Viral: OPV, measles/MR/MMR, rotavirus, varicella, yellow fever, JE (SA 14-14-2).
  • Contraindicated in pregnancy and immunodeficiency.

2. Inactivated (killed) vaccines

  • Whole organisms killed by heat or chemicals (formalin, phenol); cannot cause disease; need several doses and boosters.
  • IPV (Salk), cell-culture rabies vaccine, hepatitis A (inactivated), whole-cell pertussis (in DPT), killed oral cholera vaccine, inactivated JE vaccine, Covaxin (COVID-19).

3. Toxoids

  • Exotoxins treated with formalin to remove toxicity but keep antigenicity; usually adsorbed on alum.
  • Tetanus toxoid, diphtheria toxoid (in DPT, Td).

4. Subunit and recombinant vaccines

  • Contain only the protective antigen of the organism.
  • Hepatitis B vaccine (recombinant HBsAg made in yeast), HPV vaccine (virus-like particles), acellular pertussis, typhoid Vi polysaccharide.

5. Polysaccharide and conjugate vaccines

  • Polysaccharide – capsular polysaccharides (pneumococcal 23-valent, meningococcal); poor response in children below 2 years.
  • Conjugate – polysaccharide linked to a carrier protein – good response in infants: Hib (in pentavalent), pneumococcal conjugate vaccine (PCV), typhoid conjugate vaccine.

6. Newer vaccine technologies

  • Viral-vector vaccines – Covishield (ChAdOx1) for COVID-19.
  • mRNA vaccines – COVID-19 mRNA vaccines.
  • DNA vaccines – ZyCoV-D (India) for COVID-19.

7. Combination vaccines

  • DPT, pentavalent (DPT + hepatitis B + Hib), MMR – fewer injections and visits.

Other classifications

  • By route – oral (OPV, rotavirus), intradermal (BCG, fIPV), subcutaneous (MR, JE), intramuscular (pentavalent, PCV, Td, hepatitis B).

Nursing points Know which vaccines are live (not for pregnant or immunocompromised persons), which are freeze-sensitive, and observe all recipients for 30 minutes after vaccination.

Comparison of live and killed vaccines | Feature | Live attenuated | Inactivated (killed) | |---|---|---| | Number of doses | Usually one (plus booster) | Several doses and boosters | | Immunity | Humoral + cell-mediated, local IgA (OPV) | Mainly humoral | | Duration | Long-lasting | Shorter | | Stability | Heat-labile; strict cold chain | More stable | | Risk | May revert to virulence (vaccine-derived polio) | Cannot cause disease | | Pregnancy/immunodeficiency | Avoid | Safe |

Conclusion Vaccines range from live attenuated organisms to modern mRNA products; their type decides storage, dosing, route and contraindications.

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
unit_title: Section A: Immunity, Hypersensitivity and Immunisation
question: Explain agglutination and its types.
answer_html:
Definition Agglutination is an antigen–antibody reaction in which a particulate (insoluble or cellular) antigen combines with its specific antibody in the presence of electrolytes to form visible clumps (agglutinates). The antibody is called an agglutinin and the antigen an agglutinogen. Agglutination is more sensitive than precipitation; IgM is the most efficient agglutinating antibody.

Types of agglutination 1. Slide agglutination

  • A drop of antiserum is mixed with a bacterial suspension or blood on a slide; clumping occurs within a minute.
  • Uses: blood grouping (ABO and Rh), identification and serotyping of isolates (Salmonella, Shigella, V. cholerae O1/O139).
  • Qualitative test.

2. Tube agglutination

  • Serial dilutions of the patient's serum are mixed with a known antigen in test tubes; the highest dilution showing agglutination is the titre.
  • Quantitative test.
  • Examples: Widal test (typhoid), Weil–Felix test (rickettsial infections, using Proteus OX strains), standard agglutination test for brucellosis.

3. Passive (indirect) agglutination

  • A soluble antigen is coated on carrier particles (latex beads, RBCs, charcoal) to make it particulate.
  • Latex agglutination – CRP, rheumatoid factor, ASO, cryptococcal antigen.
  • Passive haemagglutination – TPHA (syphilis).
  • Reverse passive – antibody coated on the particle detects antigen (e.g., HBsAg tests).

4. Haemagglutination

  • Direct agglutination of RBCs – blood grouping.
  • Haemagglutination inhibition (HAI) – antibodies block the clumping of RBCs by viruses (influenza, rubella antibodies).

5. Antiglobulin (Coombs) test

  • Detects incomplete (non-agglutinating) IgG antibodies using anti-human globulin.
  • Direct Coombs test – antibodies already on RBCs (haemolytic disease of newborn, autoimmune haemolytic anaemia, transfusion reactions).
  • Indirect Coombs test – free antibodies in serum (cross-matching, antenatal antibody screening in Rh-negative mothers).

6. Co-agglutination

  • S. aureus rich in protein A is coated with antibody; it clumps when the specific antigen is present (rapid identification of bacteria).

Prozone phenomenon Very high antibody concentration may prevent visible agglutination (false negative), e.g., in brucellosis; overcome by diluting the serum.

Nursing importance Correct labelling of blood samples for grouping and cross-matching, bedside checking before transfusion, and collecting paired sera for Widal are nursing responsibilities that depend on agglutination tests.

Conclusion Agglutination is a simple, visible antigen–antibody reaction widely used in blood banks and diagnostic laboratories.

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
unit_title: Section A: Immunity, Hypersensitivity and Immunisation
question: Define antigen. Explain the properties (determinants of antigenicity) and types of antigens.
answer_html:
Definition An antigen is any substance which, when introduced into the body, stimulates the production of antibodies and/or sensitised T cells and reacts specifically with them. Strictly, a substance that stimulates an immune response is an immunogen.

1. Epitope

  • The small part of an antigen that actually combines with the antibody or T-cell receptor is the epitope (antigenic determinant); the matching part of the antibody is the paratope.

2. Properties (factors determining antigenicity)

  1. Foreignness – the substance must be foreign ("non-self"); our own proteins are normally not antigenic (self-tolerance).
  2. Molecular size – larger molecules (above 10,000 daltons) are good antigens; very small molecules are poor.
  3. Chemical nature and complexity – proteins are the best antigens, polysaccharides moderate, lipids and nucleic acids poor.
  4. Stability – rigid, stable molecules are better antigens.
  5. Degradability – must be processed by antigen-presenting cells.
  6. Route of entry – intradermal and subcutaneous routes give a good response; oral route gives local IgA response.
  7. Dose – very low or very high doses may induce tolerance.
  8. Genetic factors and age of the host; use of adjuvants (e.g., aluminium salts in DPT and Td) increases antigenicity.

3. Types of antigens (a) Complete antigens and haptens

  • Complete antigen – both immunogenic and reactive (e.g., proteins).
  • Hapten (incomplete antigen) – small molecule that cannot stimulate antibodies alone but can react with them; becomes immunogenic when attached to a carrier protein – e.g., penicillin causing allergy.

(b) Based on origin

  • Exogenous – from outside (microbes, pollen, drugs).
  • Endogenous – inside the body: autoantigens (in autoimmune diseases), alloantigens (blood-group and HLA antigens – important in transfusion and transplantation).

(c) Special antigens

  • Heterophile antigens – shared by unrelated species; basis of the Weil–Felix test and Paul–Bunnell test.
  • Superantigens – activate large numbers of T cells non-specifically, causing a cytokine storm (toxic shock syndrome toxin, streptococcal pyrogenic toxins).
  • T-dependent and T-independent antigens – proteins need T-helper cells; polysaccharides can stimulate B cells directly but give poor memory (hence conjugate vaccines for infants).

(d) Microbial antigens

  • Bacterial O (somatic), H (flagellar), K/Vi (capsular) antigens; viral surface antigens (HBsAg, haemagglutinin).

Nursing importance Antigen knowledge explains drug allergy (haptens), blood-group matching, organ transplant matching, and why some vaccines need adjuvants and boosters.

Conclusion Antigens are the triggers of immunity; their size, chemistry and foreignness decide how strongly the body responds.

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
unit_title: Section A: Immunity, Hypersensitivity and Immunisation
question: Write the types of immunoglobulins.
answer_html:
Types (classes) of immunoglobulins – five, based on the heavy chain:

  1. IgG – most abundant (75–80%); crosses placenta; secondary response.
  2. IgA – secretory antibody in milk, saliva, tears, gut and respiratory secretions; mucosal defence.
  3. IgM – largest (pentamer); first antibody in primary response; indicates recent infection.
  4. IgD – on B-cell surface; antigen receptor.
  5. IgE – binds mast cells; causes allergy (type I hypersensitivity); defence against worms.

Memory aid – "GAMED": G (most common, crosses placenta), A (secretions), M (first, largest), E (allergy), D (B-cell receptor).

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
unit_title: Section A: Immunity, Hypersensitivity and Immunisation
question: Write the classification of hypersensitivity reactions.
answer_html:
Gell and Coombs classification

  1. Type I – Anaphylactic (immediate) – IgE and mast cells; e.g., anaphylaxis, asthma, urticaria, hay fever.
  2. Type II – Cytotoxic – IgG/IgM against cell-surface antigens; e.g., ABO transfusion reaction, Rh haemolytic disease of newborn.
  3. Type III – Immune-complex – deposited complexes and complement; e.g., serum sickness, Arthus reaction, SLE, glomerulonephritis.
  4. Type IV – Delayed (cell-mediated) – sensitised T cells; e.g., Mantoux reaction, contact dermatitis, graft rejection. (Type V – stimulatory, e.g., Graves' disease, is sometimes added.)

Types I–III are immediate (antibody-mediated); type IV is delayed (24–72 hours).

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
unit_title: Section A: Immunity, Hypersensitivity and Immunisation
question: What is herd immunity?
answer_html:
Herd immunity (community immunity) is the level of resistance of a community or group to the spread of an infection, which results when a large proportion of individuals are immune (by vaccination or past infection). Immune people interrupt the chain of transmission, so even non-immune persons are indirectly protected.

Key points

  • The proportion needed depends on the infectiousness of the disease – about 95% for measles, about 80–85% for polio.
  • Applies to diseases spread from person to person (not to tetanus).
  • Basis of high immunisation coverage targets and mass campaigns (pulse polio, MR campaign).
  • Protects newborns, the elderly and immunocompromised people who cannot be vaccinated.

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
unit_title: Section A: Immunity, Hypersensitivity and Immunisation
question: What is a toxoid? Give examples.
answer_html:
Toxoid – a bacterial exotoxin that has been treated with formaldehyde (formalin) and heat so that it loses its toxicity but retains its antigenicity. When injected it stimulates the production of antitoxin antibodies (active immunity).

Examples

  1. Tetanus toxoid – in DPT, pentavalent, Td vaccines.
  2. Diphtheria toxoid – in DPT and Td.

Points: usually adsorbed on aluminium salts (adjuvant) to increase the response; given intramuscularly; freeze-sensitive – store at +2 to +8 °C; boosters are needed.

Use: prevention of tetanus and diphtheria; Td is given in pregnancy to prevent neonatal tetanus.

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
unit_title: Section A: Immunity, Hypersensitivity and Immunisation
question: What is a vaccine vial monitor (VVM)? Explain its stages.
answer_html:
Vaccine vial monitor (VVM) is a heat-sensitive label (a square inside a circle) printed on the vaccine vial or cap. The inner square darkens gradually with cumulative heat exposure, showing whether the vaccine has been exposed to too much heat and may have lost potency.

Stages

  1. Stage 1 – inner square lighter than the outer circle – use the vaccine.
  2. Stage 2 – inner square still lighter but darkening – use first (if not expired).
  3. Stage 3 – inner square matches the outer circle – do not use (discard).
  4. Stage 4 – inner square darker than the outer circle – do not use.

VVM does not indicate freeze damage or expiry – check the expiry date and do the shake test separately.

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
question: Describe the role of the nurse in the infection control programme of a hospital.
answer_html:
Introduction An infection control programme is an organised, hospital-wide system of policies, people and activities whose aim is to prevent and control health care–associated infections (HAI) among patients, staff and visitors. Nurses form the largest group of health workers and give round-the-clock bedside care, so they are the backbone of every infection control programme. In India, the programme follows the National Guidelines for Infection Prevention and Control in Healthcare Facilities (NCDC, 2020), NABH standards and the Kayakalp scheme.

A. Components of an infection control programme

  1. Hospital Infection Control Committee (HICC) and Infection Control Team (ICT) – infection control officer (microbiologist) and infection control nurses (ICN) – about one ICN per 100 beds.
  2. Written infection control manual and policies (hand hygiene, isolation, sterilisation, BMW, antibiotic policy, staff health).
  3. Surveillance of HAI and feedback.
  4. Education and training of all staff.
  5. Outbreak investigation and control.
  6. Occupational health of staff – vaccination, needle-stick management.
  7. Monitoring of CSSD, housekeeping, laundry, kitchen, BMW, water and air quality.
  8. Antimicrobial stewardship in partnership with the antibiotic committee.
  9. Audits and quality indicators.

B. Role of the staff (ward) nurse 1. Hand hygiene and standard precautions

  • Performs hand hygiene at all five moments; uses alcohol hand rub at the point of care; keeps nails short and avoids rings and watches during care.
  • Uses PPE correctly; practises respiratory hygiene and safe injection practices (one needle, one syringe, one time).
  • Acts as a role model for students, attendants and visitors.

2. Aseptic technique and care of devices

  • Inserts and maintains urinary catheters, IV cannulas, central lines and endotracheal tubes with strict asepsis.
  • Follows care bundles (CAUTI, CLABSI, VAP, SSI) and records daily whether each device is still needed.
  • Changes dressings with no-touch technique; labels lines with date of insertion.

3. Isolation and patient placement

  • Identifies patients needing contact, droplet or airborne precautions (MRSA, TB, chickenpox, COVID-19) and arranges single rooms or cohorting.
  • Displays isolation signs; restricts visitors; keeps dedicated equipment.
  • Provides protective isolation for neutropenic and burns patients.

4. Environmental hygiene

  • Supervises housekeeping staff for correct cleaning and disinfection of surfaces, beds, mattresses and equipment (high-touch areas twice daily).
  • Ensures correct dilution and contact time of disinfectants; manages blood spills with spill kits.
  • Checks that ward linen is changed and soiled linen handled safely.

5. Sterilisation and disinfection of equipment

  • Sends instruments to CSSD, checks sterility indicators, pack integrity and expiry before use.
  • Cleans and disinfects reusable items (nebuliser masks, bedpans, thermometers) as per policy.

6. Biomedical waste management

  • Segregates waste at the point of generation in colour-coded containers; never overfills sharps containers; trains Group D staff.

7. Specimen collection and laboratory liaison

  • Collects specimens aseptically, before antibiotics, labels them properly and sends them promptly.
  • Reports alert organisms (MRSA, CRE, C. difficile, TB) and critical results immediately.

8. Surveillance and reporting

  • Notices early signs of infection (fever, pus, redness at cannula site, cloudy urine) and reports them.
  • Maintains device-day and patient-day records used to calculate infection rates; informs the ICN about suspected HAIs.
  • Recognises clusters (e.g., several babies with diarrhoea in NICU) that may signal an outbreak.

9. Antimicrobial stewardship

  • Gives antibiotics on time, at correct dose and duration; reminds doctors about review after 48–72 hours and stopping prophylaxis after surgery.

10. Patient and family education

  • Teaches hand washing, cough etiquette, wound and catheter care, safe food and water, and importance of completing antibiotics.

11. Staff health and self-protection

  • Gets vaccinated (hepatitis B, influenza); reports needle-stick and splash injuries immediately; stays off duty with infectious conditions (diarrhoea, open skin lesions, conjunctivitis).

C. Special role of the infection control nurse (ICN)

  1. Surveillance – daily rounds of high-risk areas (ICU, NICU, dialysis, OT); collection of data on device-associated infections and SSIs; calculating rates and sending reports.
  2. Education – induction and in-service training on hand hygiene, PPE, BMW, bundles; preparing posters and SOPs.
  3. Audits – hand hygiene compliance, bundle compliance, environmental cleaning, BMW segregation, CSSD processes; giving feedback.
  4. Outbreak management – detecting outbreaks, helping in investigation (line listing, environmental sampling), implementing control measures.
  5. Policy implementation – drafting and updating policies with the HICC.
  6. Liaison – with microbiology, pharmacy, CSSD, housekeeping, engineering and administration.
  7. Occupational health – maintaining the needle-stick injury register, follow-up of PEP, vaccination records.
  8. Quality and accreditation – preparing for NABH and Kayakalp assessments; tracking indicators.
  9. Research – evaluating interventions and new products.

D. Role of nurse managers

  • Ensure adequate staffing (overcrowding and understaffing increase HAI), supplies of hand rub, PPE, linen and disinfectants; support training and audits; enforce policies fairly.

Example When three post-operative patients in a surgical ward develop wound infections with the same organism, the ward nurse informs the ICN; the team reviews dressing technique, OT practices and hand hygiene, finds a lapse in the dressing trolley preparation, retrains staff and the infections stop – infection control in action.

Conclusion Infection control is everybody's responsibility, but the nurse – at the bedside, in the ward management and as the infection control nurse – is its most important practitioner. Consistent, simple actions like hand hygiene, asepsis and timely reporting save lives and money.

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
question: Explain the bundle approach for the prevention of catheter-associated urinary tract infection (CAUTI), surgical site infection (SSI), ventilator-associated events (VAE) and central line–associated bloodstream infection (CLABSI).

diagram.caption: Central line insertion bundle checklist

answer_html:
Introduction Most serious hospital infections are linked to devices and procedures – urinary catheters, central venous lines, ventilators and surgery. A care bundle is a small set (3–6) of evidence-based practices which, when performed together, every time, for every patient, give much better results than when done individually. The approach was popularised by the Institute for Healthcare Improvement (IHI). Compliance is measured as "all-or-none" – the bundle counts as done only if every element is done.

A. Principles of the bundle approach

  1. Each element is simple and supported by strong evidence.
  2. Applied to a defined group of patients (e.g., all catheterised patients).
  3. Compliance is checked daily with a checklist and audited.
  4. Results (infection rates) are fed back to staff to encourage improvement.

B. CAUTI prevention bundle Insertion

  1. Insert a catheter only when truly indicated (urinary retention, accurate output monitoring in critical illness, perioperative use for selected surgeries, sacral wounds in incontinent patients, end-of-life comfort); consider alternatives (condom catheter, intermittent catheterisation).

  2. Hand hygiene and aseptic technique with sterile gloves, drape and sterile equipment; clean the meatus; use the smallest suitable catheter; sterile lubricant. Maintenance

  3. Maintain a closed, sterile drainage system; do not disconnect the catheter from the tubing.

  4. Keep urine flow unobstructed – no kinks; keep the bag below the level of the bladder and off the floor.
  5. Empty the bag regularly using a separate clean container for each patient; do not let the drain tap touch the container.
  6. Routine perineal hygiene with soap and water (no routine antiseptics or bladder irrigation).
  7. Collect urine samples from the sampling port aseptically.
  8. Review the need daily and remove the catheter as early as possible – the most important step (risk rises 3–7% per catheter-day).

C. SSI prevention bundle Before surgery

  1. Pre-operative bath with soap or chlorhexidine the night before/morning of surgery.
  2. Avoid hair removal; if necessary, use clippers (not razors) just before surgery.

  3. Treat existing infections; optimise blood sugar and nutrition; stop smoking. During surgery

  4. Prophylactic antibiotic within 60 minutes before incision (120 minutes for vancomycin), correct choice and dose; re-dose in long operations.

  5. Skin preparation with alcohol-based chlorhexidine (or povidone-iodine) allowed to dry.
  6. Maintain normothermia (≥36 °C) and adequate oxygenation; strict OT discipline (minimal traffic, doors closed).

  7. Glucose control – keep blood sugar below 180–200 mg/dl perioperatively. After surgery

  8. Sterile dressing for 24–48 hours; hand hygiene before touching the wound; stop prophylactic antibiotics within 24 hours.

  9. Surveillance for SSI up to 30 days (90 days with implants).

D. VAP / VAE prevention bundle

  1. Elevate the head of the bed 30–45° (unless contraindicated) to prevent aspiration.
  2. Daily sedation interruption ("sedation vacation") and assessment of readiness to extubate (spontaneous breathing trial).
  3. Oral care – tooth brushing and oral hygiene several times a day (chlorhexidine as per unit policy).
  4. Subglottic secretion drainage with special ET tubes; maintain cuff pressure 20–30 cm H₂O.
  5. Peptic ulcer prophylaxis and DVT prophylaxis (part of the original IHI ventilator bundle).
  6. Additional: closed suction system, avoid routine circuit changes (change only when visibly soiled or malfunctioning), drain condensate away from the patient, hand hygiene before handling the airway, early mobility and early enteral feeding.

E. CLABSI prevention bundle Insertion bundle

  1. Hand hygiene before insertion.
  2. Maximal sterile barrier precautions – cap, mask, sterile gown, sterile gloves and a large sterile drape covering the patient.
  3. Chlorhexidine (>0.5%) with alcohol for skin antisepsis, allowed to dry.
  4. Optimal site selection – subclavian preferred in adults; avoid the femoral vein.

  5. Use a checklist; empower the nurse to stop the procedure if asepsis is broken. Maintenance bundle

  6. Daily review of line necessity; remove promptly.

  7. "Scrub the hub" – disinfect needleless connectors with alcohol/chlorhexidine for 5–15 seconds before each access.
  8. Sterile transparent dressing – change every 7 days (gauze every 2 days) or if soiled, loose or damp.
  9. Change administration sets as per policy (every 4–7 days; within 24 hours for blood and lipids).
  10. Daily chlorhexidine bathing in ICU (as per policy).

F. Measuring success

  • Device-associated infection rate = (number of infections ÷ number of device-days) × 1000, e.g., CAUTI per 1,000 catheter-days.
  • Bundle compliance rate = (patients with all elements done ÷ patients audited) × 100.

G. Nurse's role

  • Nurses perform most bundle elements – positioning, oral care, catheter maintenance, dressing and hub care – and fill the daily checklists.
  • Remind doctors about removing devices; question breaks in asepsis; educate patients and families.

Conclusion Care bundles turn evidence into reliable daily practice. When every element is done for every patient every time, device-associated infections fall sharply – often to near zero in well-run ICUs.

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
question: Write a note on hospital-acquired infections (HAI).
answer_html:
Definition A hospital-acquired (health care–associated) infection is an infection that develops in a patient during the course of hospital care which was neither present nor incubating at the time of admission – usually appearing 48 hours or more after admission, within 3 days of discharge or within 30 days after surgery (90 days with implants). Infections acquired by health workers at work are also HAIs.

1. Common types

  1. Urinary tract infection – mostly catheter-associated (CAUTI).
  2. Surgical site infection (SSI).
  3. Lower respiratory tract infection / ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP).
  4. Bloodstream infection – mostly central line–associated (CLABSI).
  5. Others – C. difficile diarrhoea, skin and soft tissue infection (pressure ulcers, burns), conjunctivitis, neonatal sepsis, blood-borne viral infections.

2. Common organisms

  • Gram-negative bacilli – E. coli, Klebsiella (ESBL, carbapenem-resistant), Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Acinetobacter baumannii (common in Indian ICUs).
  • Gram-positive cocci – S. aureus (MRSA), coagulase-negative staphylococci, enterococci (VRE).
  • Fungi – Candida (including C. auris); viruses – influenza, rotavirus, norovirus, hepatitis B and C, HIV; M. tuberculosis.

3. Sources of HAI

  • Endogenous – patient's own flora (skin, gut, respiratory tract) entering through devices or wounds.
  • Exogenous – other patients and staff (especially hands), visitors, contaminated equipment, IV fluids, medicines, water (sinks, humidifiers), air (Aspergillus during construction), food and linen.

4. Risk factors

  • Patient – extremes of age, low immunity, diabetes, severe illness, malnutrition, burns, long stay.
  • Procedures and devices – catheters, ventilators, central lines, surgery.
  • Environment and practice – overcrowding, understaffing, poor hand hygiene, inadequate sterilisation, overuse of antibiotics.

5. Effects Prolonged stay, extra cost, antimicrobial resistance, disability and death; legal and reputational harm to the hospital.

6. Prevention

  1. Hand hygiene – the single most important measure.
  2. Standard and transmission-based precautions; isolation.
  3. Asepsis and care bundles for devices; remove devices early.
  4. Proper sterilisation, disinfection and environmental cleaning.
  5. Biomedical waste and laundry management.
  6. Antimicrobial stewardship.
  7. Surveillance with feedback; outbreak control.
  8. Staff training, vaccination and occupational safety.
  9. Patient and visitor education.

7. Indian initiatives

  • National Guidelines for IPC in Healthcare Facilities (NCDC, 2020) and the ICMR–AIIMS HAI surveillance network for ICUs.
  • Kayakalp awards for clean, infection-free public hospitals; NABH accreditation standards on infection control.

Conclusion HAIs are common, costly and largely preventable; strict adherence to basic infection-control practices by every nurse is the key.

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
question: Explain the sources and modes of transmission of infection.
answer_html:
Introduction For an infection to spread, the organism must leave a source, travel by a route (mode of transmission) and enter a susceptible host. Breaking any of these links prevents infection. Knowing them helps the nurse choose the right precautions.

A. Sources (reservoirs) of infection 1. Human sources

  • Cases (patients) – clinical, subclinical or latent infections (e.g., open TB patient).
  • Carriers – persons who harbour the organism without symptoms and spread it unknowingly: incubatory (measles), convalescent (typhoid after recovery), healthy carriers (nasal S. aureus in staff), chronic carriers (typhoid in the gallbladder, hepatitis B).
  • Normal flora of the patient – source of endogenous infection.

2. Animal sources (zoonoses)

  • Dogs (rabies), rats (plague, leptospirosis), cattle (brucellosis, M. bovis), pigs (JE amplifier hosts), birds (avian influenza).

3. Non-living (environmental) sources

  • Soil – tetanus, gas gangrene spores, fungi.
  • Water – cholera, typhoid, hepatitis A and E, Pseudomonas and Legionella in hospital water systems.
  • Food – food poisoning, typhoid, brucellosis.
  • Air and dust; hospital equipment and fomites.

B. Modes of transmission 1. Contact transmission (commonest in hospitals)

  • Direct contact – person to person by touching, kissing, sexual contact (MRSA, scabies, herpes, STIs); mother to baby.
  • Indirect contact – through contaminated hands of health workers, instruments, bedpans, thermometers, linen, door handles (fomites).

2. Droplet transmission

  • Large droplets (more than 5 µm) produced by coughing, sneezing, talking, suctioning; travel about 1–2 metres and fall quickly.
  • Influenza, pertussis, diphtheria, mumps, rubella, meningococcal meningitis, COVID-19.

3. Airborne transmission

  • Droplet nuclei (less than 5 µm) and dust particles that remain suspended in air for long periods and travel far.
  • Tuberculosis, measles, chickenpox, disseminated herpes zoster.

4. Vehicle (common vehicle) transmission

  • Contaminated water, food, milk, blood, IV fluids, drugs; one source infects many people (outbreaks of cholera, hepatitis A, transfusion-transmitted hepatitis B).

5. Vector-borne transmission

  • Mechanical (houseflies) or biological (mosquitoes – malaria, dengue; sandfly – kala-azar).

6. Vertical transmission

  • From mother to fetus/baby – syphilis, HIV, hepatitis B, rubella, toxoplasmosis.

7. Parenteral (inoculation)

  • Needle-stick injuries, unsafe injections, tattooing – HBV, HCV, HIV.

C. Portals of entry and exit – respiratory tract, GI tract, urogenital tract, skin and mucosa, placenta, blood.

Nursing implications Contact precautions for contact-spread organisms, masks for droplets, N95 and isolation rooms for airborne infections, safe water and food, vector control, and safe injection practices.

Conclusion Identifying the source and route of infection tells the nurse exactly where to intervene to break the chain of infection.

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
question: Explain the surveillance of hospital-acquired infections.
answer_html:
Definition Surveillance is the ongoing, systematic collection, analysis and interpretation of data on health events (here HAIs), with timely feedback to those who need to know, so that action can be taken. Without surveillance, a hospital does not know its infection problems.

1. Objectives

  • Know the baseline rates of HAI and their trends.
  • Detect outbreaks early.
  • Identify risk factors and problem areas.
  • Evaluate control measures and motivate staff through feedback.
  • Meet accreditation requirements (NABH).

2. Types of surveillance | Type | Meaning | |---|---| | Active | ICN actively looks for cases (ward rounds, records, lab reports) – more accurate | | Passive | Relies on reports sent by wards/doctors – cheaper but under-reports | | Prospective | Patients followed during stay – preferred | | Retrospective | Review of records after discharge | | Hospital-wide | All patients and infections – labour-intensive | | Targeted | High-risk areas/infections – ICU device-associated infections, SSI after specific surgeries | | Laboratory-based | Monitoring alert organisms (MRSA, CRE) | | Post-discharge | SSI after day-care surgery by phone calls/clinic visits |

3. Steps

  1. Decide what to monitor and use standard case definitions (CDC/NHSN, adopted by the ICMR HAI surveillance network in India).
  2. Collect data – numerator (number of infections) and denominator (patient-days, device-days, number of procedures).
  3. Tabulate and analyse – calculate rates and compare with previous months and benchmarks.
  4. Interpret – look for rising trends or clusters.
  5. Report and give feedback to ward staff, doctors, HICC and administration.
  6. Act and evaluate – implement corrective measures and re-check.

4. Common rates

  • CAUTI rate = (number of CAUTIs ÷ urinary catheter-days) × 1000.
  • CLABSI rate = (number of CLABSIs ÷ central line-days) × 1000.
  • VAE/VAP rate = (number of VAEs ÷ ventilator-days) × 1000.
  • SSI rate = (number of SSIs ÷ number of surgeries of that type) × 100.
  • Device utilisation ratio = device-days ÷ patient-days.

5. Role of the nurse Daily recording of device-days, early reporting of suspected infection, sending appropriate cultures, helping the ICN with data, and acting on feedback.

6. Example of feedback A monthly bar chart showing "CLABSI rate in medical ICU fell from 8 to 3 per 1,000 line-days after the insertion bundle was introduced" motivates staff far more than a written circular.

Conclusion Surveillance is the "eyes" of infection control – what is measured and fed back gets improved.

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
question: Describe the composition and functions of the hospital infection control committee and the infection control team.
answer_html:
Introduction Every hospital must have an organised structure to plan and run its infection control programme. This consists of a policy-making Hospital Infection Control Committee (HICC) and an operational Infection Control Team (ICT), as recommended by national guidelines and NABH.

A. Hospital Infection Control Committee (HICC) Composition

  • Chairperson – Head of the institution / Medical Superintendent.
  • Member-secretary – Microbiologist (Infection Control Officer).
  • Members – Nursing Superintendent/Chief Nursing Officer, infection control nurses, heads of medicine, surgery, obstetrics, paediatrics, anaesthesia/critical care, CSSD in-charge, pharmacist, hospital administrator, engineering/maintenance in-charge, housekeeping, laundry and dietary in-charge, BMW officer, occupational health representative.
  • Meets regularly – usually monthly (and urgently during outbreaks); minutes are recorded.

Functions

  1. Formulate and approve the infection control manual and policies (hand hygiene, isolation, sterilisation, BMW, linen, kitchen, staff health).
  2. Review surveillance reports and HAI rates; set targets.
  3. Approve purchase and use of disinfectants, antiseptics and equipment.
  4. Frame the hospital antibiotic policy with the antimicrobial stewardship committee.
  5. Plan education and training programmes.
  6. Take decisions during outbreaks and oversee investigation.
  7. Ensure staff health measures – immunisation, needle-stick and PEP policy.
  8. Monitor support services – CSSD, laundry, kitchen, water, air handling, construction work.
  9. Review audits and quality indicators for NABH/Kayakalp.

B. Infection Control Team (ICT) Composition

  • Infection Control Officer (ICO) – usually a microbiologist.
  • Infection Control Nurses (ICN) – about one per 100 beds.
  • Data assistant/epidemiologist where available.

Functions (day-to-day)

  • Active surveillance and calculation of HAI rates.
  • Ward rounds, audits (hand hygiene, bundle compliance, cleaning, BMW).
  • Training of staff and students.
  • Investigation and control of outbreaks.
  • Advice on isolation and alert organisms.
  • Implementation of HICC decisions and reporting back.

C. Relationship with other committees

  • Works closely with the Antimicrobial Stewardship Committee, Patient Safety/Quality Committee, BMW Management Committee, CSSD and occupational health services.
  • Reports to the hospital management and the quality department (NABH/Kayakalp).

D. Role of the nursing representative Brings ward-level problems to the committee (shortage of hand rub, PPE, linen), ensures nursing policies match HICC decisions and trains nurses accordingly.

Conclusion The HICC decides "what should be done" and the ICT ensures "it is done" – together they keep the hospital safe from infection.

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
question: Define nosocomial infection.
answer_html:
Nosocomial infection (Greek nosokomeion = hospital) is an infection acquired in a hospital or health-care facility by a patient who was admitted for some other reason; the infection was neither present nor incubating at the time of admission. It usually appears 48 hours or more after admission, or after discharge (within 30 days of surgery).

Common types: catheter-associated UTI, surgical site infection, ventilator-associated pneumonia, central line–associated bloodstream infection. Common organisms: MRSA, Klebsiella, Pseudomonas, Acinetobacter, Candida. It is now usually called health care–associated infection (HAI).

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
question: List the measures to prevent surgical site infection.
answer_html:
Measures to prevent SSI

  1. Pre-operative bath with soap/chlorhexidine; treat remote infections; control blood sugar.
  2. Avoid shaving – use clippers just before surgery if hair removal is needed.
  3. Prophylactic antibiotic within 60 minutes before incision; stop within 24 hours after surgery.
  4. Skin preparation with alcohol-based chlorhexidine; allow to dry.
  5. Strict surgical hand antisepsis, sterile gowns and gloves, sterile instruments.
  6. Maintain normothermia and good oxygenation; minimal OT traffic.
  7. Sterile dressing for 24–48 hours; hand hygiene before touching the wound.

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
question: Write two strategies to prevent catheter-associated urinary tract infection (CAUTI).
answer_html:
Strategies to prevent CAUTI

  1. Avoid unnecessary catheterisation and remove the catheter as early as possible – review the need every day (nurse-driven removal protocols).
  2. Insert aseptically and maintain a closed drainage system – hand hygiene, sterile equipment; keep the bag below bladder level and off the floor, ensure unobstructed flow and empty the bag with a clean separate container.

Other measures: daily perineal hygiene, securing the catheter, collecting samples only from the sampling port, using intermittent or condom catheters where suitable.

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
question: List the surveillance criteria for surgical site infection (SSI).
answer_html:
Superficial incisional SSI (CDC/NHSN criteria) – occurs within 30 days of surgery, involves only skin and subcutaneous tissue of the incision, and has at least one of the following:

  1. Purulent drainage from the superficial incision.
  2. Organism isolated from an aseptically obtained culture of the incision.
  3. Incision deliberately opened by the surgeon with at least one sign – pain/tenderness, localised swelling, redness or heat.
  4. Diagnosis of SSI by the surgeon/physician.

Deep incisional SSI – involves fascia and muscle; organ/space SSI – involves any organ or space opened during surgery; both are watched for 30 or 90 days (implants).

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
question: How is the device-associated infection rate calculated?
answer_html:
Device-associated infection rate = (Number of device-associated infections in a period ÷ Number of device-days in the same period) × 1000

  • Device-days = total number of days patients had the device in place (counted daily at a fixed time).
  • Expressed as infections per 1,000 device-days.

Example: 3 CAUTIs in an ICU with 600 urinary catheter-days in a month → (3 ÷ 600) × 1000 = 5 CAUTIs per 1,000 catheter-days.

Used for CAUTI, CLABSI and VAP/VAE rates; allows comparison over time and between ICUs.

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
unit_title: Section B: Isolation Precautions and Personal Protective Equipment
question: Explain standard precautions and transmission-based precautions for preventing the spread of infection in hospitals.

diagram.caption: Isolation signage for contact, droplet and airborne precautions
labels: contact – gown and gloves; droplet – surgical mask within 1–2 m; airborne – N95 respirator

answer_html:
Introduction Many patients carry infections without any signs, and many infections cannot be recognised at admission. Therefore the CDC Guideline for Isolation Precautions (2007) recommends a two-tier system:

  1. Standard precautions – applied to all patients, at all times, regardless of diagnosis.
  2. Transmission-based precautions – additional precautions for patients known or suspected to have infections spread by contact, droplet or airborne routes. (Older terms such as "universal precautions" and "standard safety measures" refer to the same idea of treating all blood and body fluids as potentially infectious.)

A. Standard precautions They assume that blood, all body fluids, secretions and excretions (except sweat), non-intact skin and mucous membranes may contain infectious agents.

1. Hand hygiene

  • At the WHO five moments; alcohol-based hand rub for routine use, soap and water when hands are visibly soiled or after caring for patients with diarrhoea (C. difficile, norovirus).

2. Personal protective equipment (PPE) – based on the anticipated exposure:

  • Gloves – when touching blood, body fluids, mucous membranes, non-intact skin or contaminated items; change between patients; hand hygiene after removal.
  • Gown/apron – when clothing may be soiled.
  • Mask, goggles or face shield – during procedures likely to generate splashes or sprays (suctioning, wound irrigation, delivery).

3. Respiratory hygiene and cough etiquette

  • Cover mouth and nose while coughing with a tissue or elbow; dispose tissues; hand hygiene; mask for coughing patients; keep at least 1 metre distance in waiting areas.

4. Safe injection practices

  • One needle, one syringe, one patient, one time; never re-use syringes; prefer single-dose vials; aseptic technique when preparing injections; never recap needles by two hands.

5. Safe handling of sharps

  • Dispose of sharps immediately at the point of use into puncture-proof containers; use safety-engineered devices; never pass sharps hand to hand.

6. Patient placement

  • Single rooms for patients who may contaminate the environment or cannot maintain hygiene.

7. Patient-care equipment and devices

  • Clean and disinfect/sterilise reusable equipment between patients; dedicated equipment for isolated patients.

8. Environmental cleaning

  • Routine cleaning and disinfection of high-touch surfaces (bed rails, tables, switches, door handles).

9. Textiles and laundry

  • Handle soiled linen with minimum agitation; bag at the point of use; do not shake.

10. Special lumbar puncture procedures – wear a surgical mask when inserting catheters or injecting into spinal/epidural spaces.

11. Worker safety – vaccination, needle-stick prevention and post-exposure management.

B. Transmission-based precautions 1. Contact precautions

  • For: MRSA, VRE, multidrug-resistant Gram-negatives (ESBL, CRE), C. difficile, scabies, lice, herpes simplex, rotavirus and other infectious diarrhoea, draining wounds, impetigo.
  • Measures
    • Single room or cohorting with patients infected by the same organism.
    • Gloves and gown on entering the room; remove before leaving; hand hygiene.
    • Dedicated equipment (stethoscope, BP cuff, thermometer); otherwise disinfect after use.
    • Limit patient transport; increase cleaning of the room.

2. Droplet precautions

  • For: influenza, pertussis, diphtheria (pharyngeal), mumps, rubella, meningococcal meningitis, mycoplasma pneumonia, adenovirus, streptococcal pharyngitis (first 24 hours of treatment), COVID-19 (with additional measures).
  • Measures
    • Single room or cohort; if shared, keep beds more than 1–2 metres apart with a curtain.
    • Surgical mask for staff within 1–2 metres of the patient.
    • Mask for the patient during transport; respiratory hygiene.

3. Airborne precautions

  • For: pulmonary/laryngeal tuberculosis, measles, chickenpox, disseminated herpes zoster; also during aerosol-generating procedures in COVID-19 and other respiratory infections.
  • Measures
    • Airborne infection isolation room (AIIR) – single room with negative pressure, at least 6–12 air changes per hour, air exhausted outside or through HEPA filters, door kept closed.
    • Where AIIR is not available – well-ventilated single room with open windows, exhaust fans.
    • N95 (or higher) respirator for staff, fit-checked every time; non-immune staff should not care for measles or chickenpox patients.
    • Surgical mask for the patient outside the room; limit movement.

C. Combined precautions Some infections need more than one type, e.g., chickenpox – airborne and contact; COVID-19 – contact and droplet with airborne precautions during aerosol-generating procedures.

D. Duration Precautions are continued till the patient is no longer infectious – e.g., sputum-positive TB until 2 weeks of effective treatment and clinical improvement (as per policy), chickenpox until all lesions crust, MRSA until cleared as per hospital policy.

E. Nurse's responsibilities

  1. Identify patients needing isolation on admission (screening questions, alert organisms).
  2. Place appropriate isolation signage on the door without revealing diagnosis.
  3. Keep PPE, hand rub and waste bins at the entrance.
  4. Explain precautions to patient and family; address feelings of loneliness and stigma; allow communication.
  5. Ensure terminal cleaning of the room after discharge.
  6. Document and communicate isolation status during transfer.

Conclusion Standard precautions protect everyone from unrecognised infection; transmission-based precautions add targeted barriers. Used together and consistently, they form the foundation of safe nursing care.

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
unit_title: Section B: Isolation Precautions and Personal Protective Equipment
question: Explain the effective use of personal protective equipment (PPE), including the sequence of donning and doffing.

diagram.caption: Sequence of donning and doffing PPE

answer_html:
Introduction Personal protective equipment (PPE) consists of specialised clothing and equipment worn by health workers to protect themselves and patients from infectious agents. PPE is effective only when the right item is chosen, worn correctly and removed without self-contamination.

1. Components and use | Item | Purpose | When used | |---|---|---| | Gloves | Protect hands | Contact with blood, body fluids, mucosa, non-intact skin | | Gown/apron | Protect skin and clothing | Splashes, contact precautions | | Surgical mask | Protects nose/mouth from droplets and splashes | Droplet precautions, sterile procedures | | N95 respirator | Filters 95% of 0.3 µm particles | Airborne precautions (TB, measles), aerosol-generating procedures | | Goggles/face shield | Protect eyes and face | Splashes, sprays, aerosols | | Cap and shoe covers | Hair and footwear protection | OT, high-risk areas |

2. Principles of effective use

  1. Select PPE by risk assessment – what exposure is expected?
  2. Perform hand hygiene before putting on and after removing PPE.
  3. Don before entering the patient's room; doff at the doorway or in the anteroom.
  4. Change gloves between patients and between dirty and clean sites on the same patient; never wash or reuse disposable gloves.
  5. Do not touch your face, mask or adjust PPE with contaminated gloves.
  6. Fit-check (seal-check) the N95 every time it is worn; fit-testing as per policy.
  7. Keep hands away from the face and limit surfaces touched.
  8. Dispose of PPE in the correct BMW bin (gloves and gowns – yellow/red as per policy).

3. Sequence of donning (putting on)

  1. Hand hygiene.
  2. Gown – fully cover the torso from neck to knees, arms to wrists; tie at back.
  3. Mask or respirator – secure ties or bands, fit the nose piece; perform seal check.
  4. Goggles or face shield.
  5. Gloves – extend over the cuffs of the gown.

4. Sequence of doffing (removing) – most contaminated items first

  1. Gloves – glove-in-glove technique (peel off the first glove holding it in the gloved hand, slide fingers of the ungloved hand under the second glove).
  2. Goggles/face shield – handle by the head band or ear pieces (back is "clean").
  3. Gown – untie, pull away from the neck and shoulders touching only the inside, roll it inside-out.
  4. Mask/respirator – remove by the ties/bands from behind, without touching the front.
  5. Hand hygiene immediately (and between steps if hands get contaminated). (Gown and gloves may be removed together as one unit.)

5. Common errors to avoid Wearing the same gloves between patients, keeping masks under the chin, touching the front of the mask, leaving the room in PPE, wearing gloves instead of hand hygiene.

Conclusion PPE is the last line of defence; its value depends on correct selection, correct sequence and careful removal.

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
unit_title: Section B: Isolation Precautions and Personal Protective Equipment
question: Describe the types of isolation and the requirements of an isolation room.
answer_html:
Definition Isolation is the separation of infected (or highly susceptible) persons from others for the period of communicability, under conditions that prevent transmission of the infectious agent.

1. Types of isolation (a) Source isolation – to prevent spread from an infected patient to others.

  • Strict isolation – highly infectious diseases spread by air and contact (e.g., viral haemorrhagic fevers, disseminated zoster).
  • Respiratory/airborne isolation – TB, measles, chickenpox.
  • Contact isolation – MRSA, scabies, infected wounds.
  • Enteric precautions – cholera, typhoid, hepatitis A, infectious diarrhoea.
  • Blood and body-fluid precautions – now covered by standard precautions.

(b) Protective (reverse) isolation – to protect a highly susceptible patient from infection coming from others: neutropenic patients on chemotherapy, bone-marrow transplant recipients, extensive burns, premature babies. Measures: single room with positive-pressure, HEPA-filtered air, strict hand hygiene, masks for staff and visitors, no fresh flowers or plants, safe food, restricting ill visitors.

(c) Category-specific and disease-specific isolation – older systems that grouped diseases into categories or gave specific instructions for each disease; now replaced by standard + transmission-based precautions.

(d) Cohort isolation – grouping patients with the same infection in one room/area, with dedicated staff, during outbreaks or when single rooms are not available.

2. Requirements of an isolation room

  1. Single room with attached toilet and hand-washing basin.
  2. Anteroom for hand hygiene, donning and doffing PPE.
  3. Ventilation – negative pressure with 6–12 or more air changes per hour for airborne infections; positive pressure for protective isolation.
  4. Door kept closed; signage on the door.
  5. Hand rub dispenser at entry; PPE stock outside; BMW bins inside.
  6. Dedicated equipment – stethoscope, BP apparatus, thermometer.
  7. Surfaces easy to clean; minimum furniture.
  8. Arrangement for linen and waste removal without contaminating corridors.
  9. Facility for communication (intercom, window) to reduce psychological isolation.

3. Nursing care Explain the reason for isolation, reduce loneliness and anxiety (phone calls, family visits with PPE), plan care to minimise entries, terminal disinfection after discharge.

4. Terminal disinfection After the patient is discharged or shifted, the room is cleaned thoroughly – linen sent as infected linen, all surfaces and equipment disinfected (e.g., 1% hypochlorite for spore-formers), curtains changed, mattresses wiped – before the next patient is admitted.

Conclusion Isolation protects other patients, staff and vulnerable patients; it must be applied with both technical precision and compassion.

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
unit_title: Section B: Isolation Precautions and Personal Protective Equipment
question: Write a note on personal protective equipment (PPE).
answer_html:
Personal protective equipment (PPE) is specialised clothing and equipment worn by health workers to create a barrier against infectious agents in blood, body fluids, droplets and air.

Components: gloves, gown/apron, surgical mask, N95 respirator, goggles/face shield, cap and shoe covers.

Key points

  • Selected according to risk (contact, droplet, airborne, splash).
  • Donning: gown → mask → goggles → gloves; doffing: gloves → goggles → gown → mask; hand hygiene before and after.
  • Single use; dispose in BMW bins; not a substitute for hand hygiene.

Wrong use of PPE (touching the face, reusing gloves) can itself spread infection.

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
unit_title: Section B: Isolation Precautions and Personal Protective Equipment
question: Explain medical asepsis.
answer_html:
Medical asepsis ("clean technique") includes all practices intended to reduce the number of microorganisms and prevent their spread from one person or place to another.

Examples

  • Hand hygiene, using clean gloves.
  • Cleaning, disinfection and proper handling of equipment and linen.
  • Isolation and barrier precautions; cough etiquette.
  • Separating clean and dirty areas; correct waste disposal.

It differs from surgical asepsis (sterile technique), which aims at the complete absence of microorganisms in sterile fields (OT, catheterisation, injections).

Purpose: to break the chain of infection in everyday ward care such as feeding, bathing, bed making and handling bedpans.

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
unit_title: Section B: Isolation Precautions and Personal Protective Equipment
question: What is cohorting?
answer_html:
Cohorting is the practice of grouping together patients who are colonised or infected with the same organism (confirmed by laboratory or clinical diagnosis) in one room or ward area, when single isolation rooms are not available, to confine their care to one area and prevent spread to other patients.

Key points

  • Often used during outbreaks (e.g., rotavirus in a paediatric ward, MRSA, COVID-19).
  • Staff cohorting – assigning dedicated nurses to care only for these patients.
  • Patients with different organisms or unknown status should not be cohorted together.
  • Beds kept at least 1–2 metres apart, with dedicated equipment.

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
unit_title: Section B: Isolation Precautions and Personal Protective Equipment
question: Differentiate between a surgical mask and an N95 respirator.
answer_html:
Feature Surgical mask N95 respirator
Purpose Protects against droplets and splashes; protects the patient from the wearer Protects the wearer against airborne particles (droplet nuclei)
Filtration Not designed to filter small particles Filters at least 95% of 0.3 µm particles
Fit Loose fitting Tight-fitting; needs seal check and fit test
Use Droplet precautions, sterile procedures TB, measles, chickenpox, aerosol-generating procedures
Duration Single use; change when damp Single use (extended use as per policy)

Note: an N95 should not be worn by the patient for transport; give the patient a surgical mask.

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
question: Describe the WHO multimodal hand hygiene improvement strategy. Add a note on monitoring hand hygiene compliance in a hospital.

diagram.caption: Five components of the WHO multimodal hand hygiene improvement strategy

answer_html:
Introduction Hand hygiene is the single most important and cheapest measure to prevent health care–associated infections. Yet studies all over the world show that health workers perform hand hygiene on average in less than half of the occasions when it is needed. Simply telling staff to wash hands does not work. In 2009 the World Health Organization published the WHO Guidelines on Hand Hygiene in Health Care and a multimodal improvement strategy – an approach that tackles the problem from several sides at once. Its global campaign "SAVE LIVES: Clean Your Hands" is observed every year on 5 May.

A. The five components of the WHO multimodal strategy

1. System change

  • Ensure the infrastructure needed for hand hygiene is available at the point of care (within arm's reach of where care is given):
    • Alcohol-based hand rub (ABHR) dispensers at every bedside, trolley, ward entrance and in pocket bottles.
    • Continuous supply of safe water, liquid soap, single-use paper towels and elbow- or foot-operated taps.
    • Ratio of at least one sink per 10 beds in general wards (one per bed in ICU, as per standards).
  • Local production of ABHR using the WHO formulations (ethanol 80% or isopropyl alcohol 75% with glycerol and hydrogen peroxide) where commercial supply is costly.

2. Training and education

  • Regular training of all health workers – doctors, nurses, students, technicians and housekeeping staff – on:
    • Why hand hygiene is important (transmission by hands).
    • The "My Five Moments for Hand Hygiene" concept.
    • Correct technique of hand rubbing (20–30 seconds) and hand washing (40–60 seconds).
    • Glove use – gloves do not replace hand hygiene.
  • Induction training for new staff and periodic refresher sessions; use of videos and demonstrations.

3. Evaluation and feedback

  • Monitoring hand hygiene practices (compliance), infrastructure, consumption of hand rub and soap, and staff knowledge and perception.
  • Giving performance feedback to staff and managers – unit-wise compliance charts displayed in the ward.
  • Periodic use of the WHO Hand Hygiene Self-Assessment Framework (HHSAF) to grade the hospital (inadequate, basic, intermediate, advanced).

4. Reminders in the workplace

  • Posters showing the five moments and the technique near sinks and dispensers.
  • Screen savers, stickers on equipment, pocket cards, announcements, "Clean Your Hands" badges.
  • Regular change of posters so that they continue to catch attention.

5. Institutional safety climate

  • Commitment of the hospital leadership – hand hygiene as a priority, adequate budget, inclusion in performance appraisal.
  • Active participation of all staff – hand hygiene champions/link nurses in each ward.
  • Patient participation – encouraging patients and relatives to remind staff ("Have you cleaned your hands?").
  • A non-punitive, positive culture of safety where staff are recognised for good practice.

B. Steps of implementation (WHO)

  1. Facility preparedness – leadership, coordinator, resources.
  2. Baseline evaluation – compliance, infrastructure, knowledge.
  3. Implementation – introducing the improvement activities.
  4. Follow-up evaluation – measuring impact.
  5. Ongoing action planning and review cycle – making hand hygiene sustainable.

C. Monitoring hand hygiene compliance 1. Direct observation (gold standard)

  • Trained observers (often the ICN or link nurses) observe staff during routine care using the WHO observation form.
  • Each opportunity (an indication under the five moments) is recorded, along with whether a hand hygiene action (rub or wash) was performed.
  • Compliance (%) = (Number of hand hygiene actions ÷ Number of opportunities) × 100.
  • Observation sessions of about 20 minutes; at least 200 opportunities per unit per period for reliable results.
  • Observers should be discreet; the Hawthorne effect (people improve when watched) should be kept in mind.

2. Indirect methods

  • Consumption of hand rub and soap per 1,000 patient-days.
  • Electronic monitoring systems (sensors on dispensers, badges).
  • Self-reporting and patient feedback (less reliable).

3. Other audits

  • Infrastructure checklist – dispensers filled, sinks functioning, posters present.
  • Knowledge questionnaires; technique assessment (e.g., using fluorescent gel and UV light).

4. Using the results

  • Display monthly compliance by profession and ward; discuss in staff meetings and HICC.
  • Recognise best-performing units; plan targeted training where compliance is low.
  • Link to HAI rates to show the benefit.

D. Barriers to compliance and solutions | Barrier | Solution | |---|---| | Lack of time, heavy workload | ABHR at point of care (takes 20–30 seconds) | | Skin irritation | Hand rubs with emollients; hand creams; good-quality soap | | Sinks far away | Bedside and pocket dispensers | | Belief that gloves are enough | Education – gloves leak and hands get contaminated on removal | | Forgetfulness | Reminders, champions, patient prompts | | Lack of role models | Senior staff and doctors leading by example |

E. Role of the nurse

  • Practise hand hygiene at every moment and model it for students and attendants.
  • Keep dispensers filled and report broken taps.
  • Act as a hand hygiene link nurse/observer; educate patients and visitors.

Conclusion Hand hygiene improves only when infrastructure, education, feedback, reminders and a strong safety culture work together. The WHO multimodal strategy provides this complete package, and regular monitoring with feedback keeps compliance high.

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
question: Explain the indications for hand hygiene in the hospital.

diagram.caption: WHO "My Five Moments for Hand Hygiene"

answer_html:
Introduction Hands of health workers are the commonest route by which organisms travel from one patient to another. The WHO describes when hand hygiene is needed through the "My Five Moments for Hand Hygiene", based on the patient zone (the patient and his immediate surroundings) and the health-care area.

A. The five moments (main indications) | Moment | When | Why | Examples | |---|---|---|---| | 1. Before touching a patient | Before contact with the patient | To protect the patient from germs on your hands | Shaking hands, taking pulse/BP, helping to move, bathing | | 2. Before a clean/aseptic procedure | Immediately before | To protect the patient from germs entering the body | Injections, IV cannulation, catheter insertion, dressing, oral care, suction, eye drops, preparing medicines | | 3. After body fluid exposure risk | Immediately after (and after removing gloves) | To protect yourself and the environment | Drawing blood, emptying urine bag, handling vomit, cleaning faeces, suctioning | | 4. After touching a patient | When leaving the patient | To protect yourself and the environment | After physical examination, giving care | | 5. After touching patient surroundings | After touching objects near the patient, even without touching the patient | To protect yourself and the environment | Changing bed linen, adjusting IV drip rate, touching bed rails, monitors, bedside table |

B. Other indications

  1. When hands are visibly dirty or soiled with blood/body fluids – wash with soap and water.
  2. Before and after removing gloves.
  3. Before handling food and medicines; before eating.
  4. After using the toilet.
  5. On arrival at and before leaving the ward/work.
  6. When moving from a contaminated body site to a clean site on the same patient.
  7. After caring for patients with diarrhoea, C. difficile or norovirus – soap and water (alcohol does not kill spores and some non-enveloped viruses).
  8. Before surgery – surgical hand antisepsis.

C. Choice of method

  • Alcohol-based hand rub (20–30 seconds) – preferred for routine hand hygiene when hands are not visibly soiled.
  • Soap and water (40–60 seconds) – visibly soiled hands, after toilet, before eating, spore-forming organisms.

D. Supporting practices Short nails, no artificial nails or rings, bare below the elbows, skin care with lotions.

Conclusion Knowing the five moments helps nurses clean their hands exactly when it matters most – protecting both patients and themselves.

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
question: Differentiate between hand washing and alcohol-based hand rub. Describe the technique of each.
answer_html:
Introduction There are two methods of routine hand hygiene: hand washing with soap and water and hand rubbing with an alcohol-based hand rub (ABHR). Both follow the same WHO movements but differ in when they are used and how long they take.

A. Differences | Feature | Hand washing | Alcohol-based hand rub | |---|---|---| | Agent | Plain or antimicrobial soap and water | 60–80% alcohol (ethanol/isopropyl) with emollient | | Duration | 40–60 seconds | 20–30 seconds | | Action | Mechanical removal of dirt and organisms | Kills most bacteria, fungi and enveloped viruses | | When preferred | Visibly soiled hands, after toilet, before food, C. difficile, norovirus | Routine hand hygiene when hands are not visibly soiled | | Need sink and towel | Yes | No – at the point of care | | Skin effect | More drying if frequent | Less irritating (contains emollients) | | Effect on spores | Removes spores physically | Does not kill spores |

B. Technique of hand rub (WHO)

  1. Apply a palmful of hand rub to cover all surfaces of the hands.
  2. Rub palm to palm.
  3. Right palm over left dorsum with interlaced fingers, and vice versa.
  4. Palm to palm with fingers interlaced.
  5. Backs of fingers to opposing palms with fingers interlocked.
  6. Rotational rubbing of the left thumb clasped in the right palm, and vice versa.
