  7. Rotational rubbing of fingertips in the opposite palm (backwards and forwards), and vice versa.
  8. Continue until hands are dry – they are then safe.

C. Technique of hand washing (WHO)

  1. Remove rings and watch; wet hands with water.
  2. Apply enough soap to cover all hand surfaces.
  3. Perform the same six rubbing steps as above (palm to palm, backs of hands, between fingers, backs of fingers, thumbs, fingertips) – include wrists.
  4. Rinse hands under running water.
  5. Dry thoroughly with a single-use towel.
  6. Use the towel to turn off the tap (if not elbow-operated).
  7. Hands are now safe.

D. Points to remember

  • Do not use hand rub and soap together one after the other.
  • Avoid very hot water (dries skin).
  • Do not top up a partially empty soap dispenser (risk of contamination).
  • Gloves are not a substitute for hand hygiene.

Conclusion Hand rub is fast and effective for routine use; hand washing is essential when hands are dirty or spores are involved. Correct technique and duration make either method effective.

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
question: Define surgical hand scrub.
answer_html:
Surgical hand scrub (surgical hand antisepsis) is the thorough cleaning of the hands and forearms up to the elbows with an antimicrobial soap (or alcohol-based surgical hand rub) performed by the surgical team before donning sterile gown and gloves, to remove transient flora and reduce resident flora for the duration of surgery.

Key points

  • Duration as per product – usually 2–6 minutes with antimicrobial soap (chlorhexidine or povidone-iodine), or surgical hand rub as per manufacturer.
  • Nails short; no jewellery; hands kept above the elbows so water drains away from hands.
  • Hands dried with a sterile towel.

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
question: What is meant by "patient zone" and "health-care area" in hand hygiene?
answer_html:
Patient zone – the patient and his immediate surroundings that are temporarily dedicated to him and get contaminated by his flora: bed, bed rails, bedside table, linen, IV pump, monitor, call bell and personal belongings.

Health-care area – all surfaces outside the patient zone in the health facility: other patients and their zones, nursing station, corridors, medicine trolleys, computers, door handles.

Importance: the five moments are based on movement between these zones – hand hygiene is needed before entering the patient zone (moments 1 and 2) and after leaving it (moments 3, 4 and 5), so that organisms are not carried from one zone to another.

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
question: Explain Spaulding's classification of patient-care items and the method of reprocessing for each category. Add a note on environmental cleaning in the hospital.

diagram.caption: Spaulding's classification of patient-care items
labels: critical (enters sterile tissue) – sterilisation; semi-critical (mucous membranes
non-intact skin) – high-level disinfection; non-critical (intact skin) – low-level disinfection or cleaning; examples for each

answer_html:
Introduction Every reusable item in a hospital – from a surgical scissor to a BP cuff – must be made safe before it is used on the next patient. Since 1968, Dr Earle H. Spaulding's classification has been used to decide how much processing each item needs. It is based on the risk of infection when the item is used: the deeper the item enters the body, the higher the level of decontamination needed.

A. Basic terms

  1. Cleaning – removal of visible dirt, blood and organic matter with water, detergent and friction; always the first step – disinfection and sterilisation fail on dirty items.
  2. Disinfection – destruction of most pathogenic microorganisms but not necessarily bacterial spores.
    • High-level disinfection (HLD) – kills all microorganisms except large numbers of spores.
    • Intermediate-level – kills bacteria including M. tuberculosis, most viruses and fungi.
    • Low-level – kills most vegetative bacteria, some viruses and fungi.
  3. Sterilisation – complete destruction of all forms of microbial life, including spores.
  4. Decontamination – any process (cleaning, disinfection, sterilisation) that makes items safe to handle.

B. Spaulding's classification 1. Critical items

  • Definition: items that enter sterile tissue or the vascular system or through which blood flows.
  • Risk: any contamination can cause serious infection.
  • Examples: surgical instruments, implants, needles, urinary catheters, cardiac and IV catheters, biopsy forceps, arthroscopes, laparoscopes, surgical dressings, sutures.
  • Method: sterilisation – steam autoclave for heat-stable items; ethylene oxide, hydrogen peroxide plasma or liquid sterilants (peracetic acid, long immersion in 2% glutaraldehyde for 10 hours) for heat-sensitive items; or purchase sterile single-use items (sterilised by gamma radiation).

2. Semi-critical items

  • Definition: items that come in contact with mucous membranes or non-intact skin but do not ordinarily penetrate sterile tissue.
  • Risk: intact mucous membranes resist spores, but are susceptible to TB bacilli and viruses.
  • Examples: flexible endoscopes (gastroscope, bronchoscope, colonoscope), laryngoscope blades, endotracheal tubes, anaesthesia and respiratory therapy equipment, vaginal specula, cystoscopes (minimum HLD), oral thermometers, ultrasound probes for internal use.
  • Method: at least high-level disinfection (sterilisation preferred where possible):
    • 2% glutaraldehyde for 20 minutes (after thorough cleaning), then rinse with sterile or filtered water and dry.
    • 0.55% ortho-phthalaldehyde (OPA), peracetic acid, hydrogen peroxide 6–7.5%.
    • Pasteurisation (hot water at 70 °C for 30 minutes) for respiratory equipment.

3. Non-critical items

  • Definition: items that touch only intact skin, not mucous membranes, or do not directly touch the patient.
  • Risk: intact skin is an effective barrier; risk is low.
  • Examples: BP cuffs, stethoscopes, bedpans, urinals, crutches, bed rails, bedside tables, patient furniture, ECG leads, pulse oximeter probes, wheelchairs.
  • Method: cleaning with detergent and low- or intermediate-level disinfection – 70% alcohol, sodium hypochlorite, quaternary ammonium compounds, phenolics; bedpans in washer-disinfectors (thermal disinfection).

Summary table | Category | Contact | Examples | Processing | |---|---|---|---| | Critical | Sterile tissue, blood | Surgical instruments, catheters, needles, implants | Sterilisation | | Semi-critical | Mucous membranes, non-intact skin | Endoscopes, laryngoscope blades, ET tubes, specula | High-level disinfection (minimum) | | Non-critical | Intact skin | BP cuff, stethoscope, bedpan, bed rails | Cleaning + low/intermediate disinfection |

C. Steps of reprocessing reusable items

  1. Point-of-use pre-cleaning – wipe off gross soil; keep instruments moist (enzymatic spray) to prevent drying of blood.
  2. Safe transport to CSSD in closed, leak-proof containers.
  3. Cleaning – manual brushing under water or ultrasonic cleaner/washer-disinfector with enzymatic detergent.
  4. Rinsing and drying.
  5. Inspection for cleanliness and damage; assembly and packing (with indicators).
  6. Disinfection or sterilisation as per category.
  7. Storage in clean, dry, dust-free areas; "first in, first out"; check pack integrity and expiry/event-related sterility.
  8. Documentation and traceability – load numbers linked to patients.

D. Environmental cleaning in the hospital 1. Principles

  • Clean before disinfecting; detergent and water remove most organisms.
  • Clean from clean to dirty areas and from top to bottom; high areas before floors.
  • Use damp dusting and wet mopping – never dry sweeping or dusting, which spreads dust and organisms into the air.
  • High-touch surfaces (bed rails, call bells, switches, door handles, IV stands, monitors, taps) cleaned more often – at least twice daily, more in ICU and isolation rooms.
  • Use colour-coded mops, cloths and buckets for different areas (e.g., toilets, patient areas, kitchen) to avoid cross-contamination – as per hospital policy.
  • Two- or three-bucket system (detergent solution, rinse water, disinfectant).
  • Prepare disinfectant solutions freshly at the correct dilution; observe contact time.

2. Agents

  • Routine: detergent and water.
  • Disinfection: sodium hypochlorite (1% for blood spills and isolation rooms; lower strength for general surfaces as per policy), 70% alcohol for small surfaces and equipment, quaternary ammonium compounds.
  • Spills of blood and body fluids: spill kit, absorb, apply 1% hypochlorite for about 10–20 minutes, wipe, discard in yellow bag.

3. Types of cleaning

  • Routine (daily) cleaning of wards.
  • Terminal cleaning after discharge or transfer, especially from isolation rooms (all surfaces, mattress, curtains changed).
  • OT cleaning – before the first case, between cases (surfaces near the table, floor around), end-of-day terminal cleaning, weekly thorough cleaning; restricted traffic.
  • Outbreak cleaning – increased frequency; sporicidal agents for C. difficile.

4. Supervision The ward sister supervises housekeeping staff, ensures supplies, uses cleaning checklists and audits (e.g., fluorescent marker method) and trains staff on PPE and dilutions.

Conclusion Spaulding's simple three-level system ensures that every item receives the right level of processing – sterilisation for critical, high-level disinfection for semi-critical and cleaning with low-level disinfection for non-critical items. Combined with regular, correct environmental cleaning, it removes the hospital environment as a source of infection.

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
question: Classify the methods of sterilisation. Explain the principle and working of the autoclave.

diagram.caption: Parts of an autoclave

answer_html:
Definition Sterilisation is the process by which an article, surface or medium is made free from all microorganisms, including bacterial spores.

A. Classification of methods of sterilisation 1. Physical methods (a) Heat – the most reliable method.

  • Dry heat (kills by oxidation and protein denaturation)
    • Red heat / flaming – inoculating loops, forceps tips.
    • Incineration – infectious waste, soiled dressings, anatomical waste.
    • Hot air oven – 160 °C for 2 hours (or 170 °C for 1 hour, 180 °C for 30 minutes); for glassware, powders, oils, petroleum jelly, metal instruments.

  • Moist heat (kills by coagulation of proteins; more efficient than dry heat)

    • Below 100 °C – pasteurisation (milk), inspissation (egg/serum media at 80–85 °C), vaccine baths.
    • At 100 °C – boiling (10–30 minutes; kills vegetative forms but not all spores – a disinfection method), Tyndallisation (steaming at 100 °C for 20 minutes on 3 successive days).
    • Above 100 °C – autoclave (steam under pressure). (b) Filtration – membrane filters (0.22 µm) for heat-sensitive liquids (sera, antibiotic solutions); HEPA filters for air in OT, ICU and biosafety cabinets. (c) Radiation

  • Ionising (gamma rays from cobalt-60) – "cold sterilisation" of disposable syringes, catheters, gloves, sutures, IV sets.

  • Non-ionising (UV rays) – surface and air disinfection in rooms and safety cabinets (poor penetration). (d) Ultrasonic vibration – used for cleaning instruments (not sterilisation).

2. Chemical methods

  • Gases – ethylene oxide (heat-sensitive items: plastics, catheters, heart-lung machine parts; needs aeration as it is toxic), formaldehyde gas, hydrogen peroxide plasma (low-temperature sterilisers).
  • Liquids – 2% glutaraldehyde (prolonged immersion – 10 hours), peracetic acid.

B. Autoclave 1. Principle

  • Water boils at 100 °C at normal atmospheric pressure. When pressure is raised, the boiling point rises.
  • At 15 pounds per square inch (psi) above atmospheric pressure (about 1.05 kg/cm²), steam reaches 121 °C.
  • Saturated steam condenses on the cooler articles, releasing a large amount of latent heat, which penetrates deeply and coagulates the proteins of all microbes, including spores.
  • Condensation also reduces volume, drawing in fresh steam.

2. Parts Pressure chamber (vertical or horizontal), lid with gasket and screw clamps, pressure gauge, safety valve, discharge (air exhaust) tap, heating element, water, perforated tray/basket, thermometer or automatic controls.

3. Working (procedure)

  1. Clean and dry articles; pack loosely in drums or wrapped trays with chemical indicators inside and autoclave tape outside.
  2. Fill water to the correct level; load articles without overcrowding so that steam can circulate.
  3. Close the lid tightly; switch on the heater with the discharge tap open.
  4. Let all the air escape until a steady jet of steam comes out (air–steam mixtures have a lower temperature) – then close the tap.
  5. Allow pressure to rise to 15 psi (121 °C) and maintain it for 15–20 minutes (holding time); at 134 °C (30 psi) only 3–4 minutes are needed (flash/high-vacuum autoclaves).
  6. Switch off; allow the pressure to fall to zero gradually before opening, to avoid wet packs and boiling over.
  7. Dry, unload, record and store.

4. Uses Surgical instruments, linen, gowns, dressings, rubber articles, culture media, laboratory and biomedical waste (red and white categories).

5. Quality control Pressure and temperature records, chemical indicators (autoclave tape, Browne's tubes), Bowie–Dick test (prevacuum autoclaves), and biological indicators – spores of Geobacillus stearothermophilus.

Conclusion Heat is the most reliable sterilising agent and the autoclave is the work-horse of every hospital, killing even spores within minutes when used correctly.

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
question: Name six disinfectants and their uses in health care.
answer_html:
Definition A disinfectant is a chemical that destroys most pathogenic microorganisms on inanimate objects; an antiseptic is a disinfectant safe enough to be used on living tissues (skin, wounds).

Six common disinfectants 1. Alcohols – 70% ethyl alcohol, isopropyl alcohol

  • Uses: skin antisepsis before injections and cannulation; alcohol-based hand rubs; disinfection of thermometers, stethoscopes, vial tops, small surfaces.
  • Points: act fast by denaturing proteins; 70% is better than absolute alcohol (water helps penetration); not sporicidal; flammable; evaporates quickly.

2. Chlorine compounds – sodium hypochlorite, bleaching powder

  • Uses: 1% sodium hypochlorite for blood and body-fluid spills, contaminated surfaces, isolation rooms, disinfection of contaminated items before disposal; lower strengths for general environmental cleaning; bleaching powder for latrines and drains; chlorine tablets for drinking water.
  • Points: broad-spectrum, cheap, sporicidal at high concentration; corrosive to metals, inactivated by organic matter; prepare fresh daily.

3. Glutaraldehyde (2%)

  • Uses: high-level disinfection of heat-sensitive semi-critical items – endoscopes, laryngoscope blades, anaesthesia equipment (20 minutes); sterilisation by immersion for 10 hours.
  • Points: activated alkaline solution, usable for about 14 days; irritant to skin, eyes and airways – use in ventilated area with PPE; rinse items with sterile water.

4. Chlorhexidine (0.5–4%)

  • Uses: surgical hand scrub (4%), skin preparation before surgery and central-line insertion (2% chlorhexidine in 70% alcohol), mouthwash for oral care (0.2%), wound cleaning (with cetrimide as Savlon), bathing in ICU.
  • Points: persistent residual action; more active against Gram-positive bacteria; avoid contact with eyes, middle ear and meninges.

5. Povidone-iodine (5–10%)

  • Uses: pre-operative skin preparation, surgical scrub (7.5%), wound and burn antisepsis, vaginal preparation, disinfection of vial tops and catheter sites.
  • Points: broad-spectrum (bacteria, viruses, fungi); needs about 2 minutes contact; stains skin; caution in iodine allergy and neonates.

6. Hydrogen peroxide (3–7.5%)

  • Uses: 3% for cleaning wounds (froth lifts debris; good against anaerobes), mouthwash; 6–7.5% as high-level disinfectant; vaporised hydrogen peroxide for room disinfection (fogging).
  • Points: decomposes into water and oxygen; avoid in closed cavities (gas embolism).

Other disinfectants

  • Phenolics (phenol, cresol, "black phenyl") – floors, toilets, drains (avoid in nurseries).
  • Quaternary ammonium compounds (cetrimide, benzalkonium) – surfaces, non-critical items.
  • Formaldehyde (formalin) – preserving tissue specimens (10% formalin); fumigation (now discouraged).

Principles of use Clean before disinfecting, use the correct dilution, observe contact time, label containers with date, never top up old solutions, and wear gloves.

Conclusion Choosing the right disinfectant at the right strength for the right purpose is a daily nursing responsibility in infection control.

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
question: Explain the methods of monitoring sterilisation (sterilisation indicators).
answer_html:
Introduction A pack that looks sterile may not be sterile. Sterilisation can fail because of air pockets, overloading, wet packs or machine faults. Therefore every sterilisation cycle must be monitored using physical, chemical and biological methods, and records kept so that items can be recalled if a failure is found.

1. Physical (mechanical) monitoring

  • Checking and recording time, temperature and pressure for every cycle using gauges, thermometers, digital displays and printouts/charts.
  • Detects obvious machine failures but does not guarantee that steam reached the inside of every pack.

2. Chemical indicators Chemicals that change colour when exposed to one or more critical conditions (temperature, time, steam).

  • External indicators (process indicators) – e.g., autoclave tape with stripes that darken; show that the pack has been through a cycle, not that it is sterile.
  • Internal indicators – placed inside each pack at the hardest-to-reach point; show that steam penetrated.
  • Integrators (multi-parameter indicators) – respond to all critical variables; closely match biological indicator results.
  • Browne's tubes – sealed tubes with red fluid that turns green after correct time–temperature exposure (older practice).
  • Bowie–Dick test – a special air-removal test for prevacuum autoclaves, done daily before the first load.

3. Biological indicators (BI) – most reliable

  • Contain highly resistant bacterial spores:
    • Geobacillus stearothermophilus – for steam autoclaves and hydrogen peroxide plasma.
    • Bacillus atrophaeus – for dry heat and ethylene oxide.
  • Method: spore strips or self-contained vials are placed in the most difficult location of the load; after the cycle they are incubated (56–60 °C for G. stearothermophilus); a control (unprocessed) BI is incubated alongside.
  • Result: no growth (no colour change) = sterilisation achieved; growth (colour change) = failure.
  • Frequency: at least weekly (preferably daily), with every load containing implants, after repairs and when a new steriliser is installed.
  • Rapid-readout BIs give results within 1–3 hours.

4. Other quality measures

  • Load records (load number, contents, operator) and labels on each pack for traceability.
  • Recall procedure when a BI is positive – quarantine and reprocess all items since the last negative BI.
  • Storage – clean, dry, closed shelves; packs checked for tears, moisture and expiry (time- or event-related sterility).
  • Regular preventive maintenance and validation of sterilisers.

Nurse's role Check the indicator colour change, integrity, dryness and date of every sterile pack before opening it; reject packs that are wet, torn or with unchanged indicators; report failures to the CSSD.

Conclusion Physical, chemical and biological indicators together give confidence that sterilisation has truly been achieved; the biological indicator is the gold standard.

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
question: List the types of sterilisation.
answer_html:
Types (methods) of sterilisation A. Physical

  1. Dry heat – flaming, incineration, hot air oven (160 °C for 2 hours).
  2. Moist heat – autoclave (121 °C, 15 psi, 15–20 minutes), Tyndallisation.
  3. Filtration – membrane filters, HEPA filters.
  4. Radiation – gamma rays (disposables), UV rays (surfaces).

B. Chemical

  1. Gases – ethylene oxide, formaldehyde, hydrogen peroxide plasma.
  2. Liquids – 2% glutaraldehyde (prolonged immersion), peracetic acid.

Most reliable method: moist heat in an autoclave; heat-sensitive items need ethylene oxide, plasma or radiation.

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
question: What is the Bowie–Dick test?
answer_html:
The Bowie–Dick test is a daily air-removal and steam-penetration test for pre-vacuum (porous load) steam sterilisers, introduced by Bowie and Dick (1963).

Method

  • A standard test pack with a chemical indicator sheet in its centre is placed alone in the empty chamber near the drain.
  • Run at 134 °C for 3.5–4 minutes every morning before the first load.

Result

  • Uniform colour change across the sheet – pass (air removed properly).
  • Lighter or uneven area in the centre – fail (air leak or poor air removal); the steriliser must not be used until repaired.

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
question: Explain the collection, labelling and transport of specimens for microbiological examination – blood culture, urine culture, pus/wound swab, throat swab and cerebrospinal fluid.

diagram.caption: Steps of blood culture collection

answer_html:
Introduction A laboratory report can only be as good as the specimen sent. A contaminated, delayed or wrongly collected specimen gives misleading results – leading to wrong antibiotics, longer stay and antimicrobial resistance. Nurses collect most specimens, so correct technique is a key nursing skill. (Sputum and stool collection were studied in Nursing Foundations; here we concentrate on other common microbiological specimens.)

A. General points for all specimens

  • Collect before starting antibiotics (or note the antibiotic and time on the form).
  • Use sterile, leak-proof, correctly labelled containers supplied by the laboratory.
  • Collect from the actual site of infection and avoid contamination with normal flora.
  • Adequate quantity; send promptly (within 1–2 hours); follow storage rules if delay is unavoidable.
  • Complete the requisition form with clinical details.
  • Follow standard precautions; place specimens in sealed bags for transport.

B. Blood culture Indications: fever with chills, suspected sepsis, endocarditis, typhoid, pneumonia, meningitis, neonatal sepsis. Procedure

  1. Explain the procedure; perform hand hygiene; wear gloves.
  2. Select a fresh venepuncture site (not from an existing IV line, except when catheter infection is being investigated as ordered).
  3. Skin antisepsis with 2% chlorhexidine in 70% alcohol (or povidone-iodine followed by alcohol), scrubbing for 30 seconds; allow it to dry completely (about 30 seconds–2 minutes). Do not touch the site again.
  4. Remove the caps of blood culture bottles and disinfect the rubber tops with 70% alcohol.
  5. Draw blood: adults 8–10 ml per bottle (one set = aerobic + anaerobic bottle, 16–20 ml); children 1–3 ml in a paediatric bottle. Correct volume is the most important factor for positive yield.
  6. Two sets from two different sites (and at different times in endocarditis) – helps to distinguish true infection from skin contaminants.
  7. Inoculate without introducing air into the anaerobic bottle; mix gently.
  8. Label each bottle (not over the barcode), with site and time of collection.
  9. Transport at room temperature within 2 hours; never refrigerate blood culture bottles.

C. Urine culture 1. Clean-catch mid-stream urine (MSU)

  • Explain to the patient; wash hands; clean the periurethral area with soap and water (not antiseptic).
  • Females separate the labia; males retract the foreskin.
  • Pass the first part of the stream into the toilet, then collect 10–20 ml of the middle stream in a sterile wide-mouthed container without touching its inside; pass the rest into the toilet.

  • First-morning sample is preferred (more concentrated). 2. Catheterised patients

  • Never collect from the urine bag.

  • Clamp the tubing below the sampling port for 10–15 minutes if needed; disinfect the sampling port with 70% alcohol; aspirate urine with a sterile needle and syringe; unclamp.
  • When a long-term catheter is changed, collect from the new catheter. 3. Infants – sterile urine bag (after cleaning) or suprapubic aspiration/catheter sample by the doctor. 4. Urine for AFB – whole early-morning sample on three consecutive days. Transport – within 1–2 hours or refrigerate at 4 °C (up to 24 hours) or use boric acid containers – otherwise bacteria multiply and give false high counts.

D. Pus and wound swabs

  • Aspirated pus in a sterile syringe is better than a swab (more organisms, anaerobes survive).
  • Remove the old dressing; clean the wound surface with sterile saline to remove surface contaminants and old exudate; do not use antiseptic before collection.
  • Swab the base or advancing edge of the wound, rotating the swab over about 1 cm² with gentle pressure (Levine technique) – not the dry eschar or surface pus.
  • Take two swabs – one for Gram stain, one for culture; place in transport medium (Stuart's or Amies).
  • For anaerobes – aspirate, expel air, cap the syringe (or use anaerobic transport medium) and send immediately.
  • Tissue biopsy from the deep wound gives the best results in chronic wounds.

E. Throat swab

  • Collect before mouthwash, antibiotics or food.
  • Seat the patient facing a good light; ask him to open the mouth and say "aah"; depress the tongue with a spatula.
  • Rub the swab firmly over both tonsils, tonsillar pillars and the posterior pharyngeal wall, avoiding the tongue, cheeks and teeth.
  • In suspected diphtheria, take swabs from under the edge of the membrane (two swabs).
  • Place in transport medium and send promptly.
  • For viral studies (influenza, COVID-19) – nasopharyngeal/oropharyngeal swab in viral transport medium (VTM), kept at 2–8 °C, with PPE (N95, face shield).

F. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF)

  • Collected by the doctor by lumbar puncture with full surgical asepsis; the nurse positions the patient (lateral with knees to chest or sitting bent forward), prepares sterile equipment and supports the patient.
  • Collect 3–4 sterile tubes (about 1–2 ml each; more – 5–10 ml – for TB and fungal culture), numbered in order: e.g., tube 1 biochemistry, tube 2 microbiology (Gram stain, culture), tube 3 cell count.
  • Send immediately by hand; never refrigerate (meningococci and Haemophilus die in the cold); inform the laboratory of the urgent sample.
  • Post-procedure: patient lies flat as advised, monitor for headache and neurological signs.

G. Labelling and documentation Each container must carry: patient's full name, age, sex, hospital number (UHID), ward/bed, type and site of specimen, date and time of collection, test required, clinical diagnosis, antibiotics given, and the collector's signature. The label goes on the container, not the lid, and must match the requisition form; high-risk specimens carry a biohazard label.

H. Common errors and their effects | Error | Effect | |---|---| | Collection after antibiotics | False-negative culture | | Poor skin antisepsis | Contaminated blood culture (skin flora) | | Urine from the drainage bag | False positive, mixed growth | | Delay at room temperature | Overgrowth or death of organisms | | Refrigerating CSF/blood culture | Death of fastidious organisms | | Unlabelled/wrongly labelled specimen | Rejection or wrong patient's report |

Conclusion Each specimen has its own correct method, container, quantity and transport condition. When the nurse collects specimens aseptically, labels them accurately and sends them quickly, the laboratory can give a true report that guides life-saving treatment.

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
question: Describe the principles of specimen collection and the nurse's responsibilities in handling patient specimens.
answer_html:
Introduction A specimen is a sample of body tissue or fluid sent to the laboratory for examination. Correct collection and handling ensure an accurate diagnosis and protect health workers from infection.

A. Principles of specimen collection

  1. Right specimen from the right site – representative of the disease process (pus from the depth of a wound, not surface exudate; deep-cough sputum, not saliva).
  2. Right time
    • Before antibiotics and antiseptics.
    • At the right stage of disease – blood culture in the first week of typhoid, early-morning sputum and urine for AFB, blood smear during fever for malaria, paired sera for serology.
  3. Right quantity – too little gives false-negative results (e.g., blood culture volume).
  4. Aseptic technique – avoid contamination with normal flora; sterile containers.
  5. Right container and preservative/transport medium – sterile screw-capped bottles, blood culture bottles, transport media (Stuart's, Cary–Blair, VTM), anticoagulants (EDTA, citrate) as required.
  6. Proper labelling and requisition with full details.
  7. Prompt transport under correct conditions (room temperature, 4 °C, or ice) as per test.
  8. Safety – treat every specimen as potentially infectious (standard precautions).

B. Nurse's responsibilities Before collection

  • Check the doctor's order and requisition; identify the patient using two identifiers.
  • Explain the procedure and obtain cooperation (e.g., how to give MSU or sputum); ensure privacy.
  • Collect the correct containers and check expiry of transport media.
  • Note whether antibiotics have already been started.

During collection

  • Perform hand hygiene; wear gloves and other PPE as required.
  • Follow the correct technique and aseptic precautions; avoid touching the inside of the container or lid.
  • Collect the right amount; close the lid tightly; wipe the outside if soiled.
  • Label the container at the bedside, in the presence of the patient – never pre-label or label later.

After collection

  • Place the specimen in a sealed leak-proof plastic bag with the form in a separate pocket; keep upright.
  • Send immediately; if delay is unavoidable, store as per laboratory instructions (urine in refrigerator; CSF and blood cultures at room temperature).
  • Use covered carrier boxes for transport; never carry specimens in pockets or hands.
  • Dispose of used materials in correct BMW bins; perform hand hygiene.
  • Document the time, type of specimen and any difficulties in the nurse's record.
  • Follow up the report; inform the doctor of critical results (positive blood culture, AFB-positive smear) without delay.

C. Safety in handling specimens

  • Avoid spills; manage spills with a spill kit and 1% hypochlorite.
  • Report needle-stick or splash injuries immediately.
  • High-risk specimens (suspected HIV, hepatitis B, TB, COVID-19) need extra care – biohazard labels, triple packaging for transport outside the hospital.

Conclusion Following these principles and responsibilities ensures that every specimen reaches the laboratory in a state that reflects the patient's true condition – safely and on time.

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
question: Explain the biosafety measures for packaging and transporting infectious specimens.

diagram.caption: Triple packaging system for infectious specimens
labels: rigid outer packaging with UN3373 label and addresses

answer_html:
Introduction Specimens may contain dangerous pathogens such as HIV, hepatitis B virus, M. tuberculosis or SARS-CoV-2. They must be packed and transported so that they do not leak, break or expose couriers, laboratory staff or the public, while keeping the organisms viable for testing. The WHO recommends the triple packaging system for transport outside the hospital.

A. Triple packaging system

  1. Primary receptacle
    • The leak-proof, watertight container holding the specimen (tube, bottle) – tightly capped, sealed with parafilm if needed and correctly labelled.
    • Wrapped in enough absorbent material (cotton, paper) to absorb the entire contents if it breaks.
  2. Secondary packaging
    • A second durable, leak-proof, watertight container (plastic container or sealed bag) that encloses one or more primary receptacles with absorbent material.
    • Request forms and documents are placed outside the secondary packaging, in a separate plastic envelope.
  3. Outer packaging
    • A rigid outer box (cardboard or insulated box) that protects the contents from physical damage during transit; ice packs or dry ice are placed here if cooling is needed.
    • Labels: sender's and receiver's names and addresses, telephone of responsible person, orientation arrows, and the hazard label – e.g., "UN3373 – Biological Substance, Category B" for most diagnostic specimens; stricter packaging (UN2814) for Category A (highly dangerous) agents.

B. Transport within the hospital

  • Specimens in sealed plastic bags with the form in a separate pocket.
  • Carried in closed, leak-proof, washable carrier boxes kept upright – not in hands or pockets; pneumatic tube systems where available.
  • Trained porters; spill kit available.
  • Leaking or broken specimens are rejected and handled with care.

C. Laboratory biosafety practices

  • Open specimens in a biosafety cabinet, especially TB and other risky specimens.
  • Wear gloves, gown and eye protection; no eating or drinking; no mouth pipetting.
  • Disinfect work surfaces after use; autoclave cultures and specimen waste before disposal.
  • Biosafety levels (BSL-1 to BSL-4) according to the risk of organisms.

D. Spill management

  1. Inform others and restrict the area.
  2. Wear PPE (gloves, gown, mask, goggles).
  3. Cover the spill with absorbent material; pour 1% sodium hypochlorite around and over it; leave for about 10–20 minutes.
  4. Pick up broken glass with forceps/scoop into a sharps container; wipe from the periphery towards the centre.
  5. Discard waste in a yellow bag; clean the area again with detergent; remove PPE and wash hands; record the incident.

Conclusion Proper packaging and careful transport protect people who handle specimens and preserve the quality of the sample – biosafety and accuracy go together.

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
question: Enumerate the purposes of labelling specimens.
answer_html:
Purposes of labelling specimens

  1. Correct patient identification – prevents reports being given to the wrong patient.
  2. Links the specimen with the requisition form and the test required.
  3. Tells the laboratory the type and site of specimen (e.g., wound swab – left leg).
  4. Records the date and time of collection – important for interpretation (delayed specimens, timing of fever, paired sera).
  5. Conveys antibiotic history and clinical diagnosis for proper processing.
  6. Warns staff about biohazard/high-risk specimens.
  7. Provides legal record and traceability; helps in quality control.

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
question: Why is a clean-catch mid-stream urine sample preferred for culture?
answer_html:
A clean-catch mid-stream urine (MSU) sample is preferred because:

  1. The first part of the stream washes out the bacteria normally present in the distal urethra and around the meatus; the middle portion represents bladder urine.
  2. Cleaning the periurethral area reduces contamination by skin and perineal flora.
  3. It avoids the risk of infection caused by catheterisation.
  4. It gives a reliable colony count – ≥10⁵ CFU/ml of a single organism indicates significant bacteriuria, whereas contaminated samples show mixed growth.
  5. It is simple and can be done by the patient after proper instruction.

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
unit_title: Section B: Biomedical Waste and Laundry Management
question: Explain biomedical waste management as per the Biomedical Waste Management Rules, 2016 – categories, colour coding, segregation, collection, storage, transport, treatment and disposal, and staff precautions.

diagram.caption: Colour coding of biomedical waste as per BMW Rules 2016
labels: lab waste; red – contaminated recyclable plastics; white translucent – sharps; blue – glassware and metallic implants; treatment and disposal for each

answer_html:
Introduction Biomedical waste (BMW) is any waste generated during the diagnosis, treatment or immunisation of human beings or animals, or in research activities related to them. About 10–25% of hospital waste is hazardous (infectious, sharp, chemical, radioactive); the rest is general waste. If not managed properly, BMW spreads HIV, hepatitis B and C, causes needle-stick injuries to rag-pickers and sanitation workers, and pollutes air, water and soil. In India it is regulated by the Bio-Medical Waste Management Rules, 2016 (amended in 2018 and 2019) under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986, monitored by the State Pollution Control Boards.

A. Steps of BMW management Generation → segregation at source → collection → storage → transport → treatment → disposal

B. Categories and colour coding (Schedule I) 1. Yellow category (non-chlorinated yellow plastic bags; separate containers for liquids)

  • (a) Human anatomical waste – tissues, organs, body parts, placenta, fetus below viability.
  • (b) Animal anatomical waste.
  • (c) Soiled waste – items contaminated with blood or body fluids: dressings, cotton swabs, plaster casts, bags with residual blood.
  • (d) Expired or discarded medicines – including cytotoxic drugs and items contaminated with them (cytotoxic label).
  • (e) Chemical waste – discarded chemicals and disinfectants.
  • (f) Chemical liquid waste – collected separately, pre-treated before discharge.
  • (g) Discarded linen, mattresses, beddings contaminated with blood or body fluids.
  • (h) Microbiology, biotechnology and clinical laboratory waste – cultures, specimens, live/attenuated vaccines, blood bags – pre-treated on site by autoclaving/disinfection.
  • Treatment: incineration or plasma pyrolysis; deep burial only in remote rural areas with permission.

2. Red category (non-chlorinated red bags/containers) – contaminated recyclable waste

  • Disposable plastic items – tubing, IV sets and bottles, catheters, urine bags, syringes without needles, vacutainers with needles cut, gloves.
  • Treatment: autoclaving or microwaving/hydroclaving followed by shredding or mutilation; the treated plastic is sent to authorised recyclers – never to landfill or for burning.

3. White (translucent) category – puncture-proof, leak-proof, tamper-proof containers

  • Waste sharps including metals – needles, syringes with fixed needles, needles from needle-cutters, scalpels, blades, other sharp metal objects.
  • Treatment: autoclaving or dry-heat sterilisation, then shredding/mutilation or encapsulation; final disposal in iron foundries or sharps pits.

4. Blue category – cardboard boxes with blue marking (or puncture-proof containers)

  • Glassware – broken or discarded contaminated glass, medicine vials and ampoules (except those contaminated with cytotoxic drugs).
  • Metallic body implants.
  • Treatment: disinfection (soaking in hypochlorite) or autoclaving, then recycling.

General (non-infectious) waste – paper, food waste, packaging – goes in black/green bins as per municipal solid waste rules.

C. Segregation

  • At the point of generation (bedside, procedure room) by the person generating waste – usually the nurse or doctor.
  • Bins of each colour at every care point, with posters showing what goes where.
  • Bags filled only up to three-fourths; never mix categories; never re-sort waste by hand.
  • Use needle cutters/destroyers; never recap needles.

D. Collection, labelling and storage

  • Bags and containers tied securely and labelled with the biohazard symbol (or cytotoxic symbol), name of the facility, date, category and weight; bar coding for tracking.
  • Collected by trained staff in closed trolleys at fixed times, via routes away from patient and food areas.
  • Stored in a separate, secure, well-ventilated storage room with a biohazard sign, away from public access.
  • Untreated BMW must not be stored for more than 48 hours.

E. Transport

  • Within the hospital – covered wheeled trolleys.
  • Outside – by the Common Bio-medical Waste Treatment Facility (CBWTF) in closed vehicles with biohazard signs; manifest/record maintained.

F. Treatment and disposal methods (summary) | Method | Used for | |---|---| | Incineration / plasma pyrolysis | Yellow category | | Autoclave, microwave, hydroclave + shredding | Red and white categories, lab waste | | Chemical disinfection (hypochlorite) | Blue (glass), liquid waste | | Encapsulation / sharps pit | Sharps | | Deep burial (permission needed) | Anatomical waste in remote areas | | Recycling (after treatment) | Plastics, glass, metal |

G. Important provisions of the Rules

  1. Phasing out of chlorinated plastic bags and gloves (burning them releases dioxins).
  2. Pre-treatment of laboratory and highly infectious waste on site.
  3. Training of all health workers at induction and at least once a year.
  4. Immunisation of all health workers and waste handlers against hepatitis B and tetanus.
  5. Records of BMW generated and treated; annual report to the State Pollution Control Board by 30 June; records kept for 5 years.
  6. Accident reporting (spills, needle-stick injuries) and corrective action.
  7. A BMW Management Committee in hospitals to review practices.

H. Staff precautions

  • Wear PPE – heavy-duty gloves, apron, mask, boots – while handling waste.
  • Never open or overfill bags; carry bags away from the body; do not drag them.
  • Hand hygiene after handling; report injuries; get vaccinated.
  • Use spill kits for leaks.

I. Role of the nurse Correct segregation at the bedside, supervising Group D staff, training students, maintaining records, ensuring supplies of bags and containers, and participating in audits (Kayakalp/NABH).

Conclusion Biomedical waste is safely managed only when every health worker segregates correctly at the source. Following the BMW Rules 2016 protects patients, staff, waste workers, the community and the environment.

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
unit_title: Section B: Biomedical Waste and Laundry Management
question: Describe the types of hospital waste with examples.
answer_html:
Introduction Hospitals generate many kinds of waste. About 75–90% is general, non-hazardous waste similar to household waste; 10–25% is hazardous and needs special handling. Classifying waste correctly is the first step in safe disposal. The WHO classification is commonly used, along with the categories of the BMW Rules 2016.

A. Non-hazardous (general) waste

  • Paper, cardboard, packaging, food waste, fruit peels, leaves, office waste.
  • Disposed of as municipal solid waste (wet and dry bins).

B. Hazardous health-care waste 1. Infectious waste – suspected to contain pathogens.

  • Dressings, swabs and bandages soiled with blood/pus; cultures and stocks from laboratories; waste from isolation wards; items contaminated with blood (blood bags, tubing).

2. Pathological (anatomical) waste

  • Human tissues, organs, body parts, placenta, fetuses, blood and body fluids, animal carcasses from laboratories.

3. Sharps

  • Needles, syringes with needles, scalpels, blades, broken glass, lancets, IV cannula stylets, infusion sets with spikes.
  • Cause cuts and needle-stick injuries – the most dangerous type for workers.

4. Pharmaceutical waste

  • Expired, unused or contaminated medicines, vaccines and sera; bottles and boxes with residues.

5. Cytotoxic (genotoxic) waste

  • Anticancer drugs and items contaminated with them (vials, syringes, gloves); urine and vomit of patients on chemotherapy.

6. Chemical waste

  • Laboratory reagents, disinfectants (glutaraldehyde, formalin), film-developing solutions, solvents, batteries.

7. Waste with high heavy-metal content

  • Mercury from broken thermometers and BP apparatus, cadmium from batteries.

8. Pressurised containers

  • Empty or partly filled gas cylinders, cartridges, aerosol cans (explode if incinerated).

9. Radioactive waste

  • Materials contaminated with radionuclides from nuclear medicine and radiotherapy (iodine-131 waste, sealed sources, contaminated linen) – managed under Atomic Energy Regulatory Board (AERB) rules.

C. Categories under BMW Rules 2016 (colour coding) | Colour | Waste | |---|---| | Yellow | Anatomical, soiled, expired medicines, chemical, lab and contaminated linen waste | | Red | Contaminated recyclable plastics (tubing, catheters, gloves, syringes without needles) | | White (translucent) | Sharps including metals | | Blue | Glassware and metallic implants |

Nursing importance Knowing the type of waste helps the nurse segregate correctly at the point of generation, which determines safe treatment and protects workers and the environment.

Conclusion Hospital waste is varied; the hazardous fraction is small but dangerous, and proper identification of each type is the foundation of safe waste management.

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
unit_title: Section B: Biomedical Waste and Laundry Management
question: Explain the importance of biomedical waste management in preventing hospital infection.
answer_html:
Introduction Biomedical waste contains blood, body fluids, pus, sharps and cultures loaded with microorganisms. Poorly managed waste is a reservoir and vehicle of infection inside and outside the hospital. Proper waste management is therefore an essential part of the infection control programme.

1. Breaks the chain of infection

  • Infectious waste is a source of organisms; safe segregation, containment and treatment remove this reservoir.
  • Prevents transmission by contact (soiled dressings), sharps (needles) and vectors (flies, rats attracted to open waste).

2. Prevents needle-stick and sharp injuries

  • Sharps disposed of at the point of use in puncture-proof containers protect nurses, doctors, ward attendants, housekeeping staff and waste handlers from HIV, hepatitis B and hepatitis C.
  • Needle cutters and destroyers prevent reuse of syringes.

3. Protects patients

  • Removes contaminated items from the patient's environment; prevents contamination of surfaces and equipment.
  • Prevents reuse and illegal recycling of syringes and IV sets – a major cause of hepatitis outbreaks in the community.

4. Protects the community and environment

  • Stops spread of infection to rag-pickers, scavengers, animals and the public.
  • Prevents contamination of soil and water (cholera, typhoid, hepatitis) and air pollution (dioxins from burning chlorinated plastics).
  • Prevents breeding of flies, mosquitoes and rodents around hospitals.

5. Reduces antimicrobial resistance spread

  • Proper treatment of laboratory cultures and pharmaceutical waste prevents release of resistant organisms and antibiotics into the environment.

6. Improves hospital hygiene and image

  • Clean wards without overflowing bins, foul smell or flies; better patient satisfaction and staff morale.
  • Essential for NABH accreditation and Kayakalp awards; avoids legal penalties under the BMW Rules 2016.

7. Economic benefit

  • Proper segregation reduces the volume of costly infectious waste treatment; recyclable plastics and glass are recovered after disinfection.

Role of the nurse Segregate at the source, use correct colour bins, never overfill or recap, supervise and train housekeeping staff, manage spills, report injuries and maintain records.

8. Real-life lessons Outbreaks of hepatitis B and C in India have been traced to reused syringes recovered from improperly disposed hospital waste – a reminder that every needle dropped in the right container protects someone outside the hospital too.

Conclusion Good waste management is good infection control – it protects patients, staff, the public and the planet.

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
unit_title: Section B: Biomedical Waste and Laundry Management
question: Describe the laundry management process in the hospital.
answer_html:
Introduction Hospital linen – bed sheets, gowns, towels, drapes – can become heavily contaminated with blood, body fluids and organisms such as S. aureus, C. difficile spores, enteric bacteria and viruses. Safe laundry management protects patients, laundry workers and the environment, and ensures a steady supply of clean linen.

1. Classification of linen

  • Clean linen – washed and ready for use.
  • Used (soiled) linen – used but not visibly soiled with body fluids.
  • Infected/foul linen – soiled with blood, faeces, vomit or other body fluids, or from isolation patients.
  • Heat-sensitive items – blankets, woollens; washed at lower temperatures with chemicals.

2. Collection at the point of use (ward)

  • Wear gloves and an apron; remove linen gently and roll it inward with soiled side inside; do not shake (disperses organisms into air).
  • Never place linen on the floor or on other patients' furniture.
  • Check for sharps and personal articles before bagging.
  • Bag linen at the bedside – used linen and infected linen in separate colour-coded bags (as per hospital policy), not more than two-thirds full; tie securely.
  • Water-soluble (alginate) bags for infected linen can be put directly into the washing machine without opening.
  • Do not sort, count or rinse soiled linen in patient-care areas.

3. Transport

  • In closed, covered trolleys – separate trolleys for clean and dirty linen; clean and disinfect trolleys regularly.
  • Separate routes or times for clean and dirty linen.

4. Processing in the laundry

  • Laundry has physically separated dirty area (receiving, weighing, sorting) and clean area (drying, ironing, folding, storage); ideally barrier washing machines.
  • Staff in the dirty area wear PPE (gloves, gown, mask, boots).
  • Washing: detergent with hot water – thermal disinfection (e.g., about 71 °C for 25 minutes, or 65 °C for 10 minutes as per guideline); lower-temperature washing with chemical disinfectants (bleach) for heat-sensitive items.
  • Infected linen is washed separately, sometimes after a pre-wash disinfection cycle.
  • Drying in tumble dryers and ironing (high heat adds further disinfection).
  • OT linen is washed, then autoclaved before use.

5. Storage and distribution of clean linen

  • In closed, clean, dry shelves or cupboards, away from dust and moisture; covered trolleys for delivery; enough stock in each ward.

6. Mattresses and pillows

  • Use impermeable covers; clean and disinfect between patients; discard damaged or contaminated mattresses as yellow-category waste.

7. Records and staff health

  • Linen inventory, condemnation of torn linen, records of issue and receipt.
  • Laundry staff trained, vaccinated (hepatitis B, tetanus) and provided hand-washing facilities.

Conclusion Safe handling from bedside to laundry and back – without shaking, with separate bags and correct thermal disinfection – keeps linen from becoming a vehicle of hospital infection.

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
unit_title: Section B: Biomedical Waste and Laundry Management
question: Write the colour coding of containers for biomedical waste.
answer_html:
Colour coding as per BMW Management Rules, 2016

  1. Yellow bag – human and animal anatomical waste, soiled waste (dressings, cotton, plaster casts), expired medicines and cytotoxic waste, chemical waste, contaminated linen, laboratory waste (after pre-treatment) → incineration.
  2. Red bag/container – contaminated recyclable plastics: tubing, IV sets, catheters, urine bags, syringes without needles, gloves → autoclave + shredding → recycling.
  3. White translucent puncture-proof container – sharps: needles, blades, scalpels, syringes with fixed needles → autoclave + shredding/encapsulation.
  4. Blue cardboard box/container – glassware (vials, ampoules, broken glass) and metallic implants → disinfection + recycling. All bags must be non-chlorinated and labelled with the biohazard symbol.

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
unit_title: Section B: Biomedical Waste and Laundry Management
question: Draw and explain the biohazard symbol and the labelling of biomedical waste.

diagram.caption: Biohazard symbol and cytotoxic hazard symbol used on BMW containers
labels: three interlocking crescents with central circle (biohazard); cytotoxic symbol with "C" and cell; label fields

answer_html:
Biohazard symbol – an internationally recognised symbol of three interlocking crescents around a central circle, printed on bags and containers of infectious biomedical waste to warn people of a biological hazard. Cytotoxic waste carries a separate cytotoxic hazard symbol.

Label on each BMW bag/container (as per BMW Rules 2016)

  • Biohazard (or cytotoxic) symbol and the word "HANDLE WITH CARE".
  • Name and address of the health-care facility (sender) and the treatment facility (receiver).
  • Category/colour of waste, date of generation, quantity/weight.
  • Bar code for tracking. Labels must be non-washable and clearly visible.

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
unit_title: Section B: Biomedical Waste and Laundry Management
question: What is the maximum period for storage of untreated biomedical waste? Mention the requirements of the storage area.
answer_html:
Maximum storage period: As per the BMW Management Rules, 2016, untreated biomedical waste must not be stored beyond 48 hours. If it must be kept longer, permission is needed and the waste must not affect human health or the environment.

Requirements of the storage area

  1. Separate, secure, lockable room away from patient-care areas, kitchen and public access.
  2. Well ventilated, well lit, with impervious, easy-to-clean floor and walls and drainage.
  3. Protected from rain, animals, birds, insects and rodents.
  4. Biohazard sign displayed; access only to authorised staff.
  5. Colour-coded bags kept separately; easy access for the CBWTF collection vehicle.

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
unit_title: Section B: Antibiotic Stewardship and Antimicrobial Resistance
question: Define antimicrobial stewardship. Explain its importance, core elements, strategies and the role of the nurse.

diagram.caption: Antimicrobial stewardship team and its interventions

answer_html:
Introduction Antibiotics are among the greatest discoveries of medicine, but their overuse and misuse has produced bacteria that no longer respond to them. India has some of the highest rates of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) and the highest antibiotic consumption in the world. Antimicrobial stewardship (AMS) is the organised effort to make every antibiotic prescription count – it is now a core part of patient safety and infection control. World AMR Awareness Week (WAAW) is observed every year from 18 to 24 November.

Definition Antimicrobial stewardship is a coordinated programme of interventions designed to improve and measure the appropriate use of antimicrobials by promoting the selection of the optimal drug, dose, route and duration – so as to cure infection while minimising toxicity, resistance and cost.

A. Importance (goals)

  1. Better patient outcomes – right drug at the right time cures infection faster.
  2. Reducing antimicrobial resistance – less unnecessary exposure, less selection of resistant strains (MRSA, ESBL, CRE).
  3. Reducing adverse effects – allergy, kidney and liver toxicity, C. difficile diarrhoea, Candida overgrowth.
  4. Reducing cost – fewer expensive broad-spectrum and reserve drugs, shorter stay.
  5. Preserving antibiotics for future generations.

B. Indian context

  • National Action Plan on AMR (NAP-AMR, 2017) with a One Health approach (human, animal and environment sectors).
  • ICMR Antimicrobial Stewardship Programme guidelines (2018) and the ICMR AMR surveillance network.
  • Schedule H1 of the Drugs and Cosmetics Rules – third- and fourth-generation cephalosporins, carbapenems and anti-TB drugs can be sold only on prescription with records.
  • "Red Line" campaign – medicines with a red vertical line on the pack should not be used without a doctor's prescription.
  • Ban on colistin as a growth promoter in animal feed (2019).

C. Core elements of a hospital AMS programme

  1. Leadership commitment – administration provides staff, time, money and IT support.
  2. Accountability – a physician leader (often an ID physician) responsible for outcomes.
  3. Pharmacy (drug) expertise – a clinical pharmacist co-leads.
  4. Action – specific interventions (below).
  5. Tracking – monitoring antibiotic use and resistance patterns.
  6. Reporting – regular feedback to doctors, nurses and the HICC.
  7. Education – of prescribers, nurses, pharmacists and patients.

The AMS team: ID physician/clinician, clinical microbiologist, clinical pharmacist, infection control nurse/ICO, intensivist, IT and administration.

D. Strategies (interventions) 1. Front-end (before prescribing)

  • Hospital antibiotic policy based on the local antibiogram (which drugs work against local bacteria).
  • Formulary restriction and pre-authorisation for reserve drugs (colistin, carbapenems, tigecycline, linezolid).

  • Clinical guidelines and order sets (e.g., surgical prophylaxis protocol). 2. Back-end (after prescribing)

  • Prospective audit and feedback – the AMS team reviews prescriptions and advises.

  • "Antibiotic time-out" at 48–72 hours – review the need, choice and duration once culture reports are available.
  • De-escalation – narrowing from broad-spectrum to a targeted drug, or stopping if no infection.
  • IV-to-oral switch when the patient can take orally and is improving.
  • Dose optimisation – for kidney function, weight, PK/PD (e.g., extended infusions).

  • Defined duration with automatic stop dates; surgical prophylaxis not beyond 24 hours. 3. Supporting measures

  • Rapid diagnostics (Gram stain, PCR, procalcitonin); cultures before antibiotics.

  • Infection prevention (fewer infections = fewer antibiotics); vaccination.
  • Following the WHO AWaRe categories – using "Access" antibiotics first.

E. Measuring stewardship

  • Days of therapy (DOT) or defined daily doses (DDD) per 1,000 patient-days.
  • Percentage of prescriptions with cultures sent; compliance with surgical prophylaxis; C. difficile rates; resistance trends.

F. Role of the nurse in antimicrobial stewardship Nurses give every antibiotic dose and are with the patient 24 hours – they are natural stewards.

  1. Collect cultures before the first dose and ensure correct specimen technique.
  2. Clarify allergy history – an unverified "penicillin allergy" leads to broader, costlier drugs.
  3. Give the first dose on time (within 1 hour in sepsis) and subsequent doses at correct intervals; correct dilution, infusion time and route; avoid missed doses.
  4. Prompt the doctor at 48–72 hours – "Culture report has come; can we narrow or stop the antibiotic?"; check stop dates.
  5. Suggest IV-to-oral switch when the patient is eating and afebrile; remove unnecessary IV lines.
  6. Monitor response and adverse effects – fever chart, diarrhoea, rash, kidney function; therapeutic drug levels (vancomycin, aminoglycosides) as ordered.
  7. Prevent infections – hand hygiene, care bundles, early removal of devices.
  8. Educate patients and families – take antibiotics exactly as prescribed, do not self-medicate, do not save leftover or share antibiotics, antibiotics do not cure colds and flu.
  9. Participate in AMS rounds, audits, data collection and awareness week activities.
  10. Accurate documentation of indication, dose times and missed doses.

Conclusion Antimicrobial stewardship ensures that antibiotics are used only when needed, in the right way and for the right time. With nurses as active partners at the bedside, stewardship protects today's patients and keeps antibiotics working for tomorrow.

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
unit_title: Section B: Antibiotic Stewardship and Antimicrobial Resistance
question: Explain antimicrobial resistance – its causes, mechanisms and prevention.
answer_html:
Definition Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) occurs when bacteria, viruses, fungi and parasites change over time and no longer respond to medicines, making infections harder to treat and increasing the risk of spread, severe illness and death. The WHO lists AMR among the top ten global public health threats.

1. Causes of AMR

  1. Overuse and misuse of antibiotics – for viral fevers, colds and diarrhoea; wrong dose or duration; unnecessary broad-spectrum drugs.
  2. Self-medication and over-the-counter sale without prescription; leftover and shared antibiotics.
  3. Poor infection prevention in hospitals – resistant bacteria spread from patient to patient.
  4. Use in animals, poultry and agriculture as growth promoters.
  5. Poor sanitation and unsafe water – spread of resistant gut bacteria.
  6. Environmental contamination with antibiotics from pharmaceutical effluents and hospital waste.
  7. Lack of rapid diagnostics; poor-quality or counterfeit drugs; few new antibiotics being developed.

2. Mechanisms of resistance | Mechanism | Example | |---|---| | Enzymatic destruction of the drug | Beta-lactamases – penicillinase, ESBL, carbapenemases (NDM-1, KPC); aminoglycoside-modifying enzymes | | Alteration of the target | Altered penicillin-binding protein (PBP2a) in MRSA; altered DNA gyrase (fluoroquinolone resistance); altered cell wall precursor in VRE | | Decreased permeability | Loss of porins in Pseudomonas (carbapenem resistance) | | Efflux pumps | Pumping out tetracyclines, fluoroquinolones | | Alternative metabolic pathway | Sulphonamide and trimethoprim resistance | | Biofilm formation | Device infections tolerant to drugs |

3. Genetic basis

  • Intrinsic resistance – natural (e.g., Mycoplasma to penicillin).
  • Acquired resistance – by mutation or by transfer of resistance genes through conjugation (plasmids), transformation and transduction; transposons spread genes rapidly between species.

4. Consequences Longer illness, higher death rates, need for costly and toxic reserve drugs (colistin), failure of surgery, cancer chemotherapy and transplants – a possible "post-antibiotic era".

5. Prevention and control

  1. Rational antibiotic use and antimicrobial stewardship – right drug, dose, duration; de-escalation.
  2. Infection prevention and control – hand hygiene, isolation of MDRO patients, care bundles.
  3. Vaccination – reduces infections and antibiotic use (pneumococcal, typhoid conjugate).
  4. Surveillance of resistance (ICMR AMR network, WHO GLASS) and antibiotic consumption.
  5. Regulation – Schedule H1, Red Line campaign, ban on growth promoters.
  6. Public education – no self-medication, complete prescribed course, awareness weeks.
  7. One Health approach – coordinated action in human health, veterinary and environmental sectors.
  8. Research and development of new antibiotics and diagnostics.

Conclusion AMR is driven largely by human behaviour; responsible antibiotic use and strict infection control by every health worker can slow it down.

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
unit_title: Section B: Antibiotic Stewardship and Antimicrobial Resistance
question: Explain the prevention of MRSA and other multidrug-resistant organisms (MDROs) in health-care settings.
answer_html:
Introduction Multidrug-resistant organisms (MDROs) are microorganisms, mainly bacteria, that are resistant to one or more classes of antimicrobial agents. Important examples are MRSA (methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus), VRE (vancomycin-resistant enterococci), ESBL-producing E. coli and Klebsiella, carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales (CRE), multidrug-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii and Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and Candida auris. They spread mainly through hands of health workers and contaminated equipment and surfaces.

A. Administrative measures

  1. Make MDRO prevention a hospital priority with policies, resources and an antibiotic policy.
  2. Flag the records of known MDRO patients so precautions start at readmission.
  3. Adequate nurse staffing; avoid overcrowding.

B. Screening and surveillance

  • Active screening of high-risk patients on admission: ICU admissions, transfers from other hospitals, patients with previous MRSA, cardiac and orthopaedic surgery patients – nasal, axillary and groin swabs for MRSA; rectal swabs for CRE/VRE.
  • Laboratory alerts for MDRO isolates; tracking rates by ward.

C. Infection control measures

  1. Hand hygiene at all five moments – the most important measure.
  2. Contact precautions – single room or cohorting, gloves and gown on entry, dedicated equipment (stethoscope, BP cuff, thermometer).
  3. Environmental cleaning – twice-daily cleaning of high-touch surfaces; terminal cleaning after discharge.
  4. Care bundles for devices; remove catheters and lines early.
  5. Limit transfers; inform the receiving unit when moving the patient.

D. Decolonisation (for MRSA)

  • Mupirocin 2% nasal ointment twice daily for 5 days and chlorhexidine body wash daily for 5 days, as per policy (pre-operative patients, outbreaks).
  • Screening and decolonisation of staff only during outbreaks.

E. Antimicrobial stewardship

  • Reduce unnecessary use of cephalosporins, fluoroquinolones and carbapenems, which select MDROs.

F. Education

  • Train staff; explain to patients and families why precautions are needed, reducing anxiety and stigma; teach hand hygiene to visitors.

G. Nurse's checklist for an MDRO patient

  • Isolation sign on the door; PPE and hand rub at the entrance.
  • Dedicated equipment kept inside the room.
  • Daily review of devices; strict aseptic care.
  • Inform laboratory, ICN and receiving departments during transfer.
  • Terminal cleaning after discharge; counsel the patient on hand hygiene at home.

Conclusion MDROs are controlled by a "bundle" of screening, hand hygiene, contact precautions, cleaning, decolonisation and wise antibiotic use.

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
unit_title: Section B: Antibiotic Stewardship and Antimicrobial Resistance
question: How can MRSA be prevented in hospitals?
answer_html:
Prevention of MRSA

  1. Hand hygiene before and after every patient contact.
  2. Screening of high-risk patients (nasal/axilla/groin swabs) on admission.
  3. Contact precautions – isolation or cohorting, gloves and gowns, dedicated equipment.
  4. Decolonisation – mupirocin nasal ointment and chlorhexidine bathing.
  5. Cleaning and disinfection of high-touch surfaces and equipment.
  6. Rational antibiotic use (antimicrobial stewardship).
  7. Aseptic care of wounds, catheters and lines; education of staff and visitors.

Staff with skin lesions should not work in high-risk areas (OT, NICU) until treated.

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
unit_title: Section B: Antibiotic Stewardship and Antimicrobial Resistance
question: List any four multidrug-resistant bacterial strains.
answer_html:
Multidrug-resistant bacterial strains

  1. MRSA – methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus.
  2. VRE – vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus.
  3. ESBL-producing E. coli and Klebsiella pneumoniae.
  4. CRE – carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales (e.g., NDM-1-producing Klebsiella).
  5. MDR Acinetobacter baumannii and Pseudomonas aeruginosa.
  6. MDR-TB/XDR-TB – Mycobacterium tuberculosis resistant to isoniazid and rifampicin (± other drugs).

These are often grouped as the "ESKAPE" pathogens – Enterococcus, S. aureus, Klebsiella, Acinetobacter, Pseudomonas, Enterobacter.

Control: hand hygiene, contact precautions, screening of high-risk patients and antimicrobial stewardship.

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
unit_title: Section B: Antibiotic Stewardship and Antimicrobial Resistance
question: Write the mechanisms of antibiotic resistance in bacteria.
answer_html:
Mechanisms of antibiotic resistance

  1. Enzymatic inactivation of the drug – beta-lactamases (ESBL, NDM-1 carbapenemase) destroy penicillins and cephalosporins.
  2. Alteration of the drug target – altered penicillin-binding protein in MRSA; altered DNA gyrase (quinolones); altered ribosomes (macrolides).
  3. Decreased permeability – loss of porin channels (Gram-negatives).
  4. Efflux pumps – drug pumped out of the cell (tetracyclines, quinolones).
  5. Alternative (bypass) metabolic pathway – sulphonamides, trimethoprim.
  6. Biofilm formation on devices.

Resistance genes are acquired by mutation or gene transfer (plasmids by conjugation, transduction, transformation).

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
unit_title: Section B: Antibiotic Stewardship and Antimicrobial Resistance
question: What is the WHO AWaRe classification of antibiotics?
answer_html:
The WHO AWaRe classification (introduced in 2017 and updated regularly) groups antibiotics into three categories to guide stewardship:

  1. Access – first- or second-choice drugs for common infections; narrow spectrum, lower resistance potential, should be widely available – e.g., amoxicillin, ampicillin, cloxacillin, gentamicin, metronidazole, doxycycline, nitrofurantoin, cefalexin.
  2. Watch – higher resistance potential; key targets of stewardship – e.g., azithromycin, ciprofloxacin, ceftriaxone, cefixime, piperacillin–tazobactam, meropenem, vancomycin.
  3. Reserve – "last resort" drugs for multidrug-resistant infections, used under strict control – e.g., colistin, polymyxin B, linezolid, tigecycline, ceftazidime–avibactam.

Countries aim for the majority (at least 60–70%) of antibiotic use to be from the Access group.

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
question: (a) Explain the types of patient restraint (3 marks). (b) State the purposes of restraint (2 marks). (c) Describe the nurse's role in patient restraint (5 marks).

diagram.caption: Restraint monitoring checklist
labels: release every 2 hours for exercise and toileting

answer_html:
Introduction A restraint is any method, device or drug used to restrict a patient's freedom of movement, physical activity or normal access to his body. Restraints are sometimes necessary to protect a confused, agitated or violent patient from injuring himself or others, or to prevent removal of life-saving tubes. But restraints also cause harm – pressure ulcers, nerve injury, falls, strangulation, loss of dignity and even death. Therefore modern patient-safety policy (NABH, JCI, Mental Healthcare Act 2017) treats restraint as a last resort, used for the shortest time, with strict monitoring.

(a) Types of restraint (3 marks) 1. Physical (mechanical) restraints – devices attached to or near the body:

  • Limb (wrist/ankle) restraints – padded cuffs tied to the bed frame; for patients pulling at tubes or lines.
  • Mitten restraints – prevent scratching and pulling of tubes while allowing arm movement (burns, eczema, confused patients).
  • Jacket/vest restraint – keeps the patient in bed or chair (risk of strangulation if wrongly applied).
  • Belt restraint – across the waist in a chair or stretcher.
  • Elbow restraints (elbow splints) – prevent children from bending elbows to reach the face or IV site (cleft-lip repair).
  • Mummy restraint – wrapping an infant in a sheet for procedures.
  • Clove-hitch restraint – a bandage knot for limb restraint.
  • Side rails, tables fixed to chairs, tucking sheets tightly – also act as restraints if they prevent the patient from leaving the bed.

2. Chemical (pharmacological) restraints

  • Drugs given mainly to control behaviour or restrict movement rather than to treat a medical condition – e.g., sedatives, antipsychotics (haloperidol), benzodiazepines.

3. Environmental restraints / seclusion

  • Seclusion – confining a patient alone in a room from which he cannot leave (mainly in psychiatric settings).
  • Locked doors, wander alarms, keeping a patient in a low bed or bean bag.

4. Manual (physical holding)

  • Staff holding the patient's limbs briefly for a procedure (e.g., child for venepuncture).

Classification by use: medical/surgical restraints (to protect tubes and devices) and behavioural restraints (for violent or self-destructive behaviour).

(b) Purposes of restraint (2 marks)

  1. To prevent the patient from injuring himself – falling from bed, hitting, scratching, interfering with wounds.
  2. To protect other patients and staff from a violent or aggressive patient.
  3. To prevent removal of life-supporting tubes and devices – endotracheal tube, central lines, IV cannula, urinary catheter, nasogastric tube, drains.
  4. To immobilise a body part during procedures and examinations (in children – lumbar puncture, IV insertion).
  5. To maintain therapeutic positioning after surgery or in traction.
  6. To allow safe transport of agitated patients.

(c) Nurse's role in patient restraint (5 marks) 1. Before applying restraint – assessment and alternatives

  • Assess the cause of agitation or confusion – pain, full bladder, hypoxia, hypoglycaemia, infection, drug withdrawal, delirium, fear – and treat it.
  • Try least-restrictive alternatives first:
    • Explain and reassure; talk calmly; reorientation (clock, calendar, familiar objects).
    • Family member or attendant to sit with the patient; one-to-one observation.
    • Bed in the lowest position, floor mats, bed alarms, keeping the patient near the nursing station.
    • Camouflaging IV lines and tubes, using abdominal binders over gastrostomy tubes, early removal of unnecessary devices.
    • Diversion activities, regular toileting, comfort measures, adequate light and sleep.
  • Use restraint only when alternatives fail and risk of harm is high.

2. Legal and ethical requirements

  • A written order from the doctor stating the reason, type, body part and duration; in emergencies the nurse may apply restraint and obtain the order within the time specified by policy (usually within 1 hour).
  • PRN (as-needed) orders for restraint are not acceptable.
  • Orders are time-limited and renewed after reassessment (e.g., every 4 hours for adults for behavioural restraint, shorter for children – as per hospital policy).
  • Explain to the patient and family the reason; obtain informed consent where possible.
  • In mental health establishments, follow the Mental Healthcare Act 2017 – restraint only to prevent imminent harm, never as punishment or for staff convenience; inform the nominated representative within 24 hours; record in the patient's file.
  • Restraint must never be used for punishment, staff convenience or as a substitute for care.

3. Correct application

  • Use the right size and type of device as per manufacturer's instructions; pad bony prominences.
  • Tie restraints to the movable bed frame (not side rails) with quick-release knots so they can be removed quickly in an emergency.
  • Allow two fingers between the restraint and the skin; avoid tightness.
  • Keep the body in good alignment; never restrain a patient flat on the back if he may vomit (risk of aspiration) – raise the head or turn to the side.
  • Never apply a jacket restraint backwards; keep side rails padded or use low beds to prevent entrapment.

4. Monitoring and care during restraint

  • Observe frequently – at least every 15 minutes (continuously for violent patients and those in seclusion):
    • Circulation – colour, warmth, pulse, capillary refill, numbness of restrained limbs.
    • Skin – redness, abrasions.
    • Breathing, consciousness and psychological status.
  • Release restraints at least every 2 hours (one limb at a time for violent patients) for range-of-motion exercises, repositioning, skin care and toileting.
  • Offer fluids and food, ensure elimination needs are met.
  • Keep the call bell within reach; ensure privacy and dignity (cover the patient).
  • Talk to and reassure the patient; involve the family.

5. Reassessment and removal

  • Reassess the need regularly; remove the restraint as soon as the patient is safe – restraint-free care is the goal.
  • After removal, discuss the episode with the patient (debriefing) and plan to prevent recurrence.

6. Documentation

  • Reason, alternatives tried, doctor's order, type of restraint, time applied and removed, monitoring findings every 15 minutes, care given (ROM, fluids, toileting), patient's response, family informed, injuries if any.
  • Report any restraint-related injury as an incident.

7. Staff training and audit

  • Regular training on de-escalation, safe application and monitoring; restraint audits as a patient safety indicator.

Conclusion Restraints may protect a patient for a short time but can also harm. The nurse's duty is to avoid them whenever possible, use the least restrictive method when necessary, follow legal requirements, monitor closely and remove them at the earliest – keeping the patient's safety and dignity at the centre.

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
question: (a) Describe vulnerable patients in the hospital (2 marks). (b) Explain the complications vulnerable patients are prone to during their hospital stay (3 marks). (c) Describe the nurse's role in preventing harm to vulnerable patients (5 marks).
answer_html:
Introduction All patients are at some risk in hospital, but certain groups cannot protect themselves, communicate their needs or make decisions, and therefore suffer more harm. Accreditation standards (NABH) require every hospital to identify vulnerable patients and protect them through special policies.

(a) Vulnerable patients (2 marks) Vulnerable patients are those who are at higher risk of harm in the hospital because of their age, physical or mental condition, dependency, or social circumstances, and who may not be able to protect themselves.

Groups

  1. Elderly (especially frail and above 65–70 years).
  2. Neonates, infants and children.
  3. Unconscious, comatose, sedated and anaesthetised patients; patients on ventilators.
  4. Patients with physical disabilities – paralysis, blindness, deafness, speech problems.
  5. Patients with mental illness, dementia, delirium or intellectual disability.
  6. Bedridden and critically ill patients.
  7. Patients on restraints.
  8. Unaccompanied patients, destitute, homeless, those who do not speak the local language.
  9. Pregnant women, immunocompromised patients (HIV, chemotherapy).
  10. Victims of abuse, assault or neglect; terminally ill patients.

(b) Complications vulnerable patients are prone to (3 marks)

  1. Falls and injuries – fractures, head injury (confusion, weakness, sedation, poor vision).
