  2. Pressure ulcers – immobility, incontinence, poor nutrition.
  3. Health care–associated infections – pneumonia, UTI, line infections (weak immunity, devices).
  4. Aspiration pneumonia – poor swallowing, unconsciousness, tube feeding.
  5. Deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism – immobility.
  6. Malnutrition and dehydration – inability to eat or drink independently.
  7. Medication errors and adverse drug reactions – multiple drugs, altered metabolism in elderly and children, dosing errors.
  8. Delirium and confusion – new environment, sleep loss, drugs.
  9. Restraint-related injuries – skin damage, nerve injury, strangulation.
  10. Burns – hot water bottles, heating pads in patients with reduced sensation.
  11. Abuse and neglect – physical, emotional, sexual or financial abuse; infant abduction.
  12. Loss of dignity, privacy and psychological distress; risk of self-harm in some psychiatric patients; wandering or leaving the hospital unnoticed (elopement).

(c) Nurse's role in preventing harm to vulnerable patients (5 marks) 1. Identification and assessment on admission

  • Identify vulnerable patients using the hospital's criteria; mark them (e.g., special wristband or bedside alert as per policy).
  • Use risk-assessment tools – Morse Fall Scale, Braden scale (pressure ulcer), nutritional screening, delirium screening (CAM), swallowing assessment – and reassess regularly and after any change.

2. Safe environment and supervision

  • Bed near the nursing station; frequent (hourly) rounding; one-to-one sitter if needed.
  • Bed in the lowest position, brakes locked, side rails as per policy, call bell and personal items within reach, night light, non-slip footwear, dry floors, clutter-free path.
  • Regular toileting schedule; help in walking.

3. Prevention of specific complications

  • Pressure ulcer prevention – 2-hourly turning, pressure-relieving mattresses, skin care, nutrition.
  • Infection prevention – hand hygiene, care bundles, oral care, early removal of devices.
  • Aspiration prevention – head end elevated 30–45° during and after feeds, swallowing assessment, correct tube position.
  • DVT prophylaxis – early mobilisation, leg exercises, stockings/drugs as ordered.
  • Nutrition and hydration – feeding assistance, intake–output charting.

4. Medication safety

  • Correct identification with two identifiers; double-check high-alert drugs; dose calculation by weight in children; review of sedatives in elderly; crushing medicines only when safe; observe for side effects.

5. Restraint minimisation

  • Use alternatives; when restraint is unavoidable, follow policy and monitor closely.

6. Communication and consent

  • Use interpreters, sign language, hearing aids, spectacles, picture boards; speak slowly and clearly.
  • Involve family members/legal guardians in decisions; obtain consent from the appropriate person.

7. Protection from abuse, neglect and abduction

  • Never leave infants unattended; matching mother–baby identification bands, controlled access to maternity and paediatric wards, Code Pink drills.
  • Watch for signs of abuse (unexplained injuries, fear); report as per law (POCSO Act for children) and hospital policy.
  • Ensure that unaccompanied patients' belongings are safely kept and documented.

8. Dignity and psychological care

  • Maintain privacy during care; respect cultural and religious needs; reassure and orient confused patients; encourage family visits.

9. Safe transfer and discharge

  • Accompany during transport; give proper handover; plan discharge with home-care teaching and follow-up.

10. Documentation, reporting and training

  • Record risk scores, preventive measures and incidents; report adverse events; take part in staff training and audits.

Conclusion Vulnerable patients depend on others for their safety. By identifying them early, assessing their risks and providing vigilant, compassionate care, nurses prevent falls, infections, pressure ulcers, medication errors and abuse – the true measure of a safe hospital.

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
question: Describe the complications of intravenous therapy and the nurse's responsibilities in preventing them.

diagram.caption: Visual Infusion Phlebitis (VIP) score
labels: resite and consider treatment; 4 – palpable venous cord

answer_html:
Introduction About 70–80% of hospitalised patients receive intravenous (IV) therapy at some time. IV lines give fluids, drugs, blood and nutrition directly into the circulation – which also means that any error or infection goes straight into the bloodstream. Most IV complications are preventable by good nursing practice.

A. Local complications 1. Phlebitis – inflammation of the vein wall.

  • Types: mechanical (large cannula, movement, poor fixation), chemical (irritant drugs – potassium chloride, some antibiotics, hypertonic fluids, rapid infusion), bacterial (poor asepsis, long dwell time).
  • Signs: pain, redness, warmth, swelling along the vein, a hard cord; graded by the Visual Infusion Phlebitis (VIP) score (0–5).

2. Infiltration

  • Leakage of a non-vesicant solution into the surrounding tissue (cannula slips out of the vein).
  • Signs: swelling, coolness, blanching, discomfort, slowing or stopping of the drip.

3. Extravasation

  • Leakage of a vesicant drug that can cause blistering and tissue necrosis – chemotherapy drugs, noradrenaline, dopamine, calcium, potassium, concentrated dextrose (above 10%), contrast media.
  • Signs: burning pain, redness, blistering, later ulceration.

4. Haematoma – bleeding into tissues at the puncture site (failed attempts, removal without pressure, anticoagulants).

5. Thrombosis and thrombophlebitis – clot in the vein, may lead to embolism.

6. Local infection/cellulitis at the insertion site – redness, pus.

7. Nerve, tendon or ligament injury – during insertion; wrong site selection.

8. Catheter occlusion – blood clot or drug precipitate blocks the cannula.

B. Systemic complications 1. Catheter-related bloodstream infection (CRBSI/CLABSI) and septicaemia

  • Fever with chills, hypotension; especially with central lines and long dwell times.

2. Circulatory (fluid) overload

  • Too much fluid or too fast, especially in elderly, children, heart and kidney patients.
  • Signs: breathlessness, cough, crepitations, raised JVP, hypertension, oedema – leading to pulmonary oedema.

3. Air embolism

  • Air entering the vein (unprimed tubing, empty bottles, loose connections, central line removal) – chest pain, breathlessness, hypotension, cyanosis, collapse.

4. Speed shock

  • Toxic reaction to a drug given too quickly (flushing, headache, chest tightness, arrhythmia, collapse).

5. Allergic reactions and anaphylaxis to drugs or blood.

6. Pyrogenic reaction – fever and rigors within 30 minutes due to contaminated fluid or tubing.

7. Catheter embolism – a broken piece of cannula travelling in the vein.

8. Electrolyte and glucose imbalance – wrong fluids or rates.

C. Nurse's responsibilities in preventing IV complications 1. Before insertion

  • Check the order – fluid, drug, volume, rate, duration; check for allergies.
  • Need for IV therapy – use oral route when possible; avoid unnecessary cannulation.
  • Explain the procedure to the patient.
  • Site selection – distal veins of the upper limb first, non-dominant arm; avoid joints, areas of infection, bruising, the side of mastectomy or AV fistula, and lower limbs in adults; choose a vein suitable for the duration and type of therapy.
  • Smallest gauge cannula that serves the purpose (e.g., 20–22 G for most fluids; 18 G for blood transfusion or rapid infusion).

2. During insertion

  • Hand hygiene, clean gloves; skin antisepsis with chlorhexidine–alcohol (or povidone-iodine), allow it to dry; do not touch the site after cleaning.
  • Insert with a no-touch technique; maximum two attempts per nurse.
  • Secure with a sterile transparent dressing; label with date, time and gauge.
  • For central lines, follow the CLABSI insertion bundle.

3. During infusion – monitoring

  • Inspect the site regularly – at least every shift (more often in children, ICU patients and with vesicant drugs) and record the VIP score.
  • Check flow rate and the correct volume infused; use infusion pumps for critical drugs, children and the elderly; calculate drop rates accurately.
  • Monitor vital signs, intake–output and signs of fluid overload (breath sounds, oedema, JVP).
  • Prime tubing completely to remove air; ensure Luer-lock connections are tight; never allow bottles to run empty; clamp lines when changing bottles.
  • Flush with saline (push–pause technique) before and after drugs and when there is incompatibility.
  • Dilute irritant drugs correctly and give over the recommended time; give vesicants only through a well-functioning cannula or central line, and watch the site closely.
  • Do not add drugs to blood; check compatibility of drugs and fluids.
  • Scrub the hub/port with alcohol before each access.
  • Change administration sets as per policy (e.g., every 72–96 hours; within 24 hours for blood, lipids and TPN).
  • Replace peripheral cannulas when clinically indicated (or as per hospital policy) and remove unnecessary cannulas immediately.

4. Patient education

  • Ask the patient to report pain, swelling, wetness or breathlessness immediately; not to adjust the flow or move the limb roughly; keep the dressing dry.

5. Management when complications occur | Complication | Immediate nursing action | |---|---| | Phlebitis | Stop and remove cannula, resite in the other limb, warm compress, elevate, document VIP score | | Infiltration | Stop infusion, remove cannula, elevate limb, warm or cold compress as per fluid, resite | | Extravasation | Stop at once, leave cannula in place, aspirate residual drug, inform doctor, give antidote if ordered (e.g., hyaluronidase), elevate, cold/warm compress as per drug, mark the area, document | | Fluid overload | Slow the infusion to keep vein open, sit the patient upright, give oxygen, inform doctor, diuretics as ordered | | Air embolism | Clamp the line, place the patient in left lateral, head-down (Trendelenburg) position, give oxygen, call for help | | Anaphylaxis | Stop infusion, keep vein open with saline, call for help, adrenaline IM as per protocol, oxygen, monitor | | Line infection | Remove/culture tip as ordered, take blood cultures, start antibiotics as ordered |

6. Documentation and reporting

  • Date, time, site, gauge, number of attempts, condition of the site, fluids and drugs given, VIP score, complications and actions; report serious events as incidents.

Conclusion IV therapy is life-saving but carries real risks. Careful site selection, aseptic insertion, accurate rate control, regular site checks with the VIP score and prompt removal of unnecessary lines allow the nurse to prevent almost all IV complications.

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
question: Explain incident reporting, root cause analysis (RCA) and corrective and preventive action (CAPA) in patient safety. Add a note on writing an incident report.

diagram.caption: Fishbone (Ishikawa) cause-and-effect diagram for a medication error
labels: effect – wrong drug given; bones – people

answer_html:
Introduction Even in the best hospitals, errors happen. The aim of patient safety is not to blame individuals but to learn from every incident and change the system so that the same error does not happen again. This is done through incident reporting, analysis by root cause analysis (RCA) and the implementation of corrective and preventive actions (CAPA), within a "just culture".

A. Key definitions

  • Incident (patient safety incident) – any unintended or unexpected event that could have or did lead to harm to a patient.
  • Near miss – an incident that did not reach the patient (caught in time) – e.g., wrong drug drawn up but noticed before giving.
  • No-harm incident – reached the patient but caused no harm.
  • Adverse event – an incident that caused harm to the patient.
  • Sentinel event – an unexpected event involving death or serious physical or psychological injury – e.g., wrong-site surgery, infant abduction, suicide of an inpatient, ABO-incompatible transfusion.
  • Never events – serious, largely preventable events that should never happen (wrong-site surgery, retained instrument, wrong-route chemotherapy).

B. Incident reporting 1. Purposes

  • To identify risks and hazards in the system.
  • To learn from errors and near misses and prevent recurrence.
  • To take immediate action for the patient's safety.
  • To fulfil legal and accreditation (NABH) requirements.

2. What to report – medication errors, falls, pressure ulcers, wrong identification, transfusion reactions, needle-stick injuries, equipment failure, IV complications, restraint injuries, patient complaints, near misses.

3. Characteristics of a good reporting system

  • Non-punitive and confidential – staff are not punished for honest errors (but reckless behaviour is dealt with fairly – "just culture").
  • Simple forms (paper or electronic), easily available.
  • Timely – reported within 24 hours (sentinel events immediately).
  • Feedback given to reporters; lessons shared.

C. Root cause analysis (RCA) Definition: a structured, systematic process to identify the basic (root) causes that led to an incident, focusing on systems and processes, not individuals. It answers three questions: What happened? Why did it happen? What can be done to prevent it? RCA is mandatory for sentinel events and is done within a fixed period (commonly about 45 days).

Steps of RCA

  1. Identify the incident and decide that an RCA is needed.
  2. Form a multidisciplinary team (doctor, nurse, pharmacist, quality manager, others) – including people who know the process but were not directly involved.
  3. Collect information – interview staff, review records, examine equipment and the site; secure evidence.
  4. Construct a timeline – the sequence of events step by step.
  5. Identify causal factors – what went wrong at each step (missed checks, poor communication).
  6. Find root causes using tools:
    • "5 Whys" – keep asking "why?" until the basic system cause is found.
    • Fishbone (Ishikawa/cause-and-effect) diagram – causes grouped under people, methods/process, equipment, environment, materials and management/policies.
    • Flow charts, barrier analysis.
  7. Develop recommendations (CAPA).
  8. Report and share learning; monitor the effect.

Example – "5 Whys" for a wrong drug given

  • Why was the wrong drug given? – Two look-alike vials were kept side by side.
  • Why? – The pharmacy stocks both in similar packs and the ward has no LASA segregation.
  • Why? – No look-alike–sound-alike (LASA) policy.
  • Root cause: absence of a LASA storage policy and labelling system.

D. Corrective and preventive action (CAPA)

  • Corrective action – action taken to eliminate the cause of an incident that has already occurred and correct its effects (e.g., remove the look-alike vial, treat the patient, inform the family).
  • Preventive action – action to prevent the problem from recurring or occurring elsewhere (e.g., LASA policy, tall-man lettering, separate storage, double-check for high-alert drugs, staff training).
  • Strength of actions – strongest actions change the system (forcing functions, standardisation, automation, e.g., barcode scanning); intermediate actions (checklists, staffing changes); weakest actions (training, warnings, new policies alone).
  • Each action has a responsible person, timeline and measure of effectiveness; follow-up audits verify success.

E. Writing an incident report Format (contents)

  1. Date, time and exact location of the incident.
  2. Patient details (name, UHID, ward) – or staff/visitor details.
  3. Type of incident (fall, medication error, etc.).
  4. Objective, factual description in chronological order – what was seen and done, in clear language, without opinions or blame ("Patient found on the floor beside bed at 2.10 a.m.", not "Patient fell because the attendant was careless").
  5. Immediate action taken – first aid, vital signs, doctor informed (name and time), investigations.
  6. Outcome – harm or no harm; condition of the patient.
  7. Witnesses and staff involved (by role).
  8. Contributing factors noticed, and suggestions.
  9. Name, designation and signature of the reporter; date and time of the report.

Points to remember

  • Write as soon as possible, legibly, without erasures; do not alter facts.
  • Record the clinical facts and care given in the patient's notes too; the incident report itself is a quality-improvement document, filed separately as per policy.
  • Inform the patient/family honestly (open disclosure) as per hospital policy.
  • Maintain confidentiality.

F. Role of the nurse Report every incident and near miss, take immediate action for the patient's safety, participate honestly in RCA, implement CAPA in the ward and encourage a learning culture.

Conclusion Incident reporting tells us what went wrong, RCA tells us why, and CAPA ensures it does not happen again. In a just culture where nurses report freely, every error becomes a lesson that makes care safer.

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
question: Explain patient safety indicators.
answer_html:
Definition Patient safety indicators (PSIs) are measurable variables used to monitor and evaluate the safety of care in a hospital, to identify problem areas and track improvement over time. They answer the question: "How safe is our care?"

1. Types (Donabedian framework)

  • Structure indicators – resources and systems: nurse–patient ratio, availability of hand rub at bedsides, trained staff, functioning equipment.
  • Process indicators – how care is given: hand hygiene compliance, bundle compliance, time-out compliance in OT, percentage of patients assessed for fall risk.
  • Outcome indicators – results of care: infection rates, falls with injury, mortality.

2. Common patient safety indicators | Area | Indicator | |---|---| | Falls | Patient falls per 1,000 patient-days; falls with injury | | Pressure injury | Incidence of hospital-acquired pressure ulcers | | Medication safety | Medication errors and adverse drug reactions per 1,000 patient-days; near misses | | Infections | CAUTI, CLABSI, VAP rates per 1,000 device-days; SSI rate per 100 surgeries | | Blood transfusion | Transfusion reactions per 100 units transfused | | Surgical safety | Wrong-site/wrong-patient surgery; retained foreign bodies; return to OT within 48 hours; surgical safety checklist compliance | | Identification | Patient identification errors | | Critical care | Unplanned return to ICU within 48 hours; re-intubation rate | | Readmission | Unplanned readmission within 30 days | | Restraint | Restraint-related injuries | | Mortality | Deaths in low-mortality conditions; in-hospital mortality | | Staff safety | Needle-stick injuries | | Process | Hand hygiene compliance; percentage of sentinel events with RCA done |

3. Uses

  • Identify risks and trends; compare units and hospitals (benchmarking).
  • Plan quality-improvement projects; evaluate interventions.
  • Required for NABH accreditation, Kayakalp and national quality programmes (NQAS).

4. Characteristics of a good indicator Relevant, measurable, valid, reliable, sensitive to change, easy to collect, and actionable.

5. Role of the nurse Collect accurate data (falls, pressure ulcers, device-days), report incidents, participate in audits and use the results to improve ward practice.

6. Example of calculation Fall rate = (number of patient falls in the month ÷ total patient-days in the month) × 1,000. If a 30-bed ward with 840 patient-days records 2 falls, the rate is (2 ÷ 840) × 1,000 = 2.4 falls per 1,000 patient-days. Tracking this every month shows whether fall-prevention measures are working.

Conclusion "What gets measured gets managed" – patient safety indicators turn safety into numbers that guide improvement.

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
question: Explain the blood transfusion safety policy and the nurse's role.
answer_html:
Introduction Blood transfusion can save lives, but errors in identification, storage or administration can cause fatal reactions such as ABO-incompatible haemolytic transfusion, transmission of infection or fluid overload. Every hospital follows a transfusion policy under the guidance of the hospital transfusion committee, and adverse events are reported to the Haemovigilance Programme of India.

1. Before transfusion

  • Clear indication and a written order (component, quantity, rate).
  • Informed consent after explaining benefits and risks.
  • Sample collection for grouping and cross-matching:
    • Identify the patient with two identifiers at the bedside.
    • Label the sample at the bedside, one patient at a time; never pre-label.
  • Blood bank tests the unit for HIV, hepatitis B and C, syphilis and malaria, and performs grouping and cross-matching.

2. Collection and storage

  • Collect blood from the blood bank only when ready to transfuse; carry in a closed, insulated carrier box.
  • Start within 30 minutes of issue; complete within 4 hours of removal from storage.
  • Storage temperatures: whole blood/packed RBCs 2–6 °C; platelets 20–24 °C with constant agitation; FFP at −18 °C or below (thawed at 37 °C before use).
  • Never keep blood in ward refrigerators or warm it in hot water; use an approved blood warmer only when ordered.

3. Bedside checking (most important step)

  • Two qualified persons check together at the bedside: patient's name, UHID, blood group, unit number, component, expiry date, compatibility label and the doctor's order; inspect the bag for leaks, clots or discolouration.
  • Ask the conscious patient to state his name and date of birth.

4. Administration

  • Record baseline vital signs.
  • Use a blood administration set with filter (170–200 µm) and an 18–20 G cannula.
  • Only normal saline may be used with blood – no dextrose (haemolysis), no Ringer's lactate (clotting due to calcium), no drugs added.
  • Start slowly and stay with the patient for the first 15 minutes; check vital signs at 15 minutes, then as per policy (hourly) and at the end.

5. Recognition and management of reactions

  • Signs: fever, chills, rash, itching, back or chest pain, breathlessness, hypotension, dark urine, bleeding.
  • Action: stop the transfusion, keep the IV line open with normal saline, inform the doctor and blood bank, recheck identification, monitor vital signs, send the blood bag, set and fresh blood and urine samples to the blood bank, document and report.

6. Documentation Unit number, time started and completed, vital signs, volume, any reaction and actions taken.

Conclusion Correct identification, safe storage, careful administration and close monitoring – especially in the first 15 minutes – make every transfusion safe.

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
question: Explain the prevention of deep vein thrombosis (DVT) in hospitalised patients.
answer_html:
Introduction Deep vein thrombosis (DVT) is the formation of a blood clot in a deep vein, usually of the legs or pelvis. A piece of the clot can break off and travel to the lungs, causing pulmonary embolism (PE), which can be fatal. Hospitalised patients – especially after surgery, trauma, stroke or prolonged bed rest – are at high risk, and venous thromboembolism (VTE) is one of the most preventable causes of hospital death.

1. Causes – Virchow's triad

  1. Stasis of blood – immobility, bed rest, paralysis, long surgery.
  2. Injury to the vein wall – surgery (especially hip/knee), trauma, IV cannulation of leg veins.
  3. Hypercoagulability – cancer, pregnancy and puerperium, oral contraceptives, dehydration, obesity, heart failure, sepsis, inherited disorders.

2. Risk assessment

  • Assess every patient on admission and periodically using tools such as the Caprini or Padua score; record the risk and the prophylaxis planned.

3. Preventive measures (a) General nursing measures

  • Early mobilisation and ambulation after surgery or illness.
  • Leg exercises – ankle pumps, foot circles, knee bending every hour while awake; active/passive range of motion for bedridden patients.
  • Adequate hydration.
  • Avoid pillows under the knees and crossing legs; avoid prolonged sitting with legs dependent.
  • Avoid IV cannulation in leg veins.
  • Deep-breathing exercises (improve venous return).

(b) Mechanical prophylaxis

  • Graduated compression stockings (GCS) – correctly measured, worn smoothly without wrinkles; remove daily for skin inspection.
  • Intermittent pneumatic compression (IPC) devices – sleeves that inflate and deflate around the calves.
  • Avoid in severe peripheral arterial disease, leg ulcers or dermatitis.

(c) Pharmacological prophylaxis (as ordered)

  • Low-molecular-weight heparin (e.g., enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneously once daily), unfractionated heparin 5,000 units subcutaneously 8–12-hourly, fondaparinux or oral anticoagulants.
  • Nurse's role: correct subcutaneous technique (abdomen, not rubbing), monitor for bleeding, platelet count, check contraindications.

4. Monitoring for DVT

  • Observe for unilateral leg swelling, pain, tenderness, warmth, redness, and measure calf circumference if suspected.
  • Sudden breathlessness, chest pain, tachycardia or haemoptysis suggest PE – an emergency.

5. Patient education Importance of moving, exercises, fluids, wearing stockings and taking anticoagulants as prescribed, especially after discharge following surgery.

Conclusion Risk assessment, early mobilisation, mechanical and drug prophylaxis together can prevent most hospital-acquired DVTs.

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
question: Explain medication reconciliation.
answer_html:
Definition Medication reconciliation is the formal process of comparing a patient's current medication orders with all the medicines the patient has been taking, to identify and resolve discrepancies – omissions, duplications, dosing errors or drug interactions – at every transition of care (admission, transfer between units, discharge).

1. Need

  • Many patients take several medicines from different doctors, including over-the-counter and herbal products.
  • Information is often lost when patients move between home, wards, ICU and other hospitals; more than half of patients have at least one unintended discrepancy at admission.
  • The WHO "Medication Without Harm" global patient safety challenge highlights transitions of care as high-risk points.

2. Steps

  1. Obtain the best possible medication history (BPMH)
    • Interview the patient and family; check prescriptions, discharge summaries, pill bottles/strips brought from home, pharmacy records.
    • Record name, dose, route, frequency, last dose taken, and allergies.
    • Include over-the-counter drugs, vitamins, herbal and Ayurvedic medicines, inhalers, eye drops, injections.
  2. Compare the BPMH with the admission/transfer/discharge orders.
  3. Identify discrepancies – intentional (documented changes) or unintentional (errors).
  4. Resolve them with the prescriber; correct the orders.
  5. Document the reconciled list and communicate it to the next care provider.
  6. At discharge – give the patient and family an updated medication list with clear instructions on which drugs to continue, stop or change, and counsel them.

3. Common discrepancies

  • Omission of a home medicine (e.g., antihypertensive, antiepileptic).
  • Duplication (brand and generic of the same drug).
  • Wrong dose, frequency or route.
  • Drug interactions with new medicines.
  • Continuing drugs that should have been stopped (e.g., anticoagulant before surgery).

4. Team roles

  • Doctor – reviews and decides; pharmacist – detailed history and checking; nurse – collects history, checks medicines brought from home, ensures correct administration, educates the patient.

5. Benefits Prevents medication errors and adverse drug events, improves continuity of care, reduces readmissions and costs.

6. Role of the nurse at each transition

  • Admission – ask the patient to bring all current medicines; list them; inform the doctor about medicines not prescribed.
  • Transfer (ICU to ward) – check that infusions and drugs stopped or started are clearly communicated.
  • Discharge – explain the final list, stopped drugs and timing; check that the patient can read and understand it.

Conclusion Medication reconciliation ensures that the patient's medication list stays complete and correct as he moves through the health-care system.

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
question: Describe the safety measures in the care of lines, drains and tubes.
answer_html:
Introduction Hospitalised patients, especially in ICU and after surgery, may have many lines (IV, central, arterial), drains (chest, surgical) and tubes (nasogastric, urinary, endotracheal, tracheostomy, PEG). Each is a portal for infection and a source of errors such as dislodgement, blockage, misconnection and wrong administration. Systematic care keeps them safe.

1. General safety principles

  • Clear indication and daily review – remove as soon as not needed.
  • Aseptic insertion and handling; hand hygiene before touching any line or tube.
  • Label each line/tube at the insertion site and near the connection: type, date of insertion, size, and for infusions – drug name.
  • Trace every line from the patient to the source before connecting or giving any medicine, and at every shift handover ("line reconciliation").
  • Secure lines and tubes with appropriate fixation devices to prevent dislodgement and traction.
  • Keep systems closed; avoid unnecessary disconnections.

2. Preventing misconnections

  • Never give enteral feeds or oral medicines through IV lines; use enteral syringes with non-Luer (ENFit) connectors for nasogastric/PEG tubes.
  • Keep IV, arterial, epidural and enteral lines separate and clearly labelled; good lighting while connecting.

3. Specific care

  • IV and central lines – site inspection, VIP score, scrub the hub, dressing care, CLABSI bundle.
  • Urinary catheter – closed drainage, bag below bladder level, unobstructed flow, catheter care, CAUTI bundle.
  • Nasogastric (Ryle's) tube – confirm position before every feed and medication (aspirate pH ≤5.5, X-ray if doubtful; the "whoosh" test is unreliable), mark the length at the nostril, check the mark each shift, head end elevated during feeds.
  • Chest drain – underwater seal bottle below chest level, check swinging and bubbling, keep clamps at bedside (do not clamp routinely), secure connections, observe for leaks.
  • Surgical drains – patency, amount and colour of drainage, keep suction as ordered, aseptic emptying.
  • Endotracheal/tracheostomy tubes – secure ties, cuff pressure, suction as needed, spare tube and obturator at bedside.

4. Monitoring and documentation

  • Record amount, colour and nature of drainage and output; report sudden changes (bright red blood, no drainage, air leak).
  • Document insertion date, size, length at the lip/nostril, site condition and any problems.

5. During movement and transport

  • Check all lines before turning or shifting; keep drainage bags below the insertion level; avoid pulling.

6. Patient and family education

  • Do not pull, kink or disconnect tubes; report pain, leakage or displacement.

Conclusion Labelling, tracing, securing, monitoring and timely removal make lines, drains and tubes safe for the patient.

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
question: Explain the safe shifting and transport of patients within the hospital.
answer_html:
Introduction Patients are often moved within the hospital – from wards to OT, ICU, radiology, dialysis or other units. Intra-hospital transport carries risks: falls, dislodgement of tubes, sudden deterioration, oxygen running out, equipment failure and loss of information. Planning and careful handling make transport safe.

1. Planning before transport

  • Assess the patient's condition and stability (vital signs, airway, oxygen needs); decide whether the benefits of transfer justify the risk.
  • Communicate with the receiving unit – confirm they are ready; give a structured handover (e.g., SBAR).
  • Decide the escort – trained nurse (and doctor for critically ill or ventilated patients); attendant for stable patients.
  • Explain the transfer to the patient and family.

2. Preparation of the patient and equipment

  • Correct identification band; complete case file, investigation reports and consent forms.
  • Secure all lines, drains and tubes; empty drainage bags; clamp tubes only as per protocol.
  • Equipment: suitable trolley or wheelchair in good condition with side rails and brakes; portable oxygen cylinder with enough oxygen (check pressure), portable monitor, suction, Ambu bag and mask, emergency drugs as needed, infusion pumps with charged batteries.
  • Infection precautions – mask for patients with respiratory infection; inform receiving unit about isolation needs.

3. Safe shifting techniques

  • Use enough staff (3–4 persons for a dependent patient); communicate and move on a count.
  • Use slide sheets, transfer boards or hoists; avoid dragging (causes skin shear).
  • Lock the wheels of the bed and trolley during transfer; bring them to the same height.
  • Log-roll patients with suspected spinal injury; support fractured limbs.
  • Use good body mechanics – bend knees, keep the back straight, hold the load close.

4. During transport

  • Keep side rails up and safety straps fastened; push the trolley with the patient's feet first, head end towards the escort.
  • Continuous observation – airway, breathing, colour, consciousness, monitor readings, IV flow.
  • Avoid delays; use dedicated lifts where available.
  • Maintain privacy and warmth (cover the patient).

5. On arrival – handover

  • Give a verbal handover (SBAR) and hand over documents; check vital signs with the receiving nurse; ensure lines and tubes are re-secured.
  • Record time of transfer, condition before and after, and any incidents.

6. Inter-hospital transfer

  • Through equipped ambulances (e.g., 108 services), with written referral notes, stabilisation before transfer and trained escort.

Conclusion Safe transport depends on planning, the right equipment, trained escorts, safe handling techniques and clear handover.

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
question: Explain communication errors in health care and the strategies to prevent them, including SBAR.
answer_html:
Introduction Communication failure is one of the leading root causes of sentinel events in hospitals. Information about patients passes between many people – doctors, nurses, pharmacists, laboratory staff, patients and families – at many points (handovers, telephone orders, transfers). Each point is a chance for misunderstanding.

1. Common communication errors

  • Incomplete or unclear handover between shifts or units.
  • Verbal and telephone orders misheard (e.g., "fifteen" vs "fifty").
  • Illegible handwriting and dangerous abbreviations ("U" for units read as zero; "QD" misread; trailing zero "5.0 mg" read as 50 mg; missing leading zero ".5" read as 5).
  • Look-alike, sound-alike drug names.
  • Failure to report critical laboratory results promptly.
  • Hierarchy – junior staff hesitant to speak up to seniors.
  • Language barriers with patients; poor explanation leading to non-adherence.
  • Information not documented or not read.

2. Strategies to prevent communication errors (a) SBAR – structured communication tool | Component | Content | Example | |---|---|---| | S – Situation | What is happening now? | "I am Nurse Asha calling about Mr Ramesh, bed 12; his BP has dropped to 80/50." | | B – Background | Relevant history | "He is day 2 after laparotomy, on IV fluids, urine output 15 ml/hour for 2 hours." | | A – Assessment | What you think the problem is | "I think he may be bleeding or going into shock." | | R – Recommendation | What you want | "Please come and see him now; should I increase the IV fluid and send Hb?" | - Used for calling doctors, handovers and transfers; makes communication brief, focused and complete.

(b) Read-back / repeat-back

  • For verbal and telephone orders and critical test results, the receiver writes down and reads back the full message, and the sender confirms.

(c) Standardised handover

  • Bedside handover with checklists (ISBAR, I-PASS), including pending tasks, risks, lines and allergies.

(d) Written communication

  • Legible, complete, dated and signed orders; avoid "do-not-use" abbreviations; use generic names, tall-man lettering for LASA drugs; electronic prescribing where available.

(e) Closed-loop communication and teamwork

  • Call-out, check-back during emergencies; "two-challenge rule" and CUS words (I am Concerned, I am Uncomfortable, this is a Safety issue) to empower staff to speak up.
  • Team briefings and huddles; surgical safety checklist in OT.

(f) Communication with patients

  • Simple language, interpreters, teach-back method, written instructions, involving family.

Conclusion Structured tools like SBAR and read-back, clear documentation and a culture where everyone can speak up reduce communication errors and protect patients.

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
question: Define adverse event, near miss and sentinel event.
answer_html:
1. Adverse event – an incident that results in harm to a patient as a result of health care (not the disease) – e.g., a fall causing a fracture, a drug reaction, wrong blood transfusion.
  2. Near miss – an incident that did not reach the patient because it was detected and corrected in time – e.g., the wrong medicine drawn up but noticed before administration. Near misses are valuable warnings.
  3. Sentinel event – an unexpected occurrence involving death or serious physical or psychological injury, or the risk thereof – e.g., wrong-site surgery, infant abduction, retained instrument, ABO-incompatible transfusion. It signals the need for immediate investigation (RCA) and response.

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
question: What are never events? Give examples.
answer_html:
Never events are serious, largely preventable patient-safety incidents that should never occur if proper preventive measures are in place.

Examples

  1. Wrong-site, wrong-procedure or wrong-patient surgery.
  2. Retained foreign object (swab, instrument) after surgery.
  3. ABO-incompatible blood transfusion.
  4. Wrong-route administration of chemotherapy (e.g., vincristine given intrathecally) or of oral/enteral medicines given intravenously.
  5. Misplaced nasogastric tube not detected before feeding.
  6. Infant discharged to the wrong family; patient falling from an unrestricted window. Every never event needs immediate reporting and root cause analysis.

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
question: Define iatrogenic injury. Give examples.
answer_html:
Iatrogenic injury (Greek iatros = physician) is harm caused to a patient as a result of medical or nursing care – by diagnosis, treatment, procedures or advice – rather than by the patient's own disease.

Examples

  1. Medication errors and adverse drug reactions.
  2. Hospital-acquired infections (CAUTI, CLABSI, SSI).
  3. Falls and pressure ulcers during hospital stay.
  4. Sciatic nerve injury from a wrongly sited intramuscular injection.
  5. Burns from hot water bottles or diathermy; pneumothorax during central line insertion.
  6. Wrong-site surgery, transfusion reactions. Prevention: protocols, checklists, correct identification, aseptic technique and incident reporting.

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
unit_title: Section B: International Patient Safety Goals
question: Explain the International Patient Safety Goals (IPSG) and the role of the nurse in achieving each goal.

diagram.caption: The six International Patient Safety Goals
labels: 5 reduce risk of health care-associated infections
6 reduce risk of harm from falls

answer_html:
Introduction The International Patient Safety Goals (IPSG) were developed by the Joint Commission International (JCI) in collaboration with the WHO to address the most common and serious problem areas in patient safety worldwide. Each goal is supported by evidence-based solutions that can be applied in every hospital. Indian accreditation (NABH) has similar standards. Nurses play the central role in achieving every goal. Our syllabus also includes clinical alarm safety, a closely related goal.

IPSG 1 – Identify patients correctly Problem: wrong-patient errors in medication, transfusion, specimen collection and surgery. Requirements

  • Use at least two patient identifiers – e.g., full name and date of birth / hospital ID (UHID) – never the bed or room number.
  • Identify the patient before giving medicines, blood and blood products, collecting specimens, performing procedures and giving diet.

  • Label specimen containers in the presence of the patient. Role of the nurse

  • Apply an identification wristband on admission and check it before every intervention; replace if missing or illegible.

  • Ask the patient to state his name and date of birth (active identification) rather than asking "Are you Mr Kumar?".
  • Take special care with unconscious, confused, newborn and same-name patients (name alert stickers); use temporary identifiers for unknown patients.

IPSG 2 – Improve effective communication Problem: misunderstanding of verbal/telephone orders, critical results and handovers. Requirements

  • For verbal and telephone orders and critical test results – the receiver writes down, reads back and gets confirmation ("write down – read back – confirm").
  • Verbal orders only in emergencies; prescriber signs within the defined time (e.g., 24 hours).
  • Standardised handover communication (SBAR/ISBAR) between shifts and units.

  • Timely reporting of critical lab values to the responsible clinician. Role of the nurse

  • Use SBAR while calling doctors; perform read-back; document the time and person informed; give complete bedside handovers.

IPSG 3 – Improve the safety of high-alert medications Problem: some drugs cause serious harm when used wrongly. High-alert medications – concentrated electrolytes (potassium chloride, potassium phosphate, sodium chloride >0.9%, magnesium sulphate ≥50%), insulin, heparin and anticoagulants, opioids, chemotherapy drugs, sedatives, neuromuscular blockers, inotropes. Requirements

  • Remove concentrated electrolytes from patient-care areas unless clinically necessary; store them separately with warning labels.
  • Look-alike, sound-alike (LASA) drugs – separate storage, tall-man lettering, labels.

  • Independent double-checks by two nurses before giving high-alert drugs; standardised concentrations; infusion pumps. Role of the nurse

  • Never give potassium chloride as an IV push; always dilute and infuse as ordered.

  • Follow the rights of medication administration; double-check calculations; monitor patients (blood sugar for insulin, bleeding for heparin, respiration for opioids).

IPSG 4 – Ensure safe surgery (correct site, correct procedure, correct patient) Requirements – Universal Protocol

  1. Pre-procedure verification – correct patient, procedure, site, consent, investigations, implants and equipment.
  2. Site marking by the surgeon with a clear, unambiguous mark (e.g., an arrow or initials) with the patient's involvement, especially for laterality (left/right) and multiple levels.
  3. "Time-out" just before the incision – the whole team stops and confirms patient, procedure and site. - Use of the WHO Surgical Safety Checklist (sign-in, time-out, sign-out). Role of the nurse
  • Check identity, consent and site marking during pre-operative preparation and OT reception; lead or participate in the checklist; count swabs and instruments; speak up if anything is wrong.

IPSG 5 – Reduce the risk of health care–associated infections Requirements

  • Adopt and implement current hand hygiene guidelines (WHO/CDC) with a hand hygiene programme and compliance monitoring.

  • Use evidence-based practices to prevent device-associated infections and SSI (bundles). Role of the nurse

  • Perform hand hygiene at the five moments; follow standard precautions and bundles; take part in audits; teach patients and visitors.

IPSG 6 – Reduce the risk of patient harm resulting from falls Requirements

  • Fall-risk assessment of all inpatients on admission, after changes in condition or medication, after a fall, and at defined intervals (e.g., Morse Fall Scale).

  • Implement fall-prevention measures for patients at risk; monitor outcomes. Role of the nurse

  • Low bed with brakes locked, side rails as per policy, call bell within reach, adequate lighting, non-slip footwear, assistance in toileting and walking, scheduled rounding, review of sedatives, fall-risk signs/bands, patient and family education; report and analyse every fall.

Additional goal – Reduce harm associated with clinical alarm systems

  • Develop an alarm management policy: set appropriate, patient-specific alarm limits; never switch off alarms; respond promptly; maintain equipment; train staff to prevent alarm fatigue.

Summary table | Goal | Key action | |---|---| | 1. Identify patients correctly | Two identifiers, wristband, active identification | | 2. Effective communication | Write down–read back–confirm, SBAR, critical results | | 3. High-alert medications | Segregation, labels, double-checks, no concentrated KCl in wards | | 4. Safe surgery | Verification, site marking, time-out, WHO checklist | | 5. Reduce HAI | Hand hygiene programme, bundles | | 6. Reduce falls | Risk assessment and prevention measures | | (Clinical alarms) | Alarm policy, appropriate limits, timely response |

Conclusion The IPSG target the commonest and most dangerous gaps in care. Because nurses identify patients, communicate orders, give medicines, prepare for surgery, prevent infections and prevent falls, they are the key to achieving these goals in every hospital.

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
unit_title: Section B: International Patient Safety Goals
question: Explain clinical alarm safety and the prevention of alarm fatigue.
answer_html:
Introduction Monitors, ventilators, infusion pumps and pulse oximeters use alarms to warn staff of dangerous changes in a patient's condition or equipment problems. But in a busy ICU each patient may trigger hundreds of alarms a day, and studies show that most (about 70–99%) are false or not clinically actionable. Staff become desensitised and may silence, ignore or switch off alarms – a dangerous situation called alarm fatigue, which has led to deaths. Reducing harm from clinical alarms is therefore a recognised patient safety goal.

1. Causes of alarm fatigue

  • Default alarm limits too narrow for the individual patient.
  • Poor electrode placement or old electrodes, loose probes, patient movement (artefacts).
  • Duplicate alarms from several devices; low-priority alarms with the same sound as critical ones.
  • Monitoring patients who do not really need it.
  • Inadequate staffing and noisy environment.

2. Consequences

  • Missed or delayed response to true emergencies (arrhythmias, apnoea, desaturation, disconnection).
  • Patient sleep disturbance, anxiety and delirium; staff stress.

3. Strategies for clinical alarm safety

  1. Hospital alarm management policy – identify the most important alarms; decide who responds and how quickly.
  2. Customise alarm limits for each patient on admission and when the condition changes (within safe ranges set by policy).
  3. Correct use of sensors – skin preparation, daily change of ECG electrodes, correct placement, properly fitting SpO₂ probes.
  4. Never disable alarms or set the volume too low; check the patient first before silencing.
  5. Use alarm delays and smart alarms where appropriate (e.g., brief SpO₂ dips).
  6. Monitor only when indicated; stop monitoring when no longer needed.
  7. Escalation systems – secondary notification to pagers or central stations; adequate staff to respond.
  8. Regular maintenance and testing of equipment by biomedical engineering.
  9. Training of staff on alarm settings and response; periodic audit of alarm data.

4. Role of the nurse Check alarm settings at the start of each shift and handover, individualise limits as ordered, respond immediately, document alarm events, report malfunctioning devices and educate families not to touch alarm buttons.

Conclusion Alarms protect patients only when they are meaningful and answered; good alarm management prevents alarm fatigue and saves lives.

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
unit_title: Section B: International Patient Safety Goals
question: Explain the methods and importance of correct patient identification.
answer_html:
Introduction Wrong-patient errors – the wrong patient receiving a drug, blood, surgery or report – are among the most serious and preventable incidents in hospitals. Correct patient identification is IPSG 1, the foundation of every other safety practice.

1. Two-identifier rule

  • At least two identifiers must be used every time – e.g., full name and date of birth, or name and hospital number (UHID/IP number).
  • Room or bed number must never be used as an identifier (patients move).

2. When to identify

  • Before giving medicines, blood and blood products, diet.
  • Before collecting specimens (label in front of the patient) and sending them.
  • Before procedures, investigations, surgery and radiological tests.
  • At admission, transfer, handover and discharge; when handing over a baby to the mother.

3. Methods

  • Identification wristband applied on admission, checked for accuracy with the patient/family; usually white for identity, with separate alert bands or stickers (allergy, fall risk) as per hospital policy.
  • Active identification – ask the patient to state his name and date of birth; compare with the wristband and the order/label.
  • Barcode scanning of wristbands with medicines and specimens where available.
  • Photographs in records (e.g., long-stay or psychiatric patients, dialysis units).

4. Special situations

  • Newborns – two identical bands (wrist and ankle) with mother's name, UHID, sex, date and time of birth applied in the delivery room before the baby leaves the mother; matched with the mother's band at every handover.
  • Unconscious or unknown patients – temporary identifier (e.g., "Unknown Male 1" with UHID) until identity is known.
  • Same or similar names – "name alert" stickers, separating beds.
  • Language barriers, confused or sedated patients – confirm with family and wristband.

5. Common causes of errors Missing or wrong wristbands, pre-labelling of tubes, distractions, emergencies, transfers, assumptions ("he answered to the name").

6. Role of the nurse Apply and check bands, never skip identification in a hurry, report identification errors as incidents, and educate patients to speak up if they are not asked.

7. Importance (summary) Prevents wrong-patient medication, transfusion, surgery and reports; protects patients legally and ethically; required for NABH/JCI accreditation.

Conclusion Two identifiers, every time, for every patient – this simple habit prevents some of the worst errors in health care.

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
unit_title: Section B: International Patient Safety Goals
question: What is "read-back"? When is it used?
answer_html:
Read-back is a communication safety technique in which the person receiving a verbal or telephone order or a critical test result writes it down and then reads the complete message back to the sender, who confirms that it is correct ("write down – read back – confirm").

Used for

  1. Verbal and telephone orders for medications and treatment (only in emergencies or when the prescriber is not present).
  2. Critical (panic) laboratory and radiology results reported by phone.
  3. Important handover information.

Points: spell out drug names and say numbers digit by digit (e.g., "one-five" for 15); the prescriber signs the order within the defined time (e.g., 24 hours). It is a key requirement of IPSG 2 – improve effective communication.

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
question: Explain hazardous material (HAZMAT) safety in hospitals, including the material safety data sheet (MSDS) and the management of chemical, mercury and cytotoxic spills.

diagram.caption: Steps of spill management
labels: collect and dispose as hazardous waste

answer_html:
Introduction Hospitals use and store many hazardous materials (HAZMAT) – disinfectants, laboratory chemicals, anaesthetic gases, anticancer drugs, mercury and radioactive substances. Accidental spills, leaks, splashes or inhalation can cause burns, poisoning, allergies, cancer, fire or explosion, and can harm patients, staff and the environment. HAZMAT safety is the programme of policies and practices for the safe identification, storage, handling, spill management and disposal of these materials, and is a requirement of NABH accreditation.

A. Hazardous materials found in hospitals | Category | Examples | |---|---| | Disinfectants and sterilants | Glutaraldehyde, formaldehyde (formalin), sodium hypochlorite, phenol, ethylene oxide, hydrogen peroxide | | Laboratory chemicals | Acids, alkalis, xylene, alcohols, staining reagents | | Cytotoxic drugs | Cyclophosphamide, methotrexate, cisplatin, 5-fluorouracil | | Anaesthetic gases | Nitrous oxide, isoflurane, sevoflurane | | Heavy metals | Mercury in old thermometers and BP apparatus, lead | | Compressed gases | Oxygen, nitrous oxide, CO₂ cylinders | | Flammables | Spirit, ether, acetone | | Radioactive materials | Iodine-131, technetium, brachytherapy sources |

B. Hazards and labelling

  • Hazards may be physical (flammable, explosive, corrosive, compressed) or health hazards (toxic, irritant, sensitiser, carcinogenic, harmful to reproduction).
  • Containers carry hazard pictograms under the Globally Harmonised System (GHS) – e.g., flame (flammable), skull and crossbones (acute toxicity), corrosion symbol, exclamation mark (irritant), health-hazard symbol (carcinogen), gas cylinder.
  • Every container must be labelled with the chemical name, hazard and date; never store chemicals in unlabelled or food containers.

C. Material Safety Data Sheet (MSDS/SDS) Definition: an MSDS (now called Safety Data Sheet, SDS) is a document supplied by the manufacturer that gives detailed information about a hazardous chemical – its hazards and how to use, store, handle and dispose of it safely, and what to do in an emergency. Contents (16 sections) – identification of product and supplier; hazard identification; composition/ingredients; first-aid measures; fire-fighting measures; accidental release (spill) measures; handling and storage; exposure controls and personal protection (PPE); physical and chemical properties; stability and reactivity; toxicological information; ecological information; disposal; transport information; regulatory information; other information. Use: an up-to-date MSDS file must be available in every area where chemicals are used (wards, OT, CSSD, laboratory, pharmacy) and staff must know where it is kept and how to read it.

D. Safe storage and handling

  1. Inventory of all hazardous materials in each department.
  2. Store in original, labelled, tightly closed containers, in cool, dry, well-ventilated areas; flammables in fire-proof cabinets away from heat and oxygen cylinders.
  3. Segregate incompatible chemicals (acids from alkalis; oxidisers from flammables; hypochlorite from acids and ammonia – they release toxic gases).
  4. Minimum quantities in clinical areas; store heavy containers on lower shelves.
  5. Use chemicals in fume hoods or ventilated areas (glutaraldehyde, formalin, xylene); scavenging systems for anaesthetic gases.
  6. Wear appropriate PPE (gloves, goggles, apron, mask) as per MSDS.
  7. Provide eye-wash stations and emergency showers reachable within about 10 seconds where corrosives are used.
  8. Cylinders – chained upright, capped, away from heat; never use oil or grease on valves.

E. Spill management – general principles

  1. Assess the spill – identify the material (label, MSDS), quantity and risk; evacuate the area if large, toxic or flammable; call the HAZMAT/emergency team (code as per hospital policy).
  2. Secure the area – warn others, keep people away, put up warning signs; remove sources of ignition; ventilate.
  3. Wear PPE – gloves, gown, goggles/face shield, mask/respirator as needed.
  4. Use the spill kit – absorbent pads or granules, neutralising agents, scoop and scraper, forceps for broken glass, disposal bags and labels.
  5. Contain and absorb from the outside towards the centre; neutralise if indicated.
  6. Collect waste into labelled bags/containers; dispose as hazardous waste.
  7. Decontaminate the area with detergent and water.
  8. Remove PPE, wash hands; give first aid to exposed persons.
  9. Report and document the incident; review causes.

F. Mercury spill management Mercury from a broken thermometer or BP apparatus vaporises at room temperature; inhaled vapour damages the nervous system and kidneys.

  1. Keep people (especially pregnant women and children) away; open windows and close inner doors; switch off fans and air-conditioning that may spread vapour.
  2. Remove jewellery (mercury binds gold); wear nitrile gloves, mask and goggles.
  3. Never use a broom or vacuum cleaner (spreads droplets and vapour) and never pour mercury down the drain.
  4. Push droplets together with stiff cardboard; pick them up with an eye dropper or syringe (without needle); use sticky tape for tiny beads; use a torch to locate shining beads.
  5. Place mercury and contaminated items in a sealed, leak-proof, wide-mouthed container with water (or use mercury-absorbing powder from the spill kit); label "Mercury waste – hazardous".
  6. Hand over to the authorised hazardous waste handler.
  7. Ventilate the room for 24 hours. Hospitals are encouraged to become mercury-free by replacing mercury devices with digital/aneroid instruments (India is a party to the Minamata Convention on mercury).

G. Cytotoxic (chemotherapy) spill management

  1. Use the chemotherapy spill kit; wear two pairs of chemotherapy-tested gloves, impermeable gown, face shield/goggles and N95 mask.
  2. Cover liquids with absorbent pads (powders with damp pads to avoid aerosols); pick up glass with a scoop.
  3. Clean the area three times with detergent followed by water, from the least to the most contaminated area.
  4. Discard all materials in yellow bags with the cytotoxic label (yellow category BMW).
  5. If skin is contaminated – wash with soap and water; eyes – irrigate for 15 minutes; report to occupational health.

H. First aid for chemical exposure

  • Skin – remove contaminated clothing; flush with running water for at least 15–20 minutes.
  • Eyes – irrigate with water/saline for at least 15 minutes, holding eyelids open; seek medical care.
  • Inhalation – move to fresh air; oxygen if needed.
  • Ingestion – do not induce vomiting unless the MSDS advises; seek medical help with the MSDS.

I. Role of the nurse Know the hazardous materials in the ward and where the MSDS and spill kit are kept, dilute and handle disinfectants correctly, use PPE, manage small spills promptly, report exposures, and participate in HAZMAT training and drills.

Conclusion HAZMAT safety depends on knowing the hazard (labels and MSDS), storing and handling materials correctly, and responding to spills quickly and safely. A well-prepared nurse protects herself, her patients and the environment.

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
question: Explain the role of the nurse during disasters.
answer_html:
Introduction A disaster is any occurrence that causes damage, loss of human life and deterioration of health services on a scale sufficient to require an extraordinary response from outside the affected community (WHO). Disasters may be natural (floods, earthquakes, cyclones, epidemics) or man-made (fire, building collapse, rail and road accidents, chemical leaks, terrorism). India manages disasters under the Disaster Management Act, 2005, through the NDMA, state and district authorities. Nurses are the largest health workforce and play key roles in every phase.

1. Preparedness phase (before disaster)

  • Participate in the hospital disaster management plan – roles, call-in lists, triage areas, extra beds, surge capacity.
  • Training and mock drills (fire, mass-casualty, earthquake evacuation, Code Yellow).
  • Maintain emergency stock – dressings, IV fluids, splints, drugs, triage tags, PPE, stretchers.
  • Identify vulnerable people in the community; community education on first aid and evacuation.

2. Response phase (during disaster)

  • Triage – sort casualties by priority using colour tags (e.g., START method):
    • Red – immediate (life-threatening but salvageable: breathing difficulty, shock, uncontrolled bleeding).
    • Yellow – delayed/urgent (serious but stable).
    • Green – minor ("walking wounded").
    • Black – dead or expectant.
  • First aid and emergency care – airway, breathing, control of bleeding, shock management, splinting, burns care, CPR.
  • Organise casualty areas, receive and register victims, maintain identification and records; track patients and bodies.
  • Infection prevention – safe water, sanitation, hand hygiene, vaccination (tetanus), prevention of epidemics in shelters.
  • Psychological first aid – reassure victims and families, especially children, elderly and pregnant women.
  • Coordinate and communicate with the incident command, doctors, police, NGOs; mobilise resources.

3. Recovery and rehabilitation phase (after disaster)

  • Continuing care of injured and chronically ill; follow-up of wounds, fractures, pregnant women and children.
  • Disease surveillance – diarrhoea, leptospirosis, malaria and respiratory infections after floods.
  • Mental health support – grief counselling, identification of post-traumatic stress disorder.
  • Help restore health services; nutrition and immunisation in camps.
  • Evaluation of the response and updating the plan.

4. Self-care of nurses Rotation of duties, rest, debriefing and support to prevent burnout.

5. Examples from India Nurses' roles were seen in the Kerala floods (2018) – relief camps, leptospirosis prophylaxis; the COVID-19 pandemic – screening, isolation wards, vaccination; and train and building disasters – triage and emergency care.

Conclusion From planning and triage to rehabilitation, nurses save lives in disasters through organised, calm and compassionate action.

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
question: Explain the 5S methodology in hospitals.
answer_html:
Introduction 5S is a Japanese workplace-organisation method (developed in the Toyota production system) that creates a clean, orderly, safe and efficient work environment. It is widely used in Indian public and private hospitals under quality programmes such as Kayakalp and NQAS to reduce waste, search time and errors. The five steps are named after five Japanese words beginning with "S".

1. Sort (Seiri)

  • Remove unnecessary items from the work area – expired drugs, broken equipment, old files, excess stock.
  • Use "red tags" to mark items whose need is doubtful; decide to keep, move or discard.
  • Example: clearing the ward store of condemned instruments and expired IV fluids.

2. Set in order (Seiton)

  • "A place for everything and everything in its place."
  • Arrange necessary items so that they are easy to find, use and return – label shelves, drawers and cupboards; colour coding; shadow boards for instruments.
  • Frequently used items kept nearest; LASA drugs stored separately.
  • Example: a standardised crash cart with drawers labelled and drugs arranged in the same order in every ward.

3. Shine (Seiso)

  • Clean the workplace and equipment regularly, and inspect while cleaning to detect problems (leaks, damage).
  • Assign cleaning responsibilities and schedules.

4. Standardise (Seiketsu)

  • Make the first three S's a routine using standard operating procedures, checklists, labels, colour codes and visual displays.
  • Same layout and labelling across all wards so staff can work anywhere.

5. Sustain (Shitsuke)

  • Build discipline and habit so that improvements last – training, regular 5S audits, feedback, recognition and leadership support.

Benefits in hospitals

  • Less time searching for supplies – more time for patients.
  • Fewer medication and equipment errors (correct drugs found quickly in emergencies).
  • Better infection control – clean, clutter-free surfaces are easier to disinfect.
  • Improved safety – no obstacles in corridors (fewer falls), fire exits kept clear.
  • Better inventory control and cost savings; improved staff morale and patient satisfaction.

Role of the nurse The ward in-charge leads 5S in her unit – organising stores, labelling, checking expiry dates, maintaining the crash cart and conducting audits.

Conclusion 5S is a simple, low-cost method that turns cluttered workplaces into safe, efficient and pleasant care areas.

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
question: Explain radiation safety in the hospital.
answer_html:
Introduction Hospitals use ionising radiation for diagnosis (X-rays, CT scans, fluoroscopy, nuclear medicine) and treatment (radiotherapy, radioactive iodine, brachytherapy). Radiation cannot be seen or felt, but excessive exposure can cause skin burns, cataract, infertility, cancer and genetic effects, and can harm the fetus. In India radiation safety is regulated by the Atomic Energy Regulatory Board (AERB).

1. Principles of radiation protection

  • Justification – every exposure must do more good than harm (no unnecessary X-rays).
  • Optimisation – ALARA – keep doses "As Low As Reasonably Achievable".
  • Dose limitation – occupational workers: 20 mSv per year averaged over 5 years (not more than 30 mSv in a single year); general public: 1 mSv per year.

2. The three protective measures – time, distance, shielding

  1. Time – minimise the time spent near the radiation source; plan care in advance; rotate staff.
  2. Distance – radiation falls according to the inverse square law (doubling the distance reduces exposure to one-fourth); stand at least 2 metres away during portable X-rays.
  3. Shielding – lead aprons (0.25–0.5 mm lead equivalent), thyroid collars, lead glasses, mobile lead screens and lead-lined walls and doors.

3. Protection of staff

  • Personal monitoring with thermoluminescent dosimeter (TLD) badges, worn at chest level under the lead apron; records reviewed regularly.
  • Do not hold patients during X-rays; if unavoidable, a relative (not pregnant) holds wearing a lead apron.
  • Pregnant staff should inform the supervisor and avoid unnecessary exposure.
  • Lead aprons hung properly (not folded) and checked periodically for cracks.

4. Protection of patients

  • Ask women of child-bearing age about LMP/pregnancy before X-rays; shield the gonads and thyroid where possible.
  • Avoid repeat X-rays by correct positioning and preparation.

5. Care of patients with radioactive sources

  • Radioactive iodine therapy – single room with attached toilet, radiation warning sign, limited visitors (no children or pregnant women), time limits for staff, disposal of body fluids as per protocol.
  • Sealed sources (brachytherapy) – keep a lead container and long-handled forceps in the room; if the source is dislodged, never touch it with hands – pick it up with forceps, place it in the container and inform the radiation safety officer.

6. Signs and controls The radiation trefoil symbol, warning lights outside X-ray rooms, restricted access and a Radiation Safety Officer (RSO) in every facility.

Conclusion Applying ALARA through time, distance and shielding, with personal monitoring, keeps radiation benefits high and risks low for patients and staff.

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
question: Explain the hospital emergency codes and their importance.
answer_html:
Introduction Hospitals use emergency codes – short coloured "code words" announced on the public address system – to alert trained staff quickly about an emergency and its location without causing panic among patients and visitors. Each hospital defines its own codes in its emergency management policy (NABH-accredited hospitals must have them), so codes may differ slightly between hospitals.

1. Commonly used codes | Code | Emergency (common meaning) | Response | |---|---|---| | Code Blue | Cardiac or respiratory arrest / medical emergency (adult) | Resuscitation team rushes with crash cart; CPR, defibrillation | | Code Red | Fire or smoke | RACE (Rescue, Alarm, Contain, Extinguish/Evacuate); fire team | | Code Pink | Infant or child abduction/missing | Exits sealed, security search, all staff watch for suspicious persons | | Code Yellow | External disaster / mass casualty | Disaster plan activated; extra staff and beds; triage areas | | Code Orange | Hazardous material (chemical) spill (some hospitals use it for external disaster) | HAZMAT team, evacuation of area, decontamination | | Code Black | Bomb threat | Security search, evacuation as instructed | | Code Grey/White | Violent or aggressive person | Security and trained staff respond | | Code Silver | Person with a weapon / hostage situation | Security and police; staff move to safety | | Code Green | Evacuation of a department or hospital | Planned evacuation routes | | Code Brown | Severe weather / internal emergency (varies) | As per plan | (Paediatric code blue and "rapid response team" calls for deteriorating patients are also common.)

2. Method of announcement

  • The code and exact location are announced clearly, usually three times – e.g., "Code Blue, Ward 5, Bed 12".
  • "All clear" is announced when the emergency is over.

3. Importance

  • Rapid, organised response by a pre-assigned team saves lives (e.g., early defibrillation in cardiac arrest).
  • Prevents panic among patients and visitors.
  • Standardises communication; everyone knows their role.
  • Required for accreditation; tested through regular mock drills.

4. Role of the nurse Know all codes and the number to dial; activate the code promptly; start first actions (CPR, RACE, securing infants); know her role in each code; participate in drills; document events.

5. Points to remember

  • Codes should be displayed on posters near telephones and in staff areas.
  • Never use a code word casually; avoid announcing details that alarm patients (e.g., "fire" is replaced by "Code Red").

Conclusion Emergency codes turn chaos into coordinated action – every nurse must know them by heart.

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
question: Explain laser safety in the operation theatre.
answer_html:
Introduction LASER (Light Amplification by Stimulated Emission of Radiation) produces a powerful, focused beam used in surgery (CO₂, Nd:YAG, argon, KTP lasers), ophthalmology, dermatology, gynaecology, urology and ENT. Surgical lasers are Class 4 – the most hazardous class. Both patients and staff can be harmed unless strict safety measures are followed.

1. Hazards

  1. Eye injury – direct or reflected beams can burn the cornea or retina and cause permanent blindness.
  2. Skin burns to the patient or staff.
  3. Fire – ignition of drapes, gauze, hair, alcohol-based skin preparations and endotracheal tubes (airway fire), especially in an oxygen-rich atmosphere.
  4. Laser plume (smoke) – contains toxic gases, carcinogens and viable viruses (e.g., HPV) and bacteria; causes respiratory irritation.
  5. Electrical hazards from high-voltage equipment.

2. Administrative controls

  • A trained Laser Safety Officer (LSO); written laser safety policy and checklist; staff training and credentialing.
  • Laser-controlled area – warning signs on all doors ("Laser in use – wear protective eyewear"), doors kept closed, windows covered.
  • Laser log of each use; key control so that only authorised users operate the machine.

3. Eye protection

  • Wavelength-specific protective eyewear (marked with wavelength and optical density) for everyone in the room.
  • Patient's eyes protected with appropriate goggles or moist eye pads.

4. Fire prevention

  • Keep a basin of sterile water/saline and a fire extinguisher ready; use moist towels/sponges around the operative site.
  • Allow alcohol-based preparations to dry completely; avoid pooling.
  • Use laser-resistant endotracheal tubes with the cuff filled with saline (often tinted with methylene blue); keep oxygen concentration as low as possible (below 30%) and avoid nitrous oxide during airway surgery.
  • Keep the laser on "standby" mode when not firing; only the surgeon controls the foot pedal.

5. Plume control

  • Smoke evacuators with suction close to the site; high-filtration (laser/N95) masks for staff.

6. Instruments

  • Use non-reflective (dull/anodised) instruments to prevent reflected beams.

7. Nurse's role Check equipment and signs before the case, distribute eyewear, protect the patient's eyes and skin, keep fire-safety items ready, operate the smoke evacuator, monitor during use and document.

Conclusion Laser surgery is safe when eyes, skin, airway and room are protected and fire and plume risks are actively controlled.

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
question: What is a material safety data sheet (MSDS)?
answer_html:
A Material Safety Data Sheet (MSDS), now called Safety Data Sheet (SDS), is a document prepared by the manufacturer or supplier of a hazardous chemical giving complete information about its hazards and safe use.

Contents include

  • Identity of the product and supplier; hazards; composition.
  • First-aid measures, fire-fighting measures, spill (accidental release) measures.
  • Handling and storage; PPE required; physical and chemical properties; toxicity; disposal and transport.

Use: MSDS must be available in every area where the chemical is used (e.g., glutaraldehyde in endoscopy, formalin in OT/lab); staff refer to it during spills and exposures.

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
question: Explain the ALARA principle.
answer_html:
ALARA stands for "As Low As Reasonably Achievable". It is the basic principle of radiation protection: every exposure to ionising radiation should be kept as low as reasonably possible, considering economic and social factors, even when it is below the legal dose limits.

ALARA is achieved by

  1. Time – minimum time near the source.
  2. Distance – maximum distance (inverse square law).
  3. Shielding – lead aprons, thyroid collars, screens. Also by avoiding unnecessary X-rays, correct technique and personal dose monitoring (TLD badges).

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
question: Define needle-stick injury. How can it be prevented? Describe the post-exposure prophylaxis and management.

diagram.caption: Post-exposure management algorithm after needle-stick injury
labels: HIV PEP within 2–72 hours for 28 days

answer_html:
Introduction Needles and other sharps are used thousands of times a day in every hospital. Needle-stick and sharps injuries (NSI) are among the commonest occupational hazards for nurses, exposing them to more than 20 blood-borne pathogens, chiefly hepatitis B virus (HBV), hepatitis C virus (HCV) and HIV. Most injuries are preventable, and correct post-exposure management greatly reduces the risk of infection.

Definition (1 mark) A needle-stick injury is a percutaneous (skin-piercing) wound caused by a needle or other sharp instrument (scalpel, lancet, broken glass, cannula stylet) that has been contaminated with blood or body fluids of a patient. Splashes of blood or body fluids on mucous membranes (eyes, mouth) or non-intact skin are managed in the same way.

A. Risk of infection after a single needle-stick exposure from an infected source | Virus | Risk | |---|---| | Hepatitis B | 6–30% (highest when the source is HBeAg-positive) | | Hepatitis C | About 1.8% | | HIV | About 0.3% (mucous membrane splash about 0.09%) | Risk is higher with hollow-bore needles, deep injury, visible blood on the device, needles used in an artery or vein, and a source with high viral load.

B. Common situations causing NSI Recapping needles, disposing of sharps late or in overfilled containers, passing sharps hand to hand, uncooperative patients, suturing, drawing blood, needles left on beds or in linen and waste, poor lighting, fatigue and haste.

C. Prevention of needle-stick injury (4 marks) 1. Elimination and substitution

  • Avoid unnecessary injections; use oral medication when possible.
  • Needle-free IV systems and connectors; use of auto-disable (AD) syringes in immunisation.

2. Engineering controls

  • Safety-engineered devices – retractable syringes, self-sheathing needles, safety IV cannulas, blunt suture needles.
  • Puncture-proof sharps containers placed at the point of use (within arm's reach), filled only to three-fourths, then closed and replaced.
  • Needle cutters/destroyers at the bedside.

3. Work-practice controls

  • Never recap needles; if unavoidable, use the one-handed scoop technique.
  • Dispose of sharps immediately after use by the person who used them.
  • Do not bend, break or remove needles by hand.
  • Do not pass sharps hand to hand – use a tray/neutral zone in OT.
  • Keep the patient informed and positioned; get help for uncooperative or restless patients and children.
  • Adequate lighting; avoid hurry; never leave sharps on beds, trays or linen.
  • Wear gloves (reduce the blood volume transferred if pricked).

4. Administrative controls

  • Sharps-injury prevention policy; training of all staff, including housekeeping and waste handlers.
  • Hepatitis B vaccination of all health workers (BMW Rules make it mandatory), with anti-HBs testing.
  • Adequate staffing and reasonable working hours.
  • NSI register, analysis of every injury and corrective action.

D. Post-exposure management (5 marks) Step 1 – Immediate first aid

  • Do not panic.
  • Wash the wound immediately with soap and running water; let it bleed freely – do not squeeze, scrub, suck or put the finger in the mouth.
  • Do not use bleach, strong antiseptics or caustic agents on the wound.
  • Splash on skin – wash with soap and water.
  • Splash in the eyes – irrigate with clean water or normal saline for several minutes, keeping eyes open; remove contact lenses.
  • Splash in the mouth – spit out, rinse the mouth repeatedly with water.

Step 2 – Report immediately

  • Inform the ward in-charge and the designated PEP/occupational health officer (or casualty medical officer) at once – time is critical.
