  • Fill the incident/NSI report form: date, time, device, procedure, depth, PPE used, source details.

Step 3 – Assess the exposure and the source

  • Type of exposure – percutaneous, mucous membrane or non-intact skin; amount of blood; depth; hollow or solid needle.
  • Source patient – check records and, with informed consent and counselling, test for HIV (rapid test), HBsAg and anti-HCV.
  • If the source is unknown (e.g., needle in waste), assess risk.

Step 4 – Baseline testing of the exposed health worker

  • HIV, HBsAg and anti-HBs titre, anti-HCV (with consent and confidentiality); pregnancy test where relevant.

Step 5 – Post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) (a) HIV PEP

  • Start as early as possible – ideally within 2 hours and not later than 72 hours after exposure; do not wait for source test results if risk is significant.
  • Current national (NACO) regimen: tenofovir 300 mg + lamivudine 300 mg + dolutegravir 50 mg (TLD), one tablet daily for 28 days.
  • Counsel about side effects (nausea, headache, fatigue) and adherence; follow up for completion.
  • If the source tests HIV-negative (and is not in the window period), PEP can be stopped.

(b) Hepatitis B prophylaxis – depends on vaccination status of the health worker | Exposed person | Action | |---|---| | Vaccinated, known responder (anti-HBs ≥10 mIU/ml) | No treatment needed | | Unvaccinated or incompletely vaccinated | Hepatitis B immunoglobulin (HBIG 0.06 ml/kg IM) as soon as possible (within 24 hours, up to 7 days) plus start/complete the hepatitis B vaccine series | | Vaccinated non-responder | HBIG (two doses one month apart) or HBIG + revaccination | | Response unknown | Test anti-HBs urgently: if adequate – nothing; if low – HBIG + vaccine booster |

(c) Hepatitis C

  • No PEP vaccine or drug is available; follow-up testing (HCV RNA at a few weeks and anti-HCV later) so that early treatment with direct-acting antivirals can be given if infection occurs.

Step 6 – Follow-up

  • HIV testing at about 6 weeks and 3 months (and later as per policy); HBV and HCV markers as indicated.
  • Advise the worker during the follow-up period to use condoms, not to donate blood, organs or semen, and to seek advice about breastfeeding and pregnancy.
  • Monitor for drug toxicity; provide psychological support – exposure causes great anxiety.
  • Confidentiality of the worker's and source's results must be maintained.

Step 7 – Documentation and prevention review

  • Record in the NSI register; analyse the cause (RCA) and take corrective action (e.g., more sharps containers, safety devices, training).

Conclusion Needle-stick injuries are common but largely preventable through safe practices, safety-engineered devices, proper sharps disposal and hepatitis B vaccination. When an injury occurs, immediate first aid, prompt reporting and timely PEP protect the nurse from life-long infection.

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
question: Explain the vaccination of health-care workers.
answer_html:
Introduction Health-care workers (HCWs) are exposed to infections through blood, respiratory secretions and contact. Vaccination protects the worker, prevents transmission to vulnerable patients and maintains a healthy workforce during outbreaks. The BMW Management Rules 2016 make immunisation of all health workers and waste handlers (hepatitis B and tetanus) the responsibility of the hospital.

1. Hepatitis B vaccine – most important

  • All HCWs at risk of exposure to blood, including students, housekeeping and laundry staff.
  • Three doses at 0, 1 and 6 months, 1 ml (20 µg) IM in the deltoid.
  • Check anti-HBs 1–2 months after the third dose: ≥10 mIU/ml = protected (no booster needed); <10 mIU/ml – repeat the 3-dose series and retest; persistent non-responders are counselled and given HBIG after any exposure.

2. Influenza vaccine

  • Every year before the influenza season – protects HCWs and reduces spread to high-risk patients.

3. Tetanus–diphtheria (Td)

  • Booster every 10 years, and after injuries as per schedule.

4. Measles–mumps–rubella (MMR)

  • Two doses (at least 28 days apart) for workers without evidence of immunity – especially those in paediatrics and maternity (rubella in pregnant staff harms the fetus).

5. Varicella (chickenpox) vaccine

  • Two doses for workers without history of chickenpox or immunity.

6. COVID-19 vaccine

  • As per national programme guidelines (HCWs were the first priority group).

7. Other vaccines in special situations

  • Hepatitis A and typhoid – food handlers and laboratory staff.
  • Meningococcal vaccine – laboratory staff handling N. meningitidis.
  • Rabies pre-exposure prophylaxis – anti-rabies clinic and laboratory workers.

8. Special considerations

  • Live vaccines (MMR, varicella) are avoided in pregnancy; women should avoid pregnancy for 1 month after them.
  • Screen immunity status at pre-employment medical examination.
  • Maintain an immunisation register and individual records; vaccines provided free of cost by the employer.
  • Encourage uptake through education; address vaccine hesitancy.

Role of the nurse Complete her own vaccinations and keep records, encourage colleagues and students, assist the occupational health service in vaccination drives and follow-up of titres.

9. Benefits Protects the worker's own health, prevents hospital outbreaks (influenza, measles, chickenpox), reduces absenteeism and maintains services during epidemics.

Conclusion Vaccinated health workers are safer workers – for themselves and for their patients.

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
question: Describe the occupational health hazards of nurses and their prevention.
answer_html:
Introduction Nurses care for others but face many risks to their own health at work – infections, chemicals, radiation, back injuries, stress and violence. Occupational health aims to protect workers through prevention, early detection and supportive services.

A. Types of occupational hazards 1. Biological hazards

  • Blood-borne infections – HBV, HCV, HIV through needle-stick and splash injuries.
  • Airborne/droplet infections – tuberculosis, influenza, COVID-19, measles, chickenpox.
  • Contact infections – MRSA, scabies, conjunctivitis.

2. Chemical hazards

  • Disinfectants (glutaraldehyde, formaldehyde, hypochlorite) – dermatitis, asthma, eye irritation.
  • Cytotoxic drugs – skin irritation, reproductive harm, cancer risk.
  • Anaesthetic gases (OT staff), latex allergy from gloves, mercury.

3. Physical hazards

  • Ionising radiation, lasers, noise, electrical hazards, burns, extremes of temperature.
  • Slips, trips and falls on wet floors.

4. Ergonomic (mechanical) hazards

  • Back injuries and musculoskeletal disorders from lifting, turning and transferring patients; prolonged standing – varicose veins, foot pain; repetitive strain from computer work.

5. Psychosocial hazards

  • Stress and burnout – heavy workload, staff shortage, emotional demands, death and suffering.
  • Shift work and night duties – sleep disturbance, fatigue, digestive problems.
  • Workplace violence – verbal and physical assault by patients or relatives; sexual harassment; bullying.

B. Prevention – hierarchy of controls

  1. Elimination/substitution – needle-free systems, mercury-free devices, latex-free gloves, safer chemicals.
  2. Engineering controls – safety-engineered sharps, ventilation and isolation rooms, fume hoods, mechanical lifting aids, lead shielding.
  3. Administrative controls – policies (IPC, sharps, HAZMAT), training, adequate staffing, reasonable shift rotation and rest breaks, job rotation, occupational health services, incident reporting.
  4. Personal protective equipment – gloves, masks, N95, gowns, goggles, lead aprons.

C. Specific measures

  • Vaccination (hepatitis B, influenza, MMR, varicella) and pre-employment and periodic health check-ups, TB screening.
  • Post-exposure prophylaxis services available 24 hours.
  • Safe patient handling – team lifting, hoists, slide sheets, correct body mechanics.
  • Workplace violence prevention – security staff, panic alarms, restricted visitor entry, de-escalation training, legal protection of health workers (several states have laws protecting medicare service persons, e.g., Maharashtra's 2010 Act); support after incidents.
  • Prevention of sexual harassment – Internal Committee under the POSH Act, 2013.
  • Stress management – counselling services, peer support, recognition, balanced rosters, recreation.

D. Role of the nurse Follow safety protocols, use PPE correctly, report injuries and hazards, look after her own health (exercise, sleep, nutrition) and support colleagues.

Conclusion A safe workplace for nurses means safer care for patients; preventing occupational hazards is a shared responsibility of the employer and every employee.

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
question: Explain employee safety indicators and the annual health check-up of health-care workers.
answer_html:
Introduction Just as hospitals measure patient safety, they must also measure employee (staff) safety. Employee safety indicators show how safe the workplace is, identify problem areas and help plan improvements. A regular annual health check-up detects health problems in staff early.

A. Employee safety indicators (examples) | Indicator | How it is expressed | |---|---| | Needle-stick/sharps injury rate | NSIs per 100 employees per year (or per 1,000 patient-days) | | Hepatitis B vaccination coverage | % of HCWs fully vaccinated with documented anti-HBs | | PEP uptake | % of exposed HCWs starting HIV PEP within 2 hours | | Occupational infections | TB, HBV, HCV, COVID-19 among staff acquired at work | | Workplace violence incidents | Number of verbal/physical assaults reported per month | | Staff injuries | Back injuries, falls, burns, chemical exposures | | Radiation exposure | % of radiation workers with doses within limits (TLD records) | | Sickness absence | Staff absenteeism rate due to illness/injury | | Training coverage | % of staff trained in fire safety, IPC, BMW, BLS | | Health check-up coverage | % of employees who completed the annual medical examination | | Staff satisfaction/burnout | Survey scores | These indicators are reviewed by the occupational health and safety committee and the HICC, and are part of NABH standards.

B. Annual health check-up of HCWs 1. Types of medical examinations

  • Pre-employment (pre-placement) – baseline health, immunity status, fitness for the job.
  • Periodic (annual) examination.
  • Post-exposure examination (after NSI, TB contact).
  • Return-to-work examination after illness.

2. Components of the annual check-up

  • History of illnesses, symptoms (cough >2 weeks, weight loss), exposures, injuries; vaccination status.
  • Physical examination – BP, weight/BMI, vision, skin (dermatitis), spine and joints.
  • Investigations – haemoglobin, blood sugar, lipid profile and others as per age; anti-HBs/HBsAg as needed; chest X-ray or symptom screening for TB in high-risk areas.
  • Job-specific tests – radiation workers (blood counts, eye check, dose record review); food handlers (stool examination, skin and nails); workers exposed to chemicals or anaesthetic gases (liver/kidney tests as advised).
  • Mental health screening – stress, burnout, sleep problems.
  • Updating vaccinations (influenza, Td).

3. Follow-up

  • Treatment or referral for problems found; job modification if needed (e.g., pregnant staff away from radiation and cytotoxics).
  • Confidential health records maintained by the occupational health service.

Conclusion Tracking safety indicators and examining staff every year keeps the workforce healthy and the workplace safe.

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
question: Explain the prevention of musculoskeletal injuries and falls among health-care workers.
answer_html:
Introduction Nursing is physically demanding. Lifting, turning, transferring and repositioning patients, prolonged standing and bending lead to back pain and other musculoskeletal disorders (MSDs) – one of the commonest causes of sickness absence among nurses. Slips, trips and falls on wet or cluttered floors also injure many staff. Most of these injuries are preventable.

A. Causes

  • Manual lifting of heavy or dependent patients, especially alone.
  • Awkward postures – bending, twisting, reaching across beds.
  • Low beds, cramped spaces, lack of lifting aids.
  • Staff shortage, fatigue, hurry, lack of training.
  • Wet floors, spills, poor lighting, cables and clutter, unsuitable footwear.

B. Prevention of musculoskeletal injuries 1. Safe patient handling and mobility programme

  • Assess every patient's mobility and plan the safest method of transfer.
  • Use mechanical aids – hoists, slide sheets, transfer boards, gait belts, electric height-adjustable beds, wheelchairs and stretchers in good condition.
  • Team lifting – never lift a heavy patient alone; move "on the count of three".
  • Encourage patients to help themselves as much as possible.

2. Principles of body mechanics

  • Keep a wide base of support (feet apart), bend the knees and hips, keep the back straight.
  • Hold the load close to the body; avoid twisting – turn with the feet.
  • Push or pull rather than lift; use body weight.
  • Raise the bed to waist height before giving care; lower it afterwards for the patient's safety.
  • Avoid overreaching; get close to the work.

3. Workplace and job design

  • Adequate staffing; rotation of heavy tasks; rest breaks.
  • Ergonomic workstations (chair and computer height) for documentation.
  • Anti-fatigue mats and comfortable, supportive footwear for prolonged standing; compression stockings to prevent varicose veins.

4. Training and fitness

  • Regular training on safe handling techniques and use of equipment.
  • Exercise to strengthen back and core muscles; maintaining healthy weight.
  • Early reporting of pain and timely physiotherapy.

C. Prevention of falls among staff

  • Keep floors clean and dry; display "wet floor" signs during mopping; clean spills immediately.
  • Good lighting in corridors, stairs and stores; clutter-free passages; secure cables.
  • Handrails on stairs; non-slip flooring in bathrooms and sluice rooms.
  • Non-slip, closed footwear; avoid running in corridors.
  • Use stable step-ladders (not chairs) for reaching high shelves; store heavy items on lower shelves.
  • Report hazards (broken tiles, leaks) to maintenance.

Conclusion Lifting aids, team work, correct body mechanics and a hazard-free environment protect nurses' backs and prevent falls – keeping them fit to care for patients.

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
question: What is the significance of the anti-HBs titre in health-care workers?
answer_html:
Anti-HBs is the antibody against hepatitis B surface antigen. It is produced after hepatitis B vaccination or recovery from infection and indicates immunity.

Significance

  1. Tested 1–2 months after the third dose of hepatitis B vaccine to confirm the response.
  2. ≥10 mIU/ml – protected (responder); no booster needed; no post-exposure treatment required after needle-stick injury.
  3. <10 mIU/ml – non-responder; repeat the 3-dose vaccine series and retest; if still low, give HBIG after any exposure.
  4. Guides post-exposure prophylaxis decisions; records must be kept in the employee health file.

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
question: What is burnout? Mention measures for its prevention.
answer_html:
Burnout is a state of physical, emotional and mental exhaustion caused by long-term, unmanaged work stress. It is marked by exhaustion, depersonalisation (feeling detached or cynical towards patients and work) and a reduced sense of accomplishment. It is common in nurses because of heavy workload, staff shortage, night shifts and emotional demands.

Prevention

  1. Adequate staffing, fair rosters and regular rest breaks.
  2. Supportive supervision, recognition and team work.
  3. Counselling and peer-support services; debriefing after stressful events.
  4. Healthy lifestyle – sleep, exercise, nutrition, hobbies, time with family.
  5. Training in stress management and time management.

subject: Applied Microbiology and Infection Control including Safety
question: What is a TLD badge? State its use.
answer_html:
A TLD (thermoluminescent dosimeter) badge is a small personal radiation-monitoring device containing crystals (e.g., lithium fluoride or calcium sulphate) that store the energy of ionising radiation; when heated in the laboratory they emit light proportional to the radiation dose received.

Use

  1. Measures the cumulative radiation dose received by workers in radiology, nuclear medicine, radiotherapy, OT (C-arm) and cath labs.
  2. Worn at chest level under the lead apron (an extra badge at the collar may be used in interventional work).
  3. Read periodically (usually every 3 months) by an accredited agency; records ensure doses stay within AERB limits and help detect unsafe practices.
